exceptions.text: Brief context note: The first-contract study covers contracts from 1987 to 1996 in campaigns where a contract was reached, and states that “the quality of the first contract that a union achieves is a direct product of their power.” The study reports how common some terms were: grievable safety clauses (safety rules workers can enforce through a formal complaint) in 55 percent of private contracts, discrimination clauses in nearly three-quarters, schedule language in one-third of private contracts, vacancy posting in more than three-quarters, job training in about one-quarter, private-sector tuition at 16 percent, and some restrictions on outsourcing in about one-third of private agreements. The factors the bill gives the panel do not require particular contract terms. Sources: , .

Brief context note: A review of Canadian first-contract arbitration states that boards and arbitrators limit awards (panel decisions) based on what the employer can afford. They also recognize that first agreements decided by arbitration should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions (new kinds of contract terms). The review describes Canadian practice, not this bill. Sources: .

Brief context note: The first-contract study collected contracts where agreement was reached and says some practices existed before organizing and were codified (written into the contract). It did not measure wage gains or the operation of local unions. Federal rules already make employers pay for most required protective equipment, and the 16-contract study reports that some clauses restate existing law. Sources: , , .

A 2009 legal review reports that experienced arbitrators generally believe interest arbitration (outside decision-makers setting contract terms) rarely departs from the status quo (the existing situation) in economic and noneconomic working conditions. A separate review of Canadian practice says first agreements decided by arbitration should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions (new kinds of contract terms). Neither review tests this bill. Sources: , .

Faster first contracts bring enforceable workplace safety rules within reach sooner.

First contracts (the first written work agreements between a new union and an employer) include safety rules that workers can enforce through complaints. A study of agreements reached in 1987–1996 found that “55 percent of private sector contracts have grievable health and safety clauses.”
These rules address specific hazards. A study of 16 contracts from 2010–2014 found: “Most contracts detail the employer’s responsibility to provide and maintain protective clothing and equipment.”

Unions also help workers report hazards without being punished: “They bargain to improve safety practices, protect their members against retaliation for reporting a violation, or make complaints on members’ behalf about hazards” .
The bill’s binding process for a first contract helps workers get and enforce these protections sooner. Protection from hazards serves [NAME]’s aim to avoid injury and illness at work.

A 2009 legal review reports: “Experienced arbitrators generally believe that interest arbitration rarely results in a departure from the status quo in terms of economic and noneconomic working conditions.” [SEP 8] Interest arbitration means outside decision-makers set contract terms, and the status quo is the existing situation. A review of Canadian practice reports “recognizing that arbitrated first agreements should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions.” [SEP 9] Breakthrough or novel provisions are new kinds of contract terms. The first-contract study says “the quality of the first contract that a union achieves is a direct product of their power” [UNC 7] . These sources do not test this bill. They also do not address settlements reached because a panel is possible, or contract terms that put existing practice into an enforceable contract.

The study does not estimate first-contract arbitration, and Treasury’s point about elections without contracts is not answered by it.

Treasury’s estimate concerns union membership: “Unions raise the wages of their members by 10 to 15 percent.” The bill’s first-contract process starts “following certification or recognition of an individual or labor organization as a representative” . The pay gap between union and non-union workers does not measure gains for workers forming a new union.

Gains from forming a new union differ from the general union pay gap. A study covering 1984–2001 compared workplaces where unions barely won or lost elections. Its wage results, from manufacturing, were different from the general pay gap: “estimates for wages are close to zero.” This is evidence that the measures differ, not an estimate of this bill’s effect.

The general union pay estimate does not establish the income gain from new first contracts on which part of the stability claim rests. This response does not answer the separate step on protecting current pay during talks.

The decision must be based on “the employer's financial status and prospects” [UNC 1] and “the wages and benefits other employers in the same business provide their employees.” [UNC 1] Canadian boards and arbitrators report “a very conservative approach to first contract awards” [UNC 8] . A 2009 review reports: “Experienced arbitrators generally believe that interest arbitration rarely results in a departure from the status quo in terms of economic and noneconomic working conditions.” [SES 14] The status quo is the existing situation. This evidence describes practice elsewhere, so it does not show that such an award could never occur.

The argument does not support its claimed added risk of awards that a defense supplier cannot afford.

The bill requires the decision to rest on “the employer's financial status and prospects” and “the wages and benefits other employers in the same business provide their employees” . The panel must use the employer’s finances and pay at similar businesses when setting terms.

A 2009 review of arbitration that sets contract terms reports: “Experienced arbitrators generally believe that interest arbitration rarely results in a departure from the status quo in terms of economic and noneconomic working conditions.” The status quo is the existing situation. This account of arbitration practice challenges the unsupported forecast of unaffordable awards.

A binding award and an unaffordable award are different claims. The argument shows that defense suppliers matter, but not why this process for setting terms would make them more likely to close. Losing a right to reject terms does not establish that missing step. This response does not show that an unaffordable award could never occur.

This concerns how often stoppages happen, at least somewhat, not how long they last. It does not assume the Canadian 50 percent figure applies. The bill does not say whether strikes or lockouts may continue during arbitration.

The Canadian systems had another rule: “In Canadian jurisdictions once an application for FCA is filed any work stoppage in progress must stop.” [SES 4] The study could not “estimate the affect of each type of FCA on incidence.” [SES 4] A legal analysis says of this bill: “The bill also raises questions about the lawfulness of strikes and lockouts during these first contract negotiations.” [SES 10] This does not answer the ordinary inference that a settlement process can reduce some first-contract stoppages.
The Canadian study does not separate the effect of the settlement incentive from the different legal rules that came with it.

First-contract arbitration lets a third party set the agreement. The study notes: “In Canadian jurisdictions once an application for FCA is filed any work stoppage in progress must stop” . H.R.5408 contains no matching requirement . It says that the panel “shall render a decision settling the dispute” .
The study says the data do not let it estimate “the affect of each type of FCA on incidence.” Here, incidence means how often first-contract strikes or lockouts occur.

The argument has not shown that the reduction found across those Canadian systems would follow from this bill’s settlement process, because those systems also had a rule stopping strikes and lockouts, which the bill lacks. This response does not answer the narrower point that arbitration gives the parties another option besides relying on a stoppage.

The Canadian estimate comes from a package of rules and a set of sectors that differ from U.S. hospitals under this bill.

The working paper behind the estimate treats health care as part of the “quasi-public sector (health, education and public administration)” . Its separate private-sector analysis uses “only first agreement work stoppages that occur in the private sector” . So the private-sector estimate does not cover hospital disputes.

The Canadian laws also contain a separate rule: “In Canadian jurisdictions once an application for FCA is filed any work stoppage in progress must stop.” FCA means first-contract arbitration. The study does not separate offering arbitration from this rule requiring strikes to stop.
H.R.5408 requires that “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” . The bill adds no matching rule stopping strikes when arbitration begins.

The reported reduction comes from a different package of rules and does not cover hospital disputes. This response does not answer the narrower inference that a settlement process can reduce the need for some first-contract hospital strikes.

The Canadian study examines first-contract arbitration. The systems it studies include a rule that directly stops strikes and lockouts: “In Canadian jurisdictions once an application for FCA is filed any work stoppage in progress must stop.”

The study’s estimate combines different systems: “There is not enough variation across Canadian jurisdictions in the use of different types of FCA to permit the analysis to estimate the affect of each type of FCA on incidence.”

H.R.5408 requires referral to a panel: “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” . The bill has no express matching rule to stop strikes. A June 11, 2026 legal analysis names the gap: “The bill also raises questions about the lawfulness of strikes and lockouts during these first contract negotiations.”

The study’s explanation about bargaining incentives does not separate the panel’s effect from the rule stopping strikes. The argument has not shown that the reported reduction carries over to this bill’s different rules.

The arbitration process covers “establishing an initial collective bargaining agreement” . Boeing’s 2024 dispute concerned an existing contract: “After ratification of a new contract in 2008, employees approved two contract extensions in 2011 and 2014.”

Boeing shows the harm of strikes, not an effect of the bill’s first-contract arbitration rule. This response does not answer the ordinary inference that a settlement process can reduce some first-contract stoppages, including in the hospital and military-support settings in the argument.

This applies only to disputes decided by a panel. The union chooses one of three panel members. Under existing law, after a real deadlock, “the employer may unilaterally change terms and conditions of employ, so long as these changes are consistent with offers that the union has rejected.” [UNC 11] So a member vote does not always decide the outcome today.

After a genuine bargaining deadlock, existing law allows an employer to make changes consistent with offers the union rejected; before that stage, rejection can return the parties to bargaining or support a strike. The Providence nurses’ contracts had expired, while other units in that dispute ratified first contracts. The Conagra report gives no amount or outcome. The Commonwealth Fund figures describe underinsured adults, not workers facing a given cost increase. The union selects one panel member. The passages read for these points give no example of workers rejecting a tentative first contract over health or safety terms. Sources: , , , , , .

The Minneapolis janitors bargained a renewal: their contract had expired in December. This example illustrates green terms and bargaining trade-offs, not a first-contract vote the bill would bypass. Under current law an employer may implement a final offer after a genuine good-faith impasse (a real deadlock in talks), and the bill requires maintaining current terms pending agreement. Panel factors can accommodate green work methods even though they do not require pollution cuts. Sources: , , .

The panel includes one union-selected and one employer-selected member, and its decision must be based partly on the size and type of the employer’s operations. The arbitrator code published by the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS), the U.S. mediation agency, says an arbitrator lacking specialized knowledge must decline, withdraw or request technical help. It says an arbitrator should comply with a party’s request to visit a work area. The code addresses voluntary arbitration and is applied to the agency’s lists of arbitrators. A 2009 review says both parties produce evidence to the arbitrator. These warnings and responses cite no record of how arbitrated rules have fit particular workplaces. Sources: , , .

The bill’s binding process does not clearly reach environmental oversight terms that have no direct link to workers’ jobs.

The argument’s enforcement step depends on specific contract language. The complaint process concerns “a violation by the Company of this Agreement” . Workers can use it for environmental duties only where those duties are in the contract.
The guide used in this argument says employers can lawfully refuse talks about optional topics “that lack a direct job nexus.” This means topics with no direct link to workers’ jobs.

The bill’s panel issues a decision “settling the dispute” . The panel bases that decision on five business and employment factors, such as “the employer's financial status and prospects” . The bill does not change which subjects employers must negotiate.

For environmental oversight with no direct job link, the argument names no way the bill’s deadlines or panel get past an employer’s lawful refusal. This response does not answer oversight terms tied to workers’ own safety and health. It also does not answer the complaint rights a first contract can create for terms it does contain.
The sources reviewed do not establish that a panel can award, or an employer must discuss, optional environmental oversight terms.

The required duty to bargain in this argument concerns safety and health. It does not establish a required way to refuse work over hazards to the environment alone.

A strike-ban clause does not add the limit this argument needs for the green-demand strikes it cites, because those strikes seek new contract terms.

The green strike in the argument took place after a contract ended: “The janitors’ contract ran out in December, but they agreed to go on working while negotiations progressed.” The bill’s arbitration rule covers “an initial collective bargaining agreement” , and its award binds “for a period of 2 years” .

Current law already limits strikes meant to rewrite terms fixed by an existing contract. The guide from the NLRB, the federal labor board, says: “The party must continue in full force and effect, without resorting to strike or lockout, all the terms and conditions of the existing contract until 60 days after the notice to the other party was given or until the date the contract is scheduled to expire, whichever is later.” This concerns changing agreed terms, not every strike during a contract.

For demands to add green contract terms, the argument has not shown what a ban clause adds beyond these existing limits. This response does not answer two things. First, an award itself ends the first-contract bargaining in which workers could strike for such terms. Second, a ban could reach work stoppages that are not aimed at changing contract terms.

A documented limit on the federal mediation agency’s services challenges the step that this process is a usable way past delay for small groups of workers.

The bill depends on the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS), the U.S. agency that helps employers and unions settle disputes: “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” .

The FMCS budget submission of April 3, 2026 says it had limited mediation to health-care groups with at least 250 represented workers and “bargaining units of 1,000 members or more for all other industries in which it has jurisdiction” .

The agency’s proposed service form, published May 15, 2026, still says of first-contract cases: “These cases will be assigned to a mediator if they meet the current criteria/metrics for case assignment.”

A supporter of the bill names the practical condition: “Without a robust, government-supported mediation and arbitration system, the Faster Labor Contracts Act would not be able to live up to its promise.”

Stopping an employer from blocking appointments does not solve this service gap for small groups seeking mediation and timely referral to a panel. This response does not show that the process is unavailable: the bill’s duty has no size limit, and the time before referral runs from the request.

The evidence describes access that is already restricted. Connecticut reports that, apart from critical-industry and class-action exceptions, negotiation services were limited to employers with “a minimum of 250 employees” . The agency’s own budget submission gives a different limit: health-care groups of 250 or more and “bargaining units of 1,000 members or more for all other industries in which it has jurisdiction” . Both accounts describe restricted access.
The bill’s first-contract duty has no employer-size limit: “the Service shall promptly communicate with the parties and use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement.”

Referral does not wait for completed mediation. The clock is the “30-day period beginning on the date on which the request for mediation is made” . If agreement has not been reached, “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” , unless the parties agree to more time.

Deciding the contract is the panel’s task, separate from the service’s mediation and referral work. Existing FMCS practice already uses a separate source of decision-makers: “Arbitrators are not FMCS employees.”

The argument has not shown how these duties would take help away from poorer unions under the already restricted system. This response does not answer added strain on groups that remain eligible for FMCS help, or the lack of a deadline at the panel stage.

The argument’s step from the power to appoint panel members to political selection rests on one advocate’s prediction.

Each side normally chooses a panel member, and the third seat remains “one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties” . The service fills “any members not selected” , so this power arises only when seats go unfilled.

The support for political selection is the statement that “there would likely be political pressure from presidential Administrations” . That passage gives no evidence about how such appointments are made.

The bill does give a federal agency those appointments. The further step, that those choices would turn on political views, is supported only by that prediction. This response does not show that such pressure would not occur.

It addresses voluntary arbitration and does not set rules for how an agency designates panel members. The sources reviewed document a 2025 executive order directing reductions at FMCS, which concerns staffing and not arbitrator selection. Sources: , .
The sources reviewed have no rules or record on how the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS) would designate panel members; the arbitrator code addresses voluntary arbitration.

The legal rulings do not establish the blanket legal defects the lawyers’ letters claim.

Hodges’s evidence concerns lawsuits seeking refunds of fees charged to nonmembers for union representation. Those claims “primarily seek retroactive application of Janus” . This means applying Janus, a U.S. Supreme Court ruling on fees for government workers, to fees already collected. That record concerns a different kind of lawsuit from challenges to contracts at private employers.

Government involvement alone does not make bargaining fees invalid. In the case Hanson, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld financial support for private railway bargaining and held that the requirement “does not violate either the First or the Fifth Amendments.”

The Janus ruling distinguishes bargaining with government employers from private workplaces: “In the public sector, core issues such as wages, pensions, and benefits are important political issues, but that is generally not so in the private sector.” The letters’ argument about government involvement does not resolve that difference.

The U.S. Supreme Court case Cedar Point does not say that every right for union representatives to enter a workplace takes property without payment. The Court separates access to closed property from “Limitations on how a business generally open to the public may treat individuals on the premises” . The legal result depends on the access granted and the place involved.

The fee and access rulings do not show the blanket legal defects the letters claim. This response does not answer the costs of hearings that do occur, or of lawsuits that use up resources even when they fail.

The bill keeps “decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” . Workers keep the way to vote a union out.
The argument’s own legal account calls an election “the preferred method for determining employees’ representational preferences.”

A signature is not always a worker’s final choice. Describing workers who signed conflicting petitions, labor lawyers explain that a secret ballot allows a final choice without others knowing it, “insulating them from retaliation from whichever side they fail to support.”

The election requirement checks the majority’s wishes through a private choice by workers, instead of leaving the employer to act on signatures. Just treatment includes protecting that choice for every worker. The argument shows that employer withdrawal can be quicker, but speed alone does not establish that confirming the majority’s wishes is unfair.

The argument treats a stronger bargaining role as acceptance of different people.
Existing law already requires employers and representatives to “meet at reasonable times and confer in good faith with respect to wages, hours, and other terms and conditions of employment” .

The bill adds a starting deadline: “Not later than 10 days after receiving a written request for collective bargaining” , which can be extended by agreement: “or within such further period as the parties agree upon” . The bill also extends the duty: “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” .

The added rules concern when talks start and how long the representative keeps its bargaining role. Giving that representative a stronger role in negotiating work terms does not by itself show greater acceptance or understanding of different people. The argument moves between these meanings of being heard without defending the link. This response does not answer the separate step about cooperation across racial lines.

The argument treats a way to settle a dispute as more mutual listening without showing the understanding it claims.

The next step applies when “the Service is not able to bring the parties to agreement by conciliation” . Then “A majority of the 3-person arbitration panel shall render a decision settling the dispute and such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years, unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.”

Choosing panel members and having economic needs weighed concern how work terms are decided. A panel can settle those terms while the groups remain unwilling to listen to or understand each other. Settlement alone therefore does not establish the mutual hearing and acceptance the argument gives it. This response does not answer the separate step that either side can now get mediation help with a difficult conversation.

The argument does not connect skipping final approval, or requiring bargaining fees, to less listening to or acceptance of people who disagree.
The union example in the argument gathers members’ views before final approval: “Our union’s bargaining process starts with a concerted effort to get feedback from you and your fellow members.”

In that example, members also elect their bargaining committee: “Your local union bylaws contain democratic voting procedures for you to elect a committee to bargain on behalf of you and your co-workers.”
Federal law protects members’ right “to meet and assemble freely with other members; and to express any views, arguments, or opinions” . The bill’s binding award leaves those protections in place.

The union must represent people who disagree fairly. The court decision in the argument describes its “statutory obligation to serve the interests of all members without hostility or discrimination toward any” .

The final vote adds power to reject terms and press for changes. Accepting people who disagree does not mean accepting their preferred terms, so the argument needs to show less hearing or acceptance of them, beyond less control over the outcome. This response does not answer that losing the vote removes one way members press negotiators to answer objections.

The same decision describes representation “on behalf of all employees in the bargaining unit” and limits required nonmember charges to “only those fees necessary to finance collective-bargaining activities” .

A bargaining fee pays for representation that must serve people who disagree too; it does not require them to agree with the union. The argument names a financial burden without showing that it makes them less heard or accepted. A reason to reject required payment needs a further link to this value.

Federal law protects members’ right “to meet and assemble freely with other members; and to express any views, arguments, or opinions” . The bill’s binding award leaves those protections in place.

The union must represent people who disagree fairly. The court decision in the argument describes its “statutory obligation to serve the interests of all members without hostility or discrimination toward any” .

The final vote adds power to reject terms and press for changes. Accepting people who disagree does not mean accepting their preferred terms, so the argument needs to show less hearing or acceptance of them, beyond less control over the outcome. This response does not answer that losing the vote removes one way members press negotiators to answer objections.

The same decision describes representation “on behalf of all employees in the bargaining unit” and limits required nonmember charges to “only those fees necessary to finance collective-bargaining activities” .

A bargaining fee pays for representation that must serve people who disagree too; it does not require them to agree with the union. The argument names a financial burden without showing that it makes them less heard or accepted. A reason to reject required payment needs a further link to this value.

Existing law requires good-faith talks while stating that this duty “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” .

After good-faith talks reach a real deadlock, an employer can put certain earlier proposals into effect without union agreement: “an employer does not violate the Act by making unilateral changes that are reasonably comprehended within his pre-impasse proposals” .
Keeping current law does not preserve a requirement that workplace terms win both groups’ acceptance. Agreement on terms is also a different test from understanding the people proposing them.

The bill requires parties to “make every reasonable effort to conclude and sign a collective bargaining agreement” . It requires the mediation service to “use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement” .

Research on Canadian first-contract arbitration (FCA) gives evidence against the predicted retreat from negotiation: “Despite this, FCA is not accessed frequently and it is even rarer for a first contract (in whole or in part) to be imposed. Together these results suggest that FCA encourages collective bargaining by creating an incentive for the parties to bargain in good faith and negotiate an agreement.” In that passage, “this” means the finding that first-contract arbitration cuts first-agreement work stoppages by at least half. That research covers systems with a work-stoppage rule that this bill does not state.

The bill’s deadlines do not excuse efforts to reach agreement. The first-contract evidence challenges the prediction that a binding last step weakens those efforts. One side’s refusal to extend talks after sincere bargaining does not itself show less willingness to understand the other group. The argument’s reason depends on that missing link, not simply on losing the power to insist on more time.

The Canadian first-contract study reports that arbitration is rarely accessed and rarely imposes a contract. It also notes that Canadian applications require any work stoppage in progress to stop, a rule not explicit in the U.S. proposal it discusses. Sources: .

The existing process gives the employer an option to stop recognizing the union: “an employer possessing such evidence may withdraw recognition when the contract expires” . That is an employer’s power, not a vote workers can themselves use to remove the union.
The bill makes removal depend on “decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” .

Section 9 of the labor law allows a petition “by an employee or group of employees” challenging the union’s continued support. If the labor board finds a question about representation, it “shall direct an election by secret ballot and shall certify the results thereof.”
The labor-board decision used in the argument calls a board-run secret vote “the preferred means of resolving questions concerning representation.”

Workers can take their changed wishes to the board without depending on the employer. An election tests the workforce’s current choice, including the views of workers who did not sign the petition. The argument does not connect losing the employer’s option to act without that vote to less listening to or acceptance of workers who reject the union.

The argument has not shown that moving labor-cost decisions to a panel makes those costs more predictable than under existing law.

At a real deadlock in talks, existing law gives the employer the “right to unilaterally implement its last, best, and final offer when the parties reach a good faith impasse.” The employer can choose the costs of the terms it puts into effect.

The bill removes that option by requiring employers “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” . A panel then chooses unresolved first-contract terms. The panel’s duty to weigh “the employer's financial status and prospects” does not tell the business what costs it will impose.

The ruling is “binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years” , but the arbitrators “have no set time to issue their award.” Those two years describe how long the ruling lasts, not when its costs become known.

The argument counts how long settled terms last without comparing the uncertainty of a panel’s choice and timing with the employer’s existing control over terms it puts into effect. The argument has not established more predictable labor costs, so its step to steadier investment and national economic activity lacks support.

Existing FMCS policy offers mediation in disputes “which imperil or threaten to imperil the national health or safety.” Health-care mediation also carries an existing duty: “the Service shall promptly communicate with the parties and use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to bring them to agreement.” The bill does not remove that policy or the health-care duty.

The added panel appointments depend on disputes staying unsettled. Referral follows only when “the Service is not able to bring the parties to agreement by conciliation” . In Canadian first-contract arbitration, the researcher Johnson finds that “the threat of having a first agreement imposed creates an incentive for the parties to reach agreement on their own.” Those Canadian systems also had a work-stoppage rule that this bill does not state.

The sources in the argument describe more demand and service limits, but not how the agency would divide staff among disputes. Existing priorities make taking staff from urgent disputes a separate step that needs support. This response does not deny that added cases would stretch a limited staff.

A documented limit on the federal mediation agency’s services challenges the step that this process is a usable way past delay for small groups of workers.

The bill depends on the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS), the U.S. agency that helps employers and unions settle disputes: “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” .

The FMCS budget submission of April 3, 2026 says it had limited mediation to health-care groups with at least 250 represented workers and “bargaining units of 1,000 members or more for all other industries in which it has jurisdiction” .

The agency’s proposed service form, published May 15, 2026, still says of first-contract cases: “These cases will be assigned to a mediator if they meet the current criteria/metrics for case assignment.”

A supporter of the bill names the practical condition: “Without a robust, government-supported mediation and arbitration system, the Faster Labor Contracts Act would not be able to live up to its promise.”

Stopping an employer from blocking appointments does not solve this service gap for small groups seeking mediation and timely referral to a panel. This response does not show that the process is unavailable: the bill’s duty has no size limit, and the time before referral runs from the request.

The legal rulings do not establish the blanket legal defects the lawyers’ letters claim.

Hodges’s evidence concerns lawsuits seeking refunds of fees charged to nonmembers for union representation. Those claims “primarily seek retroactive application of Janus” . This means applying Janus, a U.S. Supreme Court ruling on fees for government workers, to fees already collected. That record concerns a different kind of lawsuit from challenges to contracts at private employers.

Government involvement alone does not make bargaining fees invalid. In the case Hanson, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld financial support for private railway bargaining and held that the requirement “does not violate either the First or the Fifth Amendments.”

The Janus ruling distinguishes bargaining with government employers from private workplaces: “In the public sector, core issues such as wages, pensions, and benefits are important political issues, but that is generally not so in the private sector.” The letters’ argument about government involvement does not resolve that difference.

The U.S. Supreme Court case Cedar Point does not say that every right for union representatives to enter a workplace takes property without payment. The Court separates access to closed property from “Limitations on how a business generally open to the public may treat individuals on the premises” . The legal result depends on the access granted and the place involved.

The fee and access rulings do not show the blanket legal defects the letters claim. This response does not answer the costs of hearings that do occur, or of lawsuits that use up resources even when they fail.

The historical environmental actions cited come from national union bodies, and the alliance passage concerns members already active on climate. The same article states that unions face a tension, particularly those whose members work in extractive industries (industries that take resources such as coal or oil from the ground). Sources: .

The Canadian first-contract research is reported for workers generally, not by industry. Capital & Main attributes the California building trades’ refinery position to a 2014 state apprenticeship law and a Project Labor Agreement. UMWA’s organizing also includes West Virginia state employees, and state employers are outside the NLRA, the main U.S. private-sector labor law. Sources: , , , .

The bill covers private employers. AFT says “the majority of AFT members work in the public sector” [TR 23] . The SEIU political amount is decided each year by its board. Nonmembers keep a legal protection: “Section 8(a)(3) does not permit a union, over the objections of dues-paying nonmember employees, to expend funds collected from them on activities unrelated to collective-bargaining activities.” [TR 24] That protection does not reach payments by members. The sources reviewed show funding rules and positions, not a measured effect of first contracts on political spending.
