exceptions.text: A union contract (a written work agreement between an employer and a workers’ organization) can give workers a regular role in environmental oversight. The 2018 U.S. Steel contract requires “A Joint Environmental Sub-Committee of the Joint Safety and Health Committee” at each location. It says this group “will meet regularly to discuss environmental issues affecting the Company and to make appropriate recommendations.”

The company must let that group review “all non confidential environmental reports, monitoring results, analyses, materials received from the EPA and other agencies” . The EPA is the U.S. environmental agency.
The same contract requires the company to “comply with all applicable laws and regulations concerning the health and safety of Employees at work and the protection of the environment.”

Workers have a complaint process for duties in the contract: “the Union may process grievances through the grievance procedure, including arbitration” . Grievances are formal complaints, and arbitration means outside decision-makers decide. The result is binding: “A decision of the Board shall be final and binding upon the Company, the Union and all Employees concerned.”

These terms give workers information, a voice and a way to enforce environmental duties. The bill makes first contracts harder to block through delay, so it strengthens this way of challenging pollution. That serves [NAME]’s wish to protect nature.

Workers can bargain for the right to stop dangerous work: “Under the National Labor Relations Act, health and safety is a mandatory subject of collective bargaining in private sector workplaces.” A mandatory subject is one the employer must discuss if asked.

A process negotiated at Delaware City Refining Company gives workers “the authority, without fear of reprimand or retaliation, to immediately STOP any work activity that presents a hazard to you, your co-workers, the environment” .
This process protects workers’ income: “there shall be no loss of pay, seniority, or benefits during the period of refusal” .

A stronger first-contract process helps workers get these protections. Workers could then act before dangerous work harms nature, without losing pay. [NAME] values such action to defend the environment.
U.S. employers and unions may agree on climate goals. A guide to green bargaining explains that “employers and unions are still free to bargain over them.” Here, “them” means climate goals.

The guide’s contract models from other countries include “building efficiency improvements and recycling and composting programs” and “employee transit programs that promote the use of public transportation, bikes, and carpooling.”

A U.S. example shows how this can work. U.S. Steel’s contract requires joint work to “identify, analyze, and make recommendations regarding ways to conserve energy, improve energy efficiency and reduce greenhouse gas emissions” .
Contracts also fund environmental work. Minneapolis janitors won a “contract that included funding for a Labor-Management Cooperation Fund for a green education initiative” .

Climate pollution harms nature. The IPCC, an international climate science body, finds that “Human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming” and that “Hundreds of local losses of species have been driven by increases in the magnitude of heat extremes” .

The bill strengthens the process for reaching a first agreement. That helps workers bargain for environmental programs and for resources to carry them out. Saving resources and working to reduce the gases that warm the planet serve [NAME]’s care for nature.
Conservation workers also face first-contract delays. The first agreement at Audubon, a bird-protection organization, “was reached after more than two years of negotiations” .

Audubon’s agreement links its staff to protecting nature: “Audubon is committed to the mission of protecting birds and the habitats needed to sustain them” and “Audubon’s workforce is integral to the success of Audubon’s mission” .

That first contract gives practical support for staff skills: “Audubon shall support career development training that enhances the skills necessary to successfully perform the employee’s job or other Audubon career positions by providing paid leave to eligible employees” .

Pay and benefits also support conservation staffing. Defenders of Wildlife, another conservation group, tied its bargaining effort to “developing a top-tier benefits package to retain and attract top talent” . The group says the resulting agreement “optimizes staff compensation and establishes new benefits for all current and future staff.”

The bill gives newly organized conservation staff a binding way through stalled talks. This supports their efforts to get pay, benefits and training. Supporting the staff who carry out wildlife and habitat protection serves [NAME]’s value of protecting nature.

Contracts put benefits in writing in electric-vehicle battery jobs. A worker at Ultium, a battery maker, explained: “now my benefits are guaranteed in writing, ensuring financial security for my family” .

Researchers interviewed 48 union energy workers in New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania. Fear of poor pay and benefits was a barrier to supporting cleaner energy. The researchers conclude: “This analysis demonstrates that there are ways to gain their support, particularly if training, family sustaining wages and benefits, and location are integrated into transitions.”

The bill puts family needs into binding contract decisions. A panel must base its decision partly on “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” .

For clean-energy workplaces that newly form a union, a binding way to settle wages and benefits can reduce part of the financial insecurity these workers describe. Strengthening that part of the move away from fossil fuels can help build support for reducing the emissions that harm nature.
First-contract delay puts new unions at risk. Representative Scott, a member of Congress, explains: “Dragging out negotiations gives corporations a long chance to break up a union.”
Workers use unions to build environmental alliances. Researchers report that union members active on climate issues have “forged new alliances with other unions and environmentalists” .

These organizations have helped win protections for nature: “the AFL-CIO helped establish the National Wilderness Preservation System; the United Auto Workers was the leading funder of the first Earth Day and more recently supported raising emissions standards for autos.” The AFL-CIO is a national federation of unions.

Some workers organize through their union to defend nature. Limiting first-contract delay helps protect a group they can use for that action. Keeping this way into environmental campaigns open serves [NAME]’s value of taking part in protecting nature.

Winning those terms required workers to put environmental aims ahead of other benefits. Their bargainers reported: “We ultimately won, but had to compromise on the amount of funding and sacrifice other issues like additional holidays that were important to groups of the members.”

Workers normally can reject a contract. The Heritage Foundation, a policy research group, states: “Currently, nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” Ratification means a member vote to approve the contract.

The employer can start the bill’s mediation process after 90 days of talks without the union’s consent: “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.”

The panel’s five required factors concern the business and workers’ living costs and pay. None requires pollution reductions. They include “the employer's financial status and prospects” and “the wages and benefits other employers in the same business provide their employees.”

A panel can settle a first contract without pollution-reducing terms that workers would insist on before approving it. Workers cannot reject that result by a vote. Changing it during the two-year period requires the employer’s written consent. Losing that control puts workers’ ability to get such funding at risk, which gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.

Employers seek strike bans in first contracts: “One thing you can be sure of when bargaining your first contract: management will demand a contract clause barring strikes while the agreement is in effect.”

Current law leaves unions free to refuse: “Nothing in the NLRA, however, requires a union to agree to a no-strike clause.” The NLRA is the main U.S. private-sector labor law. The union can also resist through action: “the union may strike to keep it out of the contract.” Here, “it” means a no-strike clause.
The bill puts disputed contract terms within the panel’s reach. Lawyers reviewing it describe “authority to determine all terms of the parties’ first CBA” . A CBA is a union contract.
A panel can impose a strike ban that workers never accepted. This places contract limits on work stoppages beyond workers’ control.

Green demands can concern workers’ training and daily tasks. Local 26, a janitors’ union, sought a “training program for Green Technicians (including $0.20 differential) and expanded use of green cleaning.” The “differential” here is an amount of extra pay.

Strike pressure helps workers press such demands. The janitors’ bargainers explained that “the companies will simply try to ignore those demands—unless the union is willing to sacrifice and ultimately strike.”

A strike ban set by a panel can restrict work stoppages used to press work-related green demands. [NAME] values taking part in defending nature. Protecting this way of acting together on the environment gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.

Binding first-contract arbitration (a panel deciding the contract) can help new unions get contracts: “Other research has found that first-contract arbitration helped more Canadian workers sign first contracts.”

Organizing coal workers is one use for this process. The United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) says: “We are going to continue working to organize coal miners, but we must also look outside of the coal industry to grow our membership for a sustainable future” . The union also explains why growth matters: “To survive in the long term, we must grow our membership.”

Contracts can arrange regular collection of members’ dues, the payments that fund unions: “provisions that require management to automatically deduct union dues from workers’ paychecks and route them into the labor organization’s account.”
The bill’s process for binding contracts can give unions organizing coal and other fossil-fuel workers a firmer base of members and dues income.

A larger presence in oil and gas can strengthen a union’s interest in defending those industries. Writing about California politics, Capital & Main reports: “When unions organize workers in the oil and gas industry, they develop a vested interest in protecting those jobs — and can form a serious barrier to environmental justice and climate policy.”

These unions already turn resources into political pressure. CalMatters reports: “The building and construction trade unions also have long bankrolled California’s labor-friendly Democrats.” To bankroll means to give money to support someone.

That pressure has helped defeat environmental limits. CalMatters reports that “Ventura County voters sided with the oil and gas industry and the building trades unions when they overturned similar restrictions the county board of supervisors had placed on local oil wells” .

Coal unions also fight emissions limits in court. In its 2024 challenge to carbon-emission standards for coal-fired power plants, the UMWA stated: “We therefore have no choice but to file this petition, suing the EPA and stopping this rule from ever being implemented.”

Helping these unions keep members and income can strengthen organized resistance to pollution controls. That risk works against [NAME]’s aim of protecting nature from pollution and gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.

Congress states in the bill how delay can increase that gap: “The employers can use those delays to sap labor organization resolve and secure more favorable terms for the employer.” To sap resolve means to weaken a group’s determination.

Under the bill, if a first contract is not agreed, either side can move the dispute toward a binding decision by a panel. Neither side can stop the panel just by refusing to choose its members: “if the individual or labor organization or the employer fail to do so, the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.”

Both sides have a place on the panel: “with one member selected by the individual or labor organization, one member selected by the employer, and one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties.”

Workers gain a way to settle the contract that does not depend on persuading the stronger side to agree. Making their right to bargain usable protects people with less power and supports just treatment.

Existing rules allow an employer to withdraw recognition of a union (stop treating it as the workers’ representative) after a contract ends. This can happen when evidence shows that most workers no longer support the union and the union has not asked for an election in time: “If no such petition is timely filed, the employer may rely on the disaffection evidence to affect withdrawal. That evidence—assuming it establishes actual loss of majority status—will be dispositive of the union’s lack of majority status at the time of actual withdrawal; and the withdrawal of recognition will be lawful assuming no other grounds exist to find it unlawful.”

Under those rules, the union can ask for an election: “the incumbent union may file, within 45 days from the date of that announcement, an election petition” . So in this situation the bill adds a required vote where the union has not asked for one.

The bill requires that “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” . Decertification means removing the union through a federal election.
Workers keep collective representation until an election removes it. Requiring a vote before that protection ends gives workers a fairer process, and this serves [NAME]’s concern for just treatment.

Existing law lets an employer put previously offered terms into effect after good-faith talks reach a deadlock (called an impasse): “the employer may unilaterally change terms and conditions of employ, so long as these changes are consistent with offers that the union has rejected.”
The bill instead requires employers “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” .
Workers gain protection against cuts while they seek a contract. This protects people whose households cannot absorb lower pay or worse hours.
A U.S. Treasury research review finds a pay gain from union membership: “Unions raise the wages of their members by 10 to 15 percent.”

The bill requires any panel decision to consider “the employees' cost of living” and “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” .

The process for a binding contract gives workers stronger access to wage settlements, and basic living needs must be counted. This serves [NAME]’s concern for workers and dependents who are vulnerable to financial hardship.

Higher pay also supports opportunities for workers’ children: “In turn, the higher pay and job security of both unionized and nonunionized middle-class workers can further spill over to their families and communities through more stable housing, more investment in education, and other channels.”

Pay gains can spread beyond the union through competition for workers: “Nonunionized firms in competition with unionized workplaces may choose to raise wages, change hiring practices, or improve their workplace environment to attract workers.” Treasury also reports: “The empirical evidence finds that these positive spillovers exist.”

Higher income also reaches children’s education and workers outside the union. These wider gains support [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities in life, including for people beyond [NAME]’s own circle.

A U.S. study of first contracts signed in 1987–1996 found specific benefit protections: “first contracts establish, codify, and expand health insurance, pensions, and substantial paid leave benefits.”

A U.S. Treasury review cites research finding that “the higher rates of fringe benefits at newly unionized firms are the direct result of collective bargaining.” Fringe benefits are benefits beyond pay.

Helping workers reach first contracts strengthens access to care, paid time away from work and retirement income. These protections serve people at vulnerable stages of life and those who depend on their care.

The historical first-contract study found that “55 percent of private sector contracts have grievable health and safety clauses.” These let workers challenge a broken safety rule through the contract’s dispute process.

Unions bargain over safety and support workers who report hazards: “They bargain to improve safety practices, protect their members against retaliation for reporting a violation, or make complaints on members’ behalf about hazards” .
A stronger path to a contract makes enforceable safety protections easier to reach. This serves [NAME]’s concern for people exposed to harm at work.
The first-contract study found agreements requiring “discipline and discharge to be based on just cause” . Just cause means a good reason for punishing or dismissing a worker.
Contract procedures bound employers to “independent third-party review of disputes between management and employees.”

Easier access to these contracts gives workers a stronger way to get rules against unfair punishment and a hearing outside the employer’s sole control. That directly serves [NAME]’s concern that everyone receive just treatment.

Open pay scales particularly help workers with less individual bargaining power: “These types of practices, and others like publicly available pay schedules, benefit women and vulnerable workers who can be less likely to negotiate aggressively for pay raises.”
Treasury reports evidence of results: “Empirical studies have confirmed that unions have, indeed, closed race and gender gaps within firms.”

Helping workers reach contracts gives more people access to shared pay rules that reduce unequal treatment. This supports [NAME]’s concern for fair treatment and equal opportunities regardless of race or gender.
First contracts have included “anti-discrimination measures for both gender and race.” Union contracts have also protected “workers with disabilities and LGBTQ+ workers.”

Contract clauses add a way to enforce protection besides bringing a legal claim. The study explains that their enforcement takes “significantly less effort, cost, and time than claims filed under state or federal law.”

Making these contracts easier to reach gives workers facing bias a more accessible way to defend fair treatment. That serves [NAME]’s concern for vulnerable people and justice for people [NAME] does not know.
The first-contract study records rules for “the posting of schedules” . It explains that scheduling clauses give workers “predictability and control over their work schedules.”

Unpredictable hours create practical costs: “on-demand scheduling can be costly to workers who incur high costs of going to work without the ability to plan ahead, perhaps due to last-minute commuting and childcare arrangements.”
Helping workers get predictable hours reduces a barrier to holding a job while caring for dependents. This protects caregivers’ income and their opportunities to work.
Posted openings and a stated process tell workers what opportunities exist and how to seek them. Giving more workers access to these rules supports [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities.
The first-contract study found agreements “specifying job training or in-service training” . Its table of private-sector benefits also records “Tuition paid” .

Training costs matter to equal opportunities. The U.S. Treasury explains: “Income inequality often feeds back into inequality of opportunity, which impedes growth if disadvantaged people cannot access the resources necessary to acquire job skills or start businesses.”
Contract training and help with tuition open a way to gain skills for workers whose own resources limit their choices. That serves [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities in life.
Making such limits easier to reach gives workers a way to defend the jobs their households rely on. This protects people who are vulnerable to losing their income.
Either side can request mediation (outside help with talks). A binding panel decision follows if talks fail. A strike is workers stopping work; a lockout is an employer keeping workers out.

Canadian research names the bargaining incentive behind this approach: “Together these results suggest that FCA encourages collective bargaining by creating an incentive for the parties to bargain in good faith and negotiate an agreement.” FCA means first-contract arbitration.
Disrupted services also put vulnerable people at risk. A U.S. Treasury review cites research finding that “nurse strikes, though uncommon, lead to diminished patient outcomes” .

The bill gives workers another way to seek a first contract and gives both sides a reason to settle. Reducing reliance on harmful stoppages protects workers’ incomes and people who depend on their services.

Member approval is an existing safeguard under union rules. The Heritage Foundation, a policy research group, states: “Currently, nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” Ratification means a member vote to approve the contract.

The bill instead makes the panel’s vote decisive: “A majority of the 3-person arbitration panel shall render a decision settling the dispute” . The panel’s binding decision requires no approval vote by workers.

Workers live with the results of their pay, hours and workplace rules. Letting them reject terms they believe are harmful gives their needs a direct check on the outcome. Removing that safeguard weakens fair treatment in decisions that govern their income.
First-contract talks often involve beginners. The Heritage Foundation states: “newly unionized employers and newly formed unions are often inexperienced in negotiations.”

A first contract requires detailed review of many issues. Labor lawyers explain: “there are too many topics requiring in-depth discussion, negotiation, and drafting to reach agreement in that timeframe.”
Workers now use continued bargaining and economic pressure to seek better terms: “workers can use strikes to try to pull employers closer to their demands.”

The employer can start the bill’s process for binding terms even if workers object: “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” More time requires agreement: “or such additional period as the parties may agree upon” .
Workers cannot keep disputed terms open just by refusing to agree. An employer can start the move to outside decision-makers while workers still want time to study proposals or press their demands.
Representative Fine, a member of Congress, names the resulting pressure: the timetable “increases pressure on workers to settle before they have fully fought for what they deserve.”

Protecting workers who depend on their pay and benefits includes giving them a fair chance to understand and defend those needs. Pressure to accept less before they lose direct control threatens that protection.

The National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors, a business group, warns that arbitrators unfamiliar with a workplace could impose “work and safety rules that are not adequately tailored to a facility's specific operations” .

Matching prevention to the workplace matters for protecting workers. OSHA, the U.S. workplace safety agency, explains: “The process described in these recommended practices can, and should, be tailored to the needs of each workplace.”
The imposed contract lasts two years unless changed by “written consent of the parties.”

A safety rule that misses the workplace’s actual hazards can leave workers exposed to injury. Making such a rule binding despite workers’ objections puts the protection of people facing those hazards at risk.

A panel can commit a business to costs it did not agree to. Representative Walberg, a member of Congress, warns: “Those contracts could mandate spending that small employers cannot sustain, threaten jobs, kill growth, and in some cases, shut businesses down entirely.”

The bill requires decisions to consider “the employer's financial status and prospects” . The risk lies in outsiders judging those finances and operations incorrectly. Labor lawyer Robert Steptoe warns: “Panel arbitrators may not understand the business” .

A mistaken first contract can shape later ones. Steptoe explains that imposed terms “would set the standard for all future contracts because of the difficulty of unwinding the many complex provisions that go into a collective bargaining agreement.”

Costs a business cannot sustain threaten workers’ jobs and small owners’ income. Losing that income harms families with little money saved and closes opportunities to earn a living. Concern for vulnerable people gives [NAME] a reason to resist this added risk.

The bill adds required mediation and panel-related duties for the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS), the U.S. agency that helps employers and unions settle disputes: “the Service shall promptly communicate with the parties and use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement.” After failed mediation, “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” .
On June 9, lawyers King and MacDonald warned: “The FMCS does not have anywhere near the personnel to meet the obligations this legislation would impose upon it.”
A June 12 account from the State of Connecticut about the damage from the 2025 cuts confirms that “the majority of the federal agency’s employees have not returned.”
Small unions have fewer alternatives. The service is especially valuable to “small business and small unions that cannot necessarily afford to hire private mediation services.”

Moving a dispute to a panel does not create a deadline for finishing it: “The Faster Labor Contracts Act limits the amount of time that can pass before binding arbitration is invoked, but it does not limit the timeline of arbitration.”

Adding required work to a reduced agency creates competition for limited help and another source of delay. Workers whose unions cannot buy private help have fewer ways around that strain. Equal opportunity requires protecting their access to the help needed to get pay and workplace protections.

The bill normally gives each side a panel choice and calls for “one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties” . But if seats remain unfilled after the 14-day selection period, “the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.” The Service is a federal agency.

When the parties cannot fill the seats, federal choices decide who can impose their terms. Choosing arbitrators for their political views threatens workers’ access to decisions based on their circumstances and needs. Concern for just treatment gives [NAME] a reason to protect workers from that influence.

Lawyers King and MacDonald warn that compulsory arbitration requires “complex and cost-heavy hearings” . Labor lawyer Robert Steptoe names another cost: “Courts will be asked to interpret the new statute and define the limits of the arbitrators’ authority.”

King and MacDonald name a direct risk to workers’ income: “This approach will direct employer resources to litigation and potentially decrease the amount of wages and benefits an employer can provide to employees.”

Imposing terms by law also gives opponents a basis to challenge union funding. King and MacDonald argue: “The government will be involved whenever an arbitral-created contract requires fair-share fees. All of those contracts will be open to attack in our courts.” These are fees for representing workers who do not join the union.

Those fees support help for members and nonmembers. Labor-law scholar Ann Hodges explains that a fee clause “permits the union to charge a fee for representation to those who do not want to join the union and pay full union dues.” Yet “the union must represent all the employees in the unit fairly and in good faith.”

Workplace access faces a separate legal attack. King and MacDonald argue that “any time this bill imposed a contract with union access rights, it would take property and violate the Fifth Amendment.” Their claim is that requiring employers to admit union representatives takes a property right without paying for it.

Fee lawsuits can use up resources even when they fail. Reviewing earlier cases involving public-sector unions, Hodges reports that they “impose substantial litigation costs on unions that could otherwise dedicate these resources to representing workers” .

Required hearings and new legal fights can use up money for wages, benefits and representation. Challenges to funding and workplace access also put the tools of shared protection at risk. Protecting people with little individual power gives [NAME] a reason to preserve those resources and tools.

Under existing law, “upon reaching a good-faith impasse, the NLRA entitles an employer to unilaterally implement its last, best, and final offer.” This means putting that offer into effect without union agreement after talks reach a real deadlock. The NLRA is the main U.S. private-sector labor law.

The bill instead requires parties “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” . Labor lawyer Robert Steptoe explains: “This employer obligation to maintain all current terms and conditions of employment extends indefinitely beyond the point when the parties reach a good faith impasse to the date the parties reach agreement.”

The maintenance rule “applies not just to first contracts, but rather to all employers and all contracts.” The bill’s process for reaching a panel is limited to “an initial collective bargaining agreement following certification or recognition” .

Sometimes an otherwise lawful final offer would improve pay without cutting other terms. In those cases, the bill stops the employer from giving those gains on its own after a deadlock. Later contract talks have no arbitration option under this bill. Closing that way to higher pay puts low-paid workers’ living standards and chances to get ahead at risk.

Existing law allows an employer to announce, before a contract ends, that it will withdraw recognition of the union (stop treating it as the workers’ representative) after the contract ends. The employer may do so “upon receiving objective evidence that the union has actually lost majority support.”

Workers use this process. A June 2025 report describes a Sunoco driver named Fifer gathering majority support against the union: “Fifer opted to submit his petition to his employer, who withdrew recognition from the USW union in accordance with the Johnson Controls decision.” USW is the name of the union, and Johnson Controls is the 2019 labor-board decision that allows this withdrawal.

The bill requires continued bargaining “absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” . Decertification means removing the union as the workers’ representative through a federal election.

Clear majority opposition would no longer be enough for the employer to withdraw recognition; workers would have to wait for an election. That adds an obstacle to ending representation they no longer want. Just treatment includes respecting those workers’ wishes about who speaks for them.

Delay can weaken that voice. The bill states: “The employers can use those delays to sap labor organization resolve and secure more favorable terms for the employer.” To sap resolve means to weaken a group’s determination.

Talks must start within ten days of a written request from a newly recognized or certified union, unless both sides agree to more time: “Not later than 10 days after receiving a written request for collective bargaining” ; “or within such further period as the parties agree upon” .

The bill keeps the employer’s duty to bargain in place until an election removes the workers’ representative: “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” .
These rules strengthen workers’ chance to have their chosen group heard despite management’s opposition. Hearing people whose choice one dislikes puts acceptance despite disagreement into practice.

In workplaces with people of different races, continued union work gives people shared tasks across racial lines: “Union workers engage in collective action around issues of contract bargaining and workplace grievances.” The same source also names discussion with “explicitly anti-racist” messages as part of unions’ approach.

Research that followed white workers over time supports a link to accepting Black people: “our panel analysis suggests that gaining union membership between 2010 and 2016 reduced racial resentment among white workers.”
Protecting continuing union relationships also supports a setting for cooperation across racial differences. This gives [NAME] a further reason to favor protecting that voice.

The existing system already allows voluntary mediation (outside help with talks): “The FMCS provides completely free, completely voluntary contract mediation services to parties engaged in negotiations” . FMCS is the U.S. agency that helps employers and unions settle disputes.

The role of FMCS fits the problem: “In first contract mediation, a neutral third party comes in to help facilitate the bargaining process between parties that do not have a mature bargaining relationship.”

After ninety days of talks, or a longer period both sides accept, “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” The service must “promptly communicate with the parties and use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement.”

If no agreement follows within thirty days of the request, or an agreed extension, the dispute goes to a panel with “one member selected by the individual or labor organization, one member selected by the employer, and one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties.” If selection fails, “the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.”

The panel’s decision must weigh both sides’ needs: “the employer's financial status and prospects” ; “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” .

The panel’s decision provides shared rules even while disagreement remains: “such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years, unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.”

Either side gains a legal way to get help with a difficult conversation. If talks fail, each side has a place in choosing a panel that must consider their needs. [NAME] has a reason to favor this way of working with people despite disagreement.

First contracts already provide tools for this. Workers at Kickstarter, a company, voted to “ratify their first collective bargaining agreement with their employer.” Its terms say employment decisions “are not based on any protected status.” The listed traits include “religion, creed” and “political affiliation” .

Contracts give workers a way to enforce such rules: “Through procedures that address contract violations, union contracts can be used to hold employers accountable and compel them to follow anti-discrimination policies.”

Contract terms can also adapt work to people’s differences. At Santa Fe Opera, workers won rules requiring “costumes, wigs, hair coloring, shoes, and make-up that are appropriate for a range of skin tones.”

For workers seeking these terms, the bill stops a first-contract deadlock from blocking the whole contract. It strengthens their way to enforceable protection from mistreatment for who they are or what they believe, and to practical acceptance of differences. That serves [NAME]’s value of accepting people who are different.

Contracts have created regular discussions across workplace groups: “Union professionals have used their contracts to establish groups made up of managers and union members that meet regularly to discuss and address diversity issues.”
Kickstarter’s first contract gives a specific example: “To hold quarterly meetings during the work day with the participation of employees and management.”

Those meetings openly welcome different views: “Any participant may propose issues to address and invite employees who have a particular expertise or viewpoint to a meeting.” Participants agree to “maintain a respectful atmosphere at all times.”

Contracts can also require repeated learning about bias. Actors’ Equity, a union for stage actors, won a rule that “theaters will provide mandatory anti-discrimination and harassment training on at least an annual basis.”

The bill provides a way through first-contract deadlock. This helps workers turn proposals for continuing discussion and learning into workplace rules. Supporting these opportunities gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill, because [NAME] values listening to and understanding people who are different.

Contract votes give members a way to question and reject terms. UAW Local 600, an autoworkers’ union, explains that members have “a very powerful right to ask questions about any resulting tentative agreement and vote it up or down as you wish with your co-workers.”

Rejection can send disputed issues back to bargaining: “If the tentative agreement is rejected, the union may demand that the employer resume bargaining to resolve the issue(s) causing member rejection” .

In cases sent to arbitration (a panel deciding the contract), the bill makes the panel’s decision binding without requiring a member approval vote: “such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years” .

Members can support a union and still oppose particular contract terms. Arbitration skips their existing way to refuse approval and press negotiators to answer their objections. [NAME]’s wish to listen to people who disagree gives a reason to keep that way open.

Choosing a panel member does not restore a vote on the resulting contract. The bill gives the union “one member selected by the individual or labor organization” ; the panel’s majority decides the terms.

In states that permit required bargaining fees, a contract can also make nonmembers pay for representation in order to keep their jobs. The U.S. Supreme Court describes agreements “requiring all employees in the bargaining unit to pay union dues as a condition of continued employment, whether or not the employees become union members.”

This payment concerns bargaining representation. The Court limits required nonmember charges to “only those fees necessary to finance collective-bargaining activities” . Federal law also protects state bans on agreements “prohibited by State or Territorial Law” .

An imposed contract with a lawful fee clause also makes workers pay for a bargaining voice they reject. Respect for dissent gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added burden on workers who choose not to join the union.
Existing law requires both sides to “meet at reasonable times and confer in good faith” , but “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” .

The bill lets either side request mediation (outside help with talks) after 90 days of bargaining: “If after the expiration of the 90-day period beginning on the date on which bargaining is commenced, or such additional period as the parties may agree upon, the parties have failed to reach an agreement, either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.”

After the “30-day period beginning on the date on which the request for mediation is made” , unresolved disputes must go to arbitration, where a panel decides: “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” . The clock starts with the request, not with the first mediation meeting.
Mediation helps the parties find a solution they choose. The federal mediation agency describes this feature as “Parties retain control of resolution” .

Required arbitration creates a competing path. A 2008 legal analysis of an earlier first-contract arbitration proposal describes the danger that “the parties speak not to one another, but to the arbitrator.”

Failure to agree starts the bill’s process for imposed terms even after sincere, good-faith talks. A side expecting better terms from the panel gains a way to avoid further compromise with the other group.
[NAME] values listening to people with different views. That gives a reason to keep the need for both groups to work through their differences and find terms each accepts.
Extra time requires agreement: “or such additional period as the parties may agree upon” . One side’s willingness to keep seeking common ground cannot stop the other from seeking a binding award.

Construction bargaining reflects differences between places and trades. The Associated General Contractors of America, a business group, describes “local multi-employer bargaining structures that reflect regional market conditions, craft practices, and established area agreements.”

The association names the specific risk: “outside arbitration panels unfamiliar with local construction markets could impose contract terms that fail to reflect the industry or local labor standards.”
The bill lets a panel majority settle the dispute. Changes to its two-year award require both parties’ consent: “unless amended during such period by written consent of the parties.”

The bill removes the need for both sides to agree before decision-makers who may not know the local situation set binding terms. A local group whose practices are misunderstood cannot get a correction through its objection alone.

Listening to different groups includes taking their local experience and working practices seriously. The risk of overriding that knowledge gives [NAME] a reason to oppose moving final control to the panel.

The panel must consider “the size and type of the employer's operations and business” . That broad factor does not give the affected trade groups a right to reject terms that miss their local practices.

Union representation also covers people who disagree. The U.S. Supreme Court explains that the union bargains “on behalf of all employees in the bargaining unit over wages, hours, and other terms and conditions of employment” .

When a contract ends, existing law allows an employer with timely, valid proof of lost majority support to withdraw recognition. This means to stop treating the union as the workers’ bargaining representative. The NLRB, the federal labor board, states that “an employer possessing such evidence may withdraw recognition when the contract expires” .

The bill instead continues the duty until an election removes the union: “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” .

Even rejection expressed independently and strong enough for that existing process would no longer end the bargaining duty. Workers would need an election removing the union before the employer could stop bargaining with it.
Respecting people who disagree includes listening when workers reject a group’s claim to speak for them. Closing a lawful way to act on those changed wishes gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.

First contracts (the first written work agreements between a new union and an employer) include safety rules that workers can enforce through complaints. A study of agreements reached in 1987–1996 found that “55 percent of private sector contracts have grievable health and safety clauses.”
These rules address specific hazards. A study of 16 contracts from 2010–2014 found: “Most contracts detail the employer’s responsibility to provide and maintain protective clothing and equipment.”

Unions also help workers report hazards without being punished: “They bargain to improve safety practices, protect their members against retaliation for reporting a violation, or make complaints on members’ behalf about hazards” .
The bill’s binding process for a first contract helps workers get and enforce these protections sooner. Protection from hazards serves [NAME]’s aim to avoid injury and illness at work.
Existing law lets an employer put its last offer into effect after a real deadlock: “When parties reach impasse, the employer may implement its final offer.” An impasse is a deadlock in talks.
The bill instead requires employers “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” .
The bill closes that way of cutting existing health coverage, sick leave and safety rules while workers wait for an agreement. Keeping those protections serves [NAME]’s personal health and safety.
First contracts include health coverage. The first-contract study found that “first contracts establish, codify, and expand health insurance” .

Bargaining produces benefit gains. A U.S. Treasury research review finds that “the higher rates of fringe benefits at newly unionized firms are the direct result of collective bargaining.” Fringe benefits are benefits beyond pay.

A study that followed workers before and after joining a union found them “more likely to have access to health insurance” and “more likely to pay a lower portion of their healthcare expenses out-of-pocket.”
Getting these contract benefits sooner lowers a cost barrier to medical care. That directly serves [NAME]’s aim to prevent disease and protect health.

First-contract research found agreements that “provide for some sick leave benefits.” A study that followed workers before and after joining a union found them “more likely to have access to paid sick leave” .
Paid leave removes the need to lose pay in order to seek care: “Paid sick leave benefits allow workers to stay home and visit a healthcare provider when ill.”

Staying home also protects other people. A U.S. study comparing states with and without sick-leave requirements found: “We find clear evidence that sick pay mandates reduce ILI infection rates at the population level.” ILI means flu-like illness.
Getting paid sick leave sooner supports treatment and recovery and reduces exposure to sick workers. [NAME] gains a personal health reason as a worker, coworker, customer or patient.

Bargaining raises pay. A U.S. Treasury research review concludes: “All in all, the evidence points to a union wage premium of around 10 to 15 percent, with larger effects for longer tenured workers.” This compares union pay with similar non-union work.

The bill makes workers’ living needs part of a binding settlement. The panel must consider “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” .

More income buys health protection: “More affluent people have more disposable income and can more easily afford medical care and a healthy lifestyle—benefits that also extend to their children.” More income also helps pay for food: “More affluent people can more easily afford regular and nutritious meals, which tend to be more expensive and less convenient than less nutritious, calorie-dense, high-carbohydrate options and fast foods.”
Competition spreads wage gains beyond union members: “Other workers see increases in wages and improved work practices as their nonunionized workplaces compete with unionized ones for labor.”

Getting bargained pay gains sooner strengthens the means to afford care and healthy food, including through competition for workers. The reason for [NAME] is better health, with benefits that reach beyond union members.

First contracts include rules for work hours and schedule changes. The first-contract study explains: “These clauses are important because they provide workers predictability and control over their work schedules.”
Contracts also provide rest. The 16-contract study found: “Most contracts include the indicators of paid annual leave, paid rest periods, and bereavement leave.”

A randomized experiment that made schedules more stable in Gap clothing stores improved sleep: “The intervention resulted in a 6-8% increase in self rated sleep quality among workers in treatment stores.”

U.S. workplace-health experts recommend rest breaks and enough time between shifts to reduce tiredness. Their advice includes: “Consider allowing at least 10 hours between shifts, so workers can get 7–8 hours of sleep.” They also advise: “Consider allowing rest breaks of 10 to 15 minutes regularly, such as every 1–2 hours during demanding work.”
Faster contracts bring forward rules that protect sleep and recovery. These directly support [NAME]’s health and safety in ordinary working life.

The first-contract study found rules requiring a valid reason for discipline or firing, “thus constraining management’s ability to play favorites or to intimidate and threaten workers who challenge them.”
These contracts also made disputes subject to “independent third-party review of disputes between management and employees.”

Control over work and fair decisions matter for health: “Unions can address job control, decisional justice, and other work conditions that are associated with coronary heart disease, high blood pressure, musculoskeletal disorders, and stress.”
Quicker first contracts give workers tools to challenge unhealthy demands and unfair treatment. Protecting that control over working conditions serves [NAME]’s physical and mental health.

Such contracts set staffing rules that can be enforced. The first contract at Ascension Seton, a hospital in Austin, Texas, required: “In the emergency department, at least one RN will be required to work for every four patients.” RN means registered nurse.
The bill’s binding first-contract process brings a way to get staffing rules that protect patients sooner. [NAME] has a personal health reason to favor that protection when needing hospital care.

Arbitration (a panel deciding the contract) gives the two sides a way to settle a first contract without a stoppage. Evidence from Canadian private-sector first-contract laws supports this mechanism: “One study found that these laws reduced work stoppages on first-contract negotiations in the private sector by at least 50 percent.”
Hospital strikes threaten patient care. A study of New York nurses’ strikes in 1984–2004 found that “hospitals functioning during nurses’ strikes are doing so at a lower quality of patient care.”
Replacing unresolved first-contract disputes with binding settlement reduces a source of disruption in private hospitals. Avoiding that risk to care serves [NAME]’s personal safety as a patient.

Union rules normally give members a vote: “nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” A contract decided by a panel takes effect without that vote.
The panel can set “safety procedures, leave policies, and virtually every term of employment.”

The National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors, a business group, names the danger: “arbitrators could be empowered to impose work and safety rules that are not adequately tailored to a facility's specific operations” .

Workers bring knowledge needed to find those problems. OSHA, the U.S. workplace safety agency, explains: “They also often know the most about potential hazards associated with their jobs. Successful programs tap into this knowledge base.”

Approval votes let workers act on safety concerns. Reporting on Providence nurses’ rejection of a proposed contract in 2025, Northwest Labor Press states: “Oregon Nurses Association said the agreement failed because it did too little to ensure safe staffing levels or make wages competitive to help recruit and retain staff.” The nurses were in talks to renew an existing contract, which the bill’s arbitration would not reach. The example shows how an approval vote works, not a vote the bill would skip.
Skipping approval removes workers’ final chance to block a binding contract over safety problems they find. Keeping that check serves [NAME]’s wish to avoid injury.

Union rules normally give members a vote: “nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” A contract decided by a panel takes effect without that vote.
The panel can “impose wages, benefits, schedules, and workplace rules for years to come.”

Workers use approval votes to challenge such terms. The news station WDRB reported that workers at Conagra, a food company, “rejected a proposed labor contract” whose terms failed to address concerns about “forced overtime and double shifts” . The report describes an existing Teamsters union group and a 60-day “cooling-off period” . That points to talks to renew an existing contract, which the bill’s arbitration would not reach. The example shows how an approval vote works, not a vote the bill would skip.

The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), a U.S. agency, explains: “Work-related factors that can contribute to fatigue include scheduling practices, such as night shifts or extended hours, that can interfere with sleep.”
Tiredness creates injury risks: “Fatigued workers might take more risks that lead to injury or errors.”

The danger reaches ordinary road users: “The effects of work-related fatigue can also spill over into personal lives and can impact public safety, for example when fatigued workers drive on public roads.”

In first contracts decided by a panel, the bill skips this way for workers to challenge tiring schedules before accepting a binding contract. [NAME] has a safety reason to keep that check against work injuries and crashes on roads they use.

Union rules normally give members a vote: “nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” A contract decided by a panel takes effect without that vote.
The panel’s power includes “leave policies” , so it can settle paid sick leave without members’ approval.

Paid leave addresses pressure to work while sick. NIOSH, a U.S. workplace-health agency, explains: “Access to paid sick leave might reduce the pressure to work while sick out of fear of losing income.”
Research connects paid sick leave with recovery: “paid sick leave is associated with shorter worker recovery times and reduced complications from minor health problems.”
Paid sick leave also protects people around the sick worker: “Paid sick leave also enables workers to care for loved ones and can help prevent the spread of contagious diseases.”
NIOSH also found a link to injury: “workers with access to paid sick leave were 28% less likely overall to suffer nonfatal occupational injuries than workers without access to paid sick leave.”

The bill removes workers’ final chance to reject a binding contract over sick leave they find too limited. Protecting recovery, avoiding infection from sick coworkers and preventing injuries give [NAME] reasons to keep that check.

Union rules normally give members a vote: “nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” A contract decided by a panel takes effect without that vote.

The panel can impose “wages, benefits, schedules, and workplace rules” . These benefits include health coverage: the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), a union, lists “employer- provided healthcare” among union members’ benefits.

Approval votes let workers resist higher health costs. The rejected Conagra proposal “would have resulted in higher health insurance costs” . That vote came in an existing Teamsters union group, apparently in talks to renew an existing contract the bill’s arbitration would not reach. The example shows how an approval vote works.

Having insurance does not ensure affordable care. The Commonwealth Fund’s 2024 survey found: “Nearly three of five (57%) underinsured adults said they avoided getting needed health care because of its cost” . Underinsured means having coverage that does not make care affordable: “their coverage doesn’t enable affordable access to health care.”

People report worse health after delays caused by cost. In the same survey, “two of five (41%) working-age adults who reported a cost-related delay in their care said a health problem had worsened because of it.”
Skipping workers’ approval removes a check on binding health benefits they find too limited. [NAME] has a health reason to keep that check against costs that keep people from needed treatment.
First-contract deadlocks can last for years. Research found that “a third of newly organized bargaining units still do not have a first contract after three years” .
A study of Canadian first-contract arbitration (FCA), where a panel can set contract terms, found: “FCA reduces first agreement work stoppage incidence by at least 50 percent.”
The comparison uses a similar bargaining system: Canadian labor laws are “modeled on U.S. labor law.”

The shared mechanism is a reason to agree before a panel takes over. The study describes this as “creating an incentive for the parties to bargain in good faith and negotiate an agreement” . The bill provides that binding last step.
The bill gives both sides a reason to settle through bargaining and a peaceful way out when talks fail. That reduces the need to force a first agreement through a stoppage.

Disruptions reach beyond the workplace. Federal mediation helps prevent “strikes, lockouts, and other labor disruptions that can be devastating for workers and much more costly to the nation’s economy” .

First-contract bargaining reaches private companies that support the military. Workers who newly joined a union at Amentum, a defense contractor, “provide critical maintenance and supply support for military helicopter operations at the naval installation.” Their next step was clear: “Preparations are now underway to begin bargaining a first contract.”

Strikes at defense suppliers threaten military equipment. The Congressional Research Service (CRS), which does research for Congress, reported: “Boeing’s Chief Financial Officer in September said that the company’s machinists’ strike would affect the KC-46 tanker, a military version of Boeing’s commercial 767 freighter.”

First-contract disputes also cause hospital strikes. New Orleans nurses “held a three-day strike Nov. 11-13 to protest the refusal of the hospital’s owner and operator, LCMC Health, to address concerns about nursing staff retention as part of ongoing first contract bargaining” .
A study of New York hospitals found evidence that “hospitals functioning during nurses' strikes are doing so at a lower quality of patient care” .

Reducing first-contract stoppages protects steady production, military support needed to defend citizens, and medical care needed to protect their lives. These are direct interests of a secure, stable United States.
A first contract turns organizing into practical protection. First-contract arbitration (a panel deciding the contract) gives workers a “guaranteed path to get the benefits of a union contract” .

Those protections include actual safeguards against infection. Longmont United nurses won “the first acute care private-sector contract for RNs in the state of Colorado.” That contract included “Health and safety provisions to ensure nurses get the highest level of personal protective equipment when caring for patients with infectious diseases.”

Protective equipment is part of infection prevention. Guidance from the CDC, the U.S. public health agency, lists “use of gloves, gown, mask, eye protection, or face shield, depending on the anticipated exposure” .

Binding settlement gives newly organized care workers a way to get enforceable protections that an employer cannot block just by refusing to sign any contract. Strengthening this way to protect care workers and patients helps the United States defend people against disease outbreaks.

The bill makes a contract’s gains attainable and requires the panel to consider “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” .

The U.S. Treasury estimates a pay gain from union membership: “Unions raise the wages of their members by 10 to 15 percent.” Treasury also finds better benefits and work rules: “These workplace improvements contribute substantially to middle-class financial stability and worker well-being.”
Treasury links unions’ broader economic benefit to “reducing overall inequality.”

The bill also protects existing pay during bargaining. It adds a duty “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” . This closes a way of imposing cuts: existing law gives an employer a “right to unilaterally implement its last, best, and final offer when the parties reach a good faith impasse.” An impasse is a real deadlock in talks.

Financial strength has a national effect. Treasury explains that reducing inequality strengthens households, “making these Americans less sensitive to negative income shocks and thus lessening economic volatility.” Negative income shocks are sudden losses of income, and volatility means large swings.

Making gains from first contracts attainable and protecting pay during talks helps households withstand lost income. That strengthens the wider economy against swings caused by households’ financial problems, which supports U.S. stability.
The bill’s settlement is “binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years” . That gives businesses a known basis for planning labor costs.
The panel must base its decision on the business’s circumstances, including “the employer's financial status and prospects” .

The bill brings a similar planning benefit through settled, lasting terms. More predictable labor costs help companies plan staffing, spending and investment, which supports steadier economic activity across the United States.

The Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS) is the U.S. agency that helps employers and unions settle disputes. Requiring first-contract mediation when either side asks adds demand for its help. Former NLRB chair Lauren McFerran, who led the federal labor board, wrote in March 2025 about the proposal: “This mandatory requirement would presumably significantly increase the demand for the FMCS’s services, as opposed to the current, voluntary system.”

FMCS would also have to fill arbitration panel seats when the two sides do not choose members: “the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.”

The agency’s April 2026 budget reports limits on the groups of workers it serves: “FMCS limited its involvement to facilities that provide health care services with bargaining units of 250 or more members, and to bargaining units of 1,000 members or more for all other industries in which it has jurisdiction.”

The bill provides no funding for more staff. The National Restaurant Association, a business group, warns: “The FLCA also assumes a significant expansion in federal mediation capacity that has not been funded.”
FMCS describes its role: “Our mediators work tirelessly to minimize and prevent disruptions affecting utilities, health care, public safety and security.”

New required cases compete for the resources used to prevent disruptions to power and health care. That risks weakening the state’s ability to keep essential services running and protect citizens, which gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the added burden.

The labor law being changed reaches defense businesses. The NLRB, the federal labor board, applies its national-defense test to companies whose “operations exert a substantial impact on national defense” .

Representative Walberg, a member of Congress, warns that imposed contracts could “mandate spending that small employers cannot sustain, threaten jobs, kill growth, and in some cases, shut businesses down entirely.”
The U.S. Defense Department says small businesses “keep our military forces combat ready with critical parts” .

The department also warns: “Over time, a decline in the number of small businesses participating in defense acquisitions will lead to a reduction of innovative concepts, capabilities, quality of service and increased acquisition costs.”

The panel must base its decision on “the employer's financial status and prospects” . That requirement gives a supplier no right to reject the costs imposed, because the panel’s decision is binding for two years.

An unaffordable award that closes a defense supplier covered by the law threatens the supply of military parts and capabilities. Protecting those supplies serves [NAME]’s priority of a United States able to defend its citizens.

The National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors, a business group, warns that panels could “impose work and safety rules that are not adequately tailored to a facility's specific operations, creating significant operational challenges and unintended consequences.”

Distribution includes essential food and medical supplies. In its pandemic guidance, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security lists “Employees and firms supporting the distribution of food, feed, and beverage and ingredients used in these products” and “logistics and warehouse operators, distributors of medical equipment” among essential workers.
The guidance links these functions to “public health and safety, as well as economic and national security.”
The panel must use “the size and type of the employer's operations and business” in setting its terms. That factor gives neither side a right to reject a final rule that does not fit the site.

Rules that interfere with safe work at food or medical distributors put essential deliveries at risk. Protecting those deliveries helps protect citizens and keep the country stable through crises, which gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this added risk.
The panel must base its decision partly on family support: “the employees' ability to sustain themselves, their families, and their dependents on the wages and benefits they earn from the employer” .
The same Southern Baptist statement defines the marriage commitment these earnings support: “Marriage is the uniting of one man and one woman in covenant commitment for a lifetime.”

The bill gives workers a legal claim to have the costs of supporting a family counted in binding pay decisions. That supports the means to keep marriage and the roles of a father who provides and a mother who cares for children at home. [NAME] values preserving these customs.

Keeping current terms until agreement protects existing schedules after a deadlock in talks. A legal analysis names the change: “The FLCA’s second major change to the law of collective bargaining is the removal of the employer’s right to unilaterally implement its last, best, and final offer when the parties reach a good faith impasse.” FLCA is this bill; an impasse is a real deadlock.

Existing contracts protect time for worship. The 2021–25 contract at Kroger, a grocery company, gives certain groups of longtime workers this rule: “Sunday and holiday work shall be voluntary and rotated among qualified employees who are available for such work.”
The bill protects such established Sunday and holiday arrangements against changes an employer would otherwise impose after a deadlock.

First contracts also provide religious scheduling rules. University of Pennsylvania graduate workers announced: “Graduate Workers’ Agreement with the Penn administration has been ratified and it is now our first union contract.” Their agreement states: “Graduate Workers may request reasonable schedule adjustments, including switching workdays, to observe religious holidays or cultural observances not recognized by the University. Such requests shall not be unreasonably denied.”

Contracts also protect the notice families need to plan regular activities. Union workers at Bloomingdale’s main store “receive their schedules twenty-one days in advance and must be notified of any changes to the schedule at least one week in advance.”
Sunday worship is an established Christian custom. Southern Baptist teaching says the Lord’s Day “should include exercises of worship and spiritual devotion, both public and private.”

Passing on faith needs regular family time. The Christian group Focus on the Family explains: “For children to absorb God’s truths, regular times of family Bible study, devotion and worship are important.”

Keeping existing schedules protects worship routines. A binding process for first contracts strengthens workers’ means to get religious holiday and advance-notice rules. Both serve [NAME]’s commitment to keeping Christian customs and teaching them to children.

Paid parental leave is a specific first-contract benefit. The first agreement for Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago workers includes: “Four weeks of paid parental leave upon the birth or adoption of a child” .

Lack of leave is a reported reason for seeking abortion in the United States. A mother interviewed in a U.S. study explained: “My work doesn't offer maternity leave” . She added: “If I took time off I would lose my job so there's just no way.”
Southern Baptist teaching makes protecting unborn life a religious duty: “We should speak on behalf of the unborn and contend for the sanctity of all human life from conception to natural death.”
Christian pro-life writers John Stonestreet and Roberto Rivera apply that duty to supporting parents through leave policies: “We should also back policies that will encourage women to choose life.”

Binding first-contract settlement strengthens workers’ way to paid parental leave. For parents who observe the religious rule against abortion, that reduces the work and income pressure the mother describes and helps them continue that observance.

This tradition calls for public action, not only private belief: “we urge all Southern Baptists to advocate in the public square for laws and policies that reflect the moral order revealed in Scripture and nature” .

The Service Employees International Union (SEIU), a national union, pledges to “do everything in our power to keep abortion and all reproductive healthcare services safe, legal, and accessible for everyone” .

First contracts can add to SEIU’s income, because one national payment is not owed for “members who have not achieved a first collective bargaining agreement.” A firmer income and membership base strengthens an organization working against a teaching [NAME]’s tradition calls on Christians to support in law. Preserving that teaching gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this effect.

The Southern Baptist Convention teaches: “Marriage is a lifelong covenant between one man and one woman” . The Convention calls for “the overturning of laws and court rulings, including Obergefell v. Hodges, that defy God’s design for marriage and family” . Obergefell is the U.S. Supreme Court decision recognizing same-sex marriage.

The AFL-CIO, a national group of unions, lobbied for the opposite policy: “The AFL-CIO urges you to vote in support of HR 8404, the Respect for Marriage Act. This legislation is essential to securing marriage equality for same-gender couples” .

Paying members support the federation as well as their own unions. The AFL-CIO’s constitution requires payment “upon the full paid-up membership of each affiliated national or international union” . The American Federation of Teachers (AFT), a union, confirms: “The AFT is affiliated with American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations” .

Protecting paying membership in affiliated unions supports a federation that lobbied in 2022 for a marriage policy this Christian tradition seeks to change. Unless that position has changed, strengthening the federation conflicts with [NAME]’s aim of keeping its inherited view of marriage.

The Southern Baptist Convention teaches: “God made every person in his image as either male or female in accord with his good design for humanity” . The Convention calls for laws that “recognize the biological reality of male and female” .

The May 2025 policy of the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), a union, seeks “strong state and national protections for LGBTQIA+ youth and adults” , including “Equitable access to facilities that match gender identities” and “Policies that allow transgender athletes to compete in the sports teams that they identify with” .

AFT sets aside part of each member’s payment for political work , and it represents some private-sector workers this bill covers . Strengthening AFT’s member-funded political work supports efforts to change public rules away from the understanding of sex [NAME] seeks to preserve.

School aid helps families carry out that role. The Association of Christian Schools International reports: “School choice programs in Kansas, along with scholarships CCS itself provides, enable the school to welcome students who were previously unable to afford tuition” .
The report connects access to religious practice: “Because of school choice, some students are shepherded by Christian educators for the first time, which has made a positive impact in the home.”

The American Federation of Teachers (AFT), a union, pledges to “assist our affiliates in lobbying state governments, and will support affiliated unions in opposing school vouchers and voucher-like programs” . These are forms of aid for schooling outside the public system.

AFT sets aside part of each member’s payment for political work , and it represents some private-sector workers this bill covers . Stronger AFT resources support an opponent of aid that makes Christian schooling affordable. Preserving families’ ability to teach and practice their faith gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that effect.
The U.S. Supreme Court described the foster care of Catholic Social Services (CSS) as “continuing the centuries-old mission of the Catholic Church to serve Philadelphia’s needy children.”

The court’s account states: “CSS holds the religious belief that marriage is a sacred bond between a man and a woman.” The Southern Baptist Convention’s Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission explains that the ruling lets faith-based providers “continue serving children and families according to their convictions.”

A 2022 resolution of the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), a union, lists “Fulton v. City of Philadelphia (2021)” among the rulings it condemns, then pledges to “work to reverse both these decisions of the court and their impact” .

AFT sets aside part of each member’s payment for political work , and it represents some private-sector workers this bill covers . If AFT keeps that pledge, strengthening it supports opposition to protection for practicing inherited Christian beliefs while serving others. [NAME]’s concern for following religious customs reaches this freedom to act on faith, as well as the beliefs themselves.

Contract approval is an existing union practice. The Heritage Foundation, a policy research group, states: “nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” Ratification means a vote to approve the contract.

The American Federation of Teachers (AFT), a union, seeks “transgender-inclusive healthcare” “during bargaining negotiations with employers” . Its 2025 policy also calls for “gender-affirming medical care” to “be fully covered by medical insurance” .

Choosing coverage is itself a religious practice in this tradition. GuideStone, a Southern Baptist body, warns: “you could be required to pay premiums that go toward other members’ coverage that directly conflicts with your faith — even when you don’t personally use a medical product or service that goes against your convictions.” GuideStone explains its own approach: “GuideStone health plans exclude coverage for gender dysphoria treatments, including sex change surgery or related sex hormones.”
For a contract set by the panel, the panel’s decision “shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years” . Members’ approval is no longer required for those terms to take effect.

Even where most workers would reject such coverage in order to follow their faith, a panel can make it part of their contract. The bill removes their shared vote as a way to keep shared health coverage in line with inherited Christian teaching.

The factors the bill gives the panel do not require particular contract terms. Sources: , .

They also recognize that first agreements decided by arbitration should not contain breakthrough or novel provisions (new kinds of contract terms). The review describes Canadian practice, not this bill. Sources: .

Faster first contracts bring enforceable workplace safety rules within reach sooner.

First contracts (the first written work agreements between a new union and an employer) include safety rules that workers can enforce through complaints. A study of agreements reached in 1987–1996 found that “55 percent of private sector contracts have grievable health and safety clauses.”
These rules address specific hazards. A study of 16 contracts from 2010–2014 found: “Most contracts detail the employer’s responsibility to provide and maintain protective clothing and equipment.”

Unions also help workers report hazards without being punished: “They bargain to improve safety practices, protect their members against retaliation for reporting a violation, or make complaints on members’ behalf about hazards” .
The bill’s binding process for a first contract helps workers get and enforce these protections sooner. Protection from hazards serves [NAME]’s aim to avoid injury and illness at work.
