The income gain in the argument depends on a general union pay estimate that differs from evidence on new unionization.

Treasury’s estimate concerns union membership: “Unions raise the wages of their members by 10 to 15 percent.” The bill’s first-contract process starts “following certification or recognition of an individual or labor organization as a representative” . The pay gap between union and non-union workers does not measure gains for workers forming a new union.

Gains from forming a new union differ from the general union pay gap. A study covering 1984–2001 compared workplaces where unions barely won or lost elections. Its wage results, from manufacturing, were different from the general pay gap: “estimates for wages are close to zero.” This is evidence that the measures differ, not an estimate of this bill’s effect.

The general union pay estimate does not establish the income gain from new first contracts on which part of the stability claim rests. This response does not answer the separate step on protecting current pay during talks.

This concerns how often stoppages happen, at least somewhat, not how long they last. It does not assume the Canadian 50 percent figure applies. The bill does not say whether strikes or lockouts may continue during arbitration.

The Canadian systems had another rule: “In Canadian jurisdictions once an application for FCA is filed any work stoppage in progress must stop.” [SES 4] The study could not “estimate the affect of each type of FCA on incidence.” [SES 4] A legal analysis says of this bill: “The bill also raises questions about the lawfulness of strikes and lockouts during these first contract negotiations.” [SES 10] This does not answer the ordinary inference that a settlement process can reduce some first-contract stoppages.
The Canadian study does not separate the effect of the settlement incentive from the different legal rules that came with it.

First-contract arbitration lets a third party set the agreement. The study notes: “In Canadian jurisdictions once an application for FCA is filed any work stoppage in progress must stop” . H.R.5408 contains no matching requirement . It says that the panel “shall render a decision settling the dispute” .
The study says the data do not let it estimate “the affect of each type of FCA on incidence.” Here, incidence means how often first-contract strikes or lockouts occur.

The argument has not shown that the reduction found across those Canadian systems would follow from this bill’s settlement process, because those systems also had a rule stopping strikes and lockouts, which the bill lacks. This response does not answer the narrower point that arbitration gives the parties another option besides relying on a stoppage.

A strike-ban clause does not add the limit this argument needs for the green-demand strikes it cites, because those strikes seek new contract terms.

The green strike in the argument took place after a contract ended: “The janitors’ contract ran out in December, but they agreed to go on working while negotiations progressed.” The bill’s arbitration rule covers “an initial collective bargaining agreement” , and its award binds “for a period of 2 years” .

Current law already limits strikes meant to rewrite terms fixed by an existing contract. The guide from the NLRB, the federal labor board, says: “The party must continue in full force and effect, without resorting to strike or lockout, all the terms and conditions of the existing contract until 60 days after the notice to the other party was given or until the date the contract is scheduled to expire, whichever is later.” This concerns changing agreed terms, not every strike during a contract.

For demands to add green contract terms, the argument has not shown what a ban clause adds beyond these existing limits. This response does not answer two things. First, an award itself ends the first-contract bargaining in which workers could strike for such terms. Second, a ban could reach work stoppages that are not aimed at changing contract terms.

The bill depends on the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS), the U.S. agency that helps employers and unions settle disputes: “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” .

The FMCS budget submission of April 3, 2026 says it had limited mediation to health-care groups with at least 250 represented workers and “bargaining units of 1,000 members or more for all other industries in which it has jurisdiction” .

The agency’s proposed service form, published May 15, 2026, still says of first-contract cases: “These cases will be assigned to a mediator if they meet the current criteria/metrics for case assignment.”

A supporter of the bill names the practical condition: “Without a robust, government-supported mediation and arbitration system, the Faster Labor Contracts Act would not be able to live up to its promise.”

Stopping an employer from blocking appointments does not solve this service gap for small groups seeking mediation and timely referral to a panel. This response does not show that the process is unavailable: the bill’s duty has no size limit, and the time before referral runs from the request.

The evidence describes access that is already restricted. Connecticut reports that, apart from critical-industry and class-action exceptions, negotiation services were limited to employers with “a minimum of 250 employees” . The bill’s first-contract duty has no employer-size limit: “the Service shall promptly communicate with the parties and use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement.”

Deciding the contract is the panel’s task, separate from the service’s mediation and referral work. Existing FMCS practice already uses a separate source of decision-makers: “Arbitrators are not FMCS employees.”

The argument has not shown how these duties would take help away from poorer unions under the already restricted system. This response does not answer added strain on groups that remain eligible for FMCS help, or the lack of a deadline at the panel stage.

The argument’s step from the power to appoint panel members to political selection rests on one advocate’s prediction.

Each side normally chooses a panel member, and the third seat remains “one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties” . The service fills “any members not selected” , so this power arises only when seats go unfilled.

The support for political selection is the statement that “there would likely be political pressure from presidential Administrations” . That passage gives no evidence about how such appointments are made.

The bill does give a federal agency those appointments. The further step, that those choices would turn on political views, is supported only by that prediction. This response does not show that such pressure would not occur.

It addresses voluntary arbitration and does not set rules for how an agency designates panel members. The argument’s step from the power to appoint panel members to political selection rests on one advocate’s prediction.

Each side normally chooses a panel member, and the third seat remains “one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties” . The service fills “any members not selected” , so this power arises only when seats go unfilled.

The support for political selection is the statement that “there would likely be political pressure from presidential Administrations” . That passage gives no evidence about how such appointments are made.

The bill does give a federal agency those appointments. The further step, that those choices would turn on political views, is supported only by that prediction. This response does not show that such pressure would not occur.

The legal rulings do not establish the blanket legal defects the lawyers’ letters claim.

Hodges’s evidence concerns lawsuits seeking refunds of fees charged to nonmembers for union representation. Those claims “primarily seek retroactive application of Janus” . This means applying Janus, a U.S. Supreme Court ruling on fees for government workers, to fees already collected. That record concerns a different kind of lawsuit from challenges to contracts at private employers.

Government involvement alone does not make bargaining fees invalid. In the case Hanson, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld financial support for private railway bargaining and held that the requirement “does not violate either the First or the Fifth Amendments.”

The Janus ruling distinguishes bargaining with government employers from private workplaces: “In the public sector, core issues such as wages, pensions, and benefits are important political issues, but that is generally not so in the private sector.” The letters’ argument about government involvement does not resolve that difference.

The U.S. Supreme Court case Cedar Point does not say that every right for union representatives to enter a workplace takes property without payment. The Court separates access to closed property from “Limitations on how a business generally open to the public may treat individuals on the premises” . The legal result depends on the access granted and the place involved.

The fee and access rulings do not show the blanket legal defects the letters claim. This response does not answer the costs of hearings that do occur, or of lawsuits that use up resources even when they fail.

The bill keeps “decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” . Workers keep the way to vote a union out.
The argument’s own legal account calls an election “the preferred method for determining employees’ representational preferences.”

A signature is not always a worker’s final choice. Describing workers who signed conflicting petitions, labor lawyers explain that a secret ballot allows a final choice without others knowing it, “insulating them from retaliation from whichever side they fail to support.”

The election requirement checks the majority’s wishes through a private choice by workers, instead of leaving the employer to act on signatures. Just treatment includes protecting that choice for every worker. The argument shows that employer withdrawal can be quicker, but speed alone does not establish that confirming the majority’s wishes is unfair.

The argument treats a stronger bargaining role as acceptance of different people.
Existing law already requires employers and representatives to “meet at reasonable times and confer in good faith with respect to wages, hours, and other terms and conditions of employment” .

The bill adds a starting deadline: “Not later than 10 days after receiving a written request for collective bargaining” , which can be extended by agreement: “or within such further period as the parties agree upon” . The bill also extends the duty: “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” .

The added rules concern when talks start and how long the representative keeps its bargaining role. Giving that representative a stronger role in negotiating work terms does not by itself show greater acceptance or understanding of different people. The argument moves between these meanings of being heard without defending the link. This response does not answer the separate step about cooperation across racial lines.

Federal law protects members’ right “to meet and assemble freely with other members; and to express any views, arguments, or opinions” . The bill’s binding award leaves those protections in place.

The union must represent people who disagree fairly. The court decision in the argument describes its “statutory obligation to serve the interests of all members without hostility or discrimination toward any” .

The final vote adds power to reject terms and press for changes. Accepting people who disagree does not mean accepting their preferred terms, so the argument needs to show less hearing or acceptance of them, beyond less control over the outcome. This response does not answer that losing the vote removes one way members press negotiators to answer objections.

The same decision describes representation “on behalf of all employees in the bargaining unit” and limits required nonmember charges to “only those fees necessary to finance collective-bargaining activities” .

A bargaining fee pays for representation that must serve people who disagree too; it does not require them to agree with the union. The argument names a financial burden without showing that it makes them less heard or accepted. A reason to reject required payment needs a further link to this value.

The argument does not establish that arbitration reduces efforts to understand the other side, and current law does not ensure terms both sides accept.
Existing law requires good-faith talks while stating that this duty “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” .

After good-faith talks reach a real deadlock, an employer can put certain earlier proposals into effect without union agreement: “an employer does not violate the Act by making unilateral changes that are reasonably comprehended within his pre-impasse proposals” .
Keeping current law does not preserve a requirement that workplace terms win both groups’ acceptance. Agreement on terms is also a different test from understanding the people proposing them.

The bill requires parties to “make every reasonable effort to conclude and sign a collective bargaining agreement” . It requires the mediation service to “use its best efforts, by mediation and conciliation, to secure an agreement” .

Research on Canadian first-contract arbitration (FCA) gives evidence against the predicted retreat from negotiation: “Despite this, FCA is not accessed frequently and it is even rarer for a first contract (in whole or in part) to be imposed. Together these results suggest that FCA encourages collective bargaining by creating an incentive for the parties to bargain in good faith and negotiate an agreement.” In that passage, “this” means the finding that first-contract arbitration cuts first-agreement work stoppages by at least half. That research covers systems with a work-stoppage rule that this bill does not state.

The bill’s deadlines do not excuse efforts to reach agreement. The first-contract evidence challenges the prediction that a binding last step weakens those efforts. One side’s refusal to extend talks after sincere bargaining does not itself show less willingness to understand the other group. The argument’s reason depends on that missing link, not simply on losing the power to insist on more time.

The Canadian first-contract study reports that arbitration is rarely accessed and rarely imposes a contract. It also notes that Canadian applications require any work stoppage in progress to stop, a rule not explicit in the U.S. proposal it discusses. Sources: .

The bill removes workers’ approval check on tiring schedules that threaten safety at work and on the road.

Union rules normally give members a vote: “nearly all union constitutions and bylaws require union members’ ratification of collective bargaining agreements before they are signed and enforced.” A contract decided by a panel takes effect without that vote.
The panel can “impose wages, benefits, schedules, and workplace rules for years to come.”

Workers use approval votes to challenge such terms. The news station WDRB reported that workers at Conagra, a food company, “rejected a proposed labor contract” whose terms failed to address concerns about “forced overtime and double shifts” . The report describes an existing Teamsters union group and a 60-day “cooling-off period” . That points to talks to renew an existing contract, which the bill’s arbitration would not reach. The example shows how an approval vote works, not a vote the bill would skip.

The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), a U.S. agency, explains: “Work-related factors that can contribute to fatigue include scheduling practices, such as night shifts or extended hours, that can interfere with sleep.”

People report worse health after delays caused by cost. In the same survey, “two of five (41%) working-age adults who reported a cost-related delay in their care said a health problem had worsened because of it.”
Skipping workers’ approval removes a check on binding health benefits they find too limited. [NAME] has a health reason to keep that check against costs that keep people from needed treatment.

The bill skips contract votes that make negotiators answer to union members who disagree.

Contract votes give members a way to question and reject terms. UAW Local 600, an autoworkers’ union, explains that members have “a very powerful right to ask questions about any resulting tentative agreement and vote it up or down as you wish with your co-workers.”

Rejection can send disputed issues back to bargaining: “If the tentative agreement is rejected, the union may demand that the employer resume bargaining to resolve the issue(s) causing member rejection” .

In cases sent to arbitration (a panel deciding the contract), the bill makes the panel’s decision binding without requiring a member approval vote: “such decision shall be binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years” .

Members can support a union and still oppose particular contract terms. Arbitration skips their existing way to refuse approval and press negotiators to answer their objections. [NAME]’s wish to listen to people who disagree gives a reason to keep that way open.

Choosing a panel member does not restore a vote on the resulting contract. The bill gives the union “one member selected by the individual or labor organization” ; the panel’s majority decides the terms.

In states that permit required bargaining fees, a contract can also make nonmembers pay for representation in order to keep their jobs. The U.S. Supreme Court describes agreements “requiring all employees in the bargaining unit to pay union dues as a condition of continued employment, whether or not the employees become union members.”

This payment concerns bargaining representation. The Court limits required nonmember charges to “only those fees necessary to finance collective-bargaining activities” . Federal law also protects state bans on agreements “prohibited by State or Territorial Law” .

An imposed contract with a lawful fee clause also makes workers pay for a bargaining voice they reject. Respect for dissent gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added burden on workers who choose not to join the union.
The argument about fees applies only in states permitting such fee clauses and only if a panel’s award contains one. The sources reviewed do not show a panel would include one.
This applies to the general duty to bargain, not only to first contracts. It does not remove the right of workers to vote a union out.
The argument treats a stronger bargaining role as acceptance of different people.
Existing law already requires employers and representatives to “meet at reasonable times and confer in good faith with respect to wages, hours, and other terms and conditions of employment” .

The bill adds a starting deadline: “Not later than 10 days after receiving a written request for collective bargaining” , which can be extended by agreement: “or within such further period as the parties agree upon” . The bill also extends the duty: “an employer's duty to collectively bargain shall continue absent decertification of the representative following an election conducted pursuant to section 9” .

The added rules concern when talks start and how long the representative keeps its bargaining role. Giving that representative a stronger role in negotiating work terms does not by itself show greater acceptance or understanding of different people. The argument moves between these meanings of being heard without defending the link. This response does not answer the separate step about cooperation across racial lines.

The argument’s own legal account calls an election “the preferred method for determining employees’ representational preferences.”

A signature is not always a worker’s final choice. Describing workers who signed conflicting petitions, labor lawyers explain that a secret ballot allows a final choice without others knowing it, “insulating them from retaliation from whichever side they fail to support.”

The election requirement checks the majority’s wishes through a private choice by workers, instead of leaving the employer to act on signatures. Just treatment includes protecting that choice for every worker. The argument shows that employer withdrawal can be quicker, but speed alone does not establish that confirming the majority’s wishes is unfair.

The bill risks jobs and income by letting outsiders set costs a business cannot sustain.

A panel can commit a business to costs it did not agree to. Representative Walberg, a member of Congress, warns: “Those contracts could mandate spending that small employers cannot sustain, threaten jobs, kill growth, and in some cases, shut businesses down entirely.”

The bill requires decisions to consider “the employer's financial status and prospects” . The risk lies in outsiders judging those finances and operations incorrectly. Labor lawyer Robert Steptoe warns: “Panel arbitrators may not understand the business” .

A mistaken first contract can shape later ones. Steptoe explains that imposed terms “would set the standard for all future contracts because of the difficulty of unwinding the many complex provisions that go into a collective bargaining agreement.”

Costs a business cannot sustain threaten workers’ jobs and small owners’ income. Losing that income harms families with little money saved and closes opportunities to earn a living. Concern for vulnerable people gives [NAME] a reason to resist this added risk.

At a real deadlock in talks, existing law gives the employer the “right to unilaterally implement its last, best, and final offer when the parties reach a good faith impasse.” The employer can choose the costs of the terms it puts into effect.

The bill removes that option by requiring employers “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” . A panel then chooses unresolved first-contract terms. The panel’s duty to weigh “the employer's financial status and prospects” does not tell the business what costs it will impose.

The ruling is “binding upon the parties for a period of 2 years” , but the arbitrators “have no set time to issue their award.” Those two years describe how long the ruling lasts, not when its costs become known.

The argument counts how long settled terms last without comparing the uncertainty of a panel’s choice and timing with the employer’s existing control over terms it puts into effect. The argument has not established more predictable labor costs, so its step to steadier investment and national economic activity lacks support.

The argument’s step from the power to appoint panel members to political selection rests on one advocate’s prediction.

Each side normally chooses a panel member, and the third seat remains “one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties” . The service fills “any members not selected” , so this power arises only when seats go unfilled.

The support for political selection is the statement that “there would likely be political pressure from presidential Administrations” . That passage gives no evidence about how such appointments are made.

The bill does give a federal agency those appointments. The further step, that those choices would turn on political views, is supported only by that prediction. This response does not show that such pressure would not occur.

The arbitrator code published by the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS), the U.S. mediation agency, lists honesty, integrity, impartiality and general competence as qualifications for arbitrators. It addresses voluntary arbitration and does not set rules for how an agency designates panel members. The sources reviewed document a 2025 executive order directing reductions at FMCS, which concerns staffing and not arbitrator selection. Sources: , .
The sources reviewed have no rules or record on how the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS) would designate panel members; the arbitrator code addresses voluntary arbitration.
The legal rulings do not establish the blanket legal defects the lawyers’ letters claim.

Hodges’s evidence concerns lawsuits seeking refunds of fees charged to nonmembers for union representation. Those claims “primarily seek retroactive application of Janus” . This means applying Janus, a U.S. Supreme Court ruling on fees for government workers, to fees already collected. That record concerns a different kind of lawsuit from challenges to contracts at private employers.

Government involvement alone does not make bargaining fees invalid. In the case Hanson, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld financial support for private railway bargaining and held that the requirement “does not violate either the First or the Fifth Amendments.”

The Janus ruling distinguishes bargaining with government employers from private workplaces: “In the public sector, core issues such as wages, pensions, and benefits are important political issues, but that is generally not so in the private sector.” The letters’ argument about government involvement does not resolve that difference.

The U.S. Supreme Court case Cedar Point does not say that every right for union representatives to enter a workplace takes property without payment. The Court separates access to closed property from “Limitations on how a business generally open to the public may treat individuals on the premises” . The legal result depends on the access granted and the place involved.

The fee and access rulings do not show the blanket legal defects the letters claim. This response does not answer the costs of hearings that do occur, or of lawsuits that use up resources even when they fail.
