exceptions.text: The evidence does not settle whether transgender women who train and compete keep the speed and power advantage this fairness argument needs.

The review says the effects on people who train are not known. GAHT means hormone treatment that matches gender identity: “the effects of GAHT on these parameters, or indeed athletic performance in transgender people who engage in training and competition, remain unknown.”
The review does not say whether the compared groups trained the same amount: “The levels of physical activity of the transwomen compared with cisgender women in the studies were not reported.”

A 2024 study measured athletes at one point in time and found mixed results. Compared with cisgender women athletes, transgender women athletes had “higher absolute handgrip strength” but “lower relative jump height” . Relative jump height takes body weight into account.

Strength kept by people who are not athletes does not show an advantage among trained athletes in a speed or power event. The one athlete study points in both directions. Its authors write: “Sports-specific studies are necessary to inform policy-making.” This response does not show that no advantage exists. It also does not address places without hormone limits.

A 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine systematic review (52 studies) reports pooled comparisons of transgender women and cisgender women as similar on relative lean mass, upper-body and lower-body strength and maximal oxygen consumption. The statistical ranges for those comparisons include zero (no difference), and certainty is rated low or very low. Its conclusion states higher lean mass with comparable fitness and calls the evidence mostly low certainty. A later correction removed three studies, added one and said the main conclusions were unchanged. These are averages for body composition and fitness. The text in this project's evidence collection reports no result by sport for absolute mass, speed, collisions or injuries. Sources: , .
The review came after the comparison date but before the evidence cutoff. Sources: , .

A 2026 review says: “Current evidence is mostly low certainty and has heterogenous quality but does not support theories of inherent athletic advantages for transgender women over cisgender.” These sources do not rule out an advantage in a particular sport.
Protecting a place does not by itself show that opportunity has become more equal. This reason depends on the fairness claim in Point 1.

The bill’s practice exception requires that “no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.”
Where a place is limited, the bill decides which student holds it. That shows who keeps the benefit. It does not show that this division of places is fairer.

The mental-health finding is about access to a good program: “Girls who play sport in positive environments report significantly lower levels of anxiety and depression than those who previously played or never played.”
The leadership finding is about benefits people connect to playing: “Half of women (48.6%) credit the skills acquired through sports for their leadership development.”

These benefits go to whoever holds the place. They do not answer who has a fair claim to it. This reason adds to [NAME]’s equal-opportunity concern only as far as the fairness claim in Point 1 holds. This response does not dispute that some female athletes would keep places and their benefits under the bill.
For students who have gone through male puberty, listing the benefits of a lost team place does not show that the eligibility rule denies equal opportunity.

Fair opportunity can require limits on who enters a sports category. In the Clark case, a court upheld keeping boys off a girls’ volleyball team because “due to average physiological differences, males would displace females to a substantial extent if they were allowed to compete for positions on the volleyball team.” The reason was a real difference affecting fair competition, not just that separate teams exist.

Having been eligible under a testosterone limit does not show equal competitive conditions. Reviewing physical traits after male puberty, researchers Hilton and Lundberg reported that “the muscular advantage enjoyed by transgender women is only minimally reduced when testosterone is suppressed.”

Equal opportunity requires a fair basis for eligibility, not keeping every existing route to scholarships, learning or admission. For these students, the argument must show why this boundary unfairly blocks comparable students. Naming benefits and affected identities does not supply that step.

This response depends on the disputed claim that an advantage remains. A 2026 review reports: “Current evidence is mostly low certainty and has heterogenous quality but does not support theories of inherent athletic advantages for transgender women over cisgender.”
This response does not reach students who have not gone through male puberty, sports where no advantage has been shown, or eligible girls deterred by uncertainty about intersex variations.
NCAA eligibility on the comparison date used sport-specific testosterone thresholds. NCAA is the main college sports organization. Sources: , .
The evidence does not establish that the bill would lead to bodily examinations or to sexual abuse resulting from them.
H.R.28 restricts participation in programs “designated for women or girls.” Its text adds no requirement for bodily examinations.

AP describes questions about records and knowledge: investigators sought “to find out who knew the girl was transgender and when and how her records were changed.” That account reports no bodily examination.
Florida’s birth-sex law gives a way to decide eligibility from records: a birth certificate is accepted if its sex statement “was filed at or near the time of the student's birth.”

The step to bodily examinations and sexual abuse rests on an organization’s warning, not on a documented case in this evidence. This response does not answer the documented privacy harms from records checks and interviews, or the disrupted schooling that followed.

Idaho's statute included a separate sex-dispute verification process, which the Ninth Circuit described as allowing gynecological exams. The same court reported that most states with categorical bans verified sex through a birth certificate. Sources: , .

The complaint explains the school’s religious objection to playing that game: “it would be affirming that sex is mutable, in violation of its beliefs.” Mutable means able to change. That explains the objection. It does not make meeting the school’s demand an act of accepting people across differences.

Accepting people despite disagreement does not mean adopting their demands about others. The UNESCO declaration on tolerance, an international statement, makes this clear: “It means that one is free to adhere to one's own convictions and accepts that others adhere to theirs.”

H.R.28 would make it unlawful for federally funded programs to allow “a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.” The same rule would apply across covered programs, whether or not anyone objects. The bill's definition rests on “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.”

The forfeit explains why the school wants a different rule for who may compete. It does not show why respecting these girls gives [NAME] a tolerance-based reason to impose that rule on other participants.

The training exception begins: “Nothing in this subsection shall be construed to prohibit” . The exception leaves shared training possible under stated conditions. It does not require any cooperation across differences.
Permission to train together does not supply the missing link between enforcing the objection and accepting people despite disagreement.
The cited study does not establish that the team places protected by the bill give practice in accepting different people.

The change the study reports from team play is that it “made players more collectivistic in response to a values questionnaire.” Collectivistic means putting the group’s goals first. The questionnaire’s example of that outlook was “I agree with Emily, learning to play as a team is more important.” That measures how much a player values team goals. Accepting people with different beliefs is a different outcome. The result neither shows nor rules out such acceptance.

The player’s statement, “I’m learning—I learn from my team—cooperation, tolerance, and patience.” , appears in an account of what she learned about how groups work. In the same passage she complains about team unity and says, “I think we need team bonding.”

The link from a team place to practice in accepting different people rests on one player’s brief use of the word tolerance, in a passage about team unity. This response does not dispute that she names tolerance as something she learned, or that the teams included players of many ethnic backgrounds.
The change the study measured over the season was toward collectivistic responses (putting the group's goals first). It did not measure acceptance of others. Sources: .

Accepting people across disagreements leaves room to disagree about rules. [NAME] can listen to a student, understand the student’s situation and accept the student while reaching a different view about team eligibility. The research defining this value says it concerns “accepting and understanding those with life-styles and beliefs different from one’s own.”

The bill sets a rule for sports eligibility: “For the purposes of this subsection, sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” A decision under that rule does not show how classmates regard or listen to the student.

Treating eligibility itself as acceptance assumes the point in question. This response does not answer the claims that exclusion reduces contact and team-linked chances to build understanding, adds stigma, or removes a school’s choice to include.
The one team-place example given does not show lost access to healthy exercise.
Starling “was bumped down to the JV team.” JV means junior varsity.
The report adds that “she was moved back up to the varsity cross-country team, only missing that one meet. ML remains on the team as well.” ML is the transgender runner in this report.
Starling kept access to school sports, and both runners ended up on the varsity team. Losing varsity status for one meet does not show less exercise or lost health benefits.

That research is about girls added to sports, while the example is about a girl who stayed active. The evidence given does not support the step from being moved down to exercising less. This response does not address a girl cut from a team with limited places and no other place to play.
The inference for a girl with no other team is the argument's own reasoning. The example itself shows a girl who stayed active.
The bill limits its new definition of sex to “the purposes of this subsection” .
The bill's definition of athletic activities “includes, but is not limited to, all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.”

Representative Walberg quotes Gaines describing the exposure: “that man walked into the women's locker room at your university and saw me undress down to full nudity.” A locker room is a room for changing clothes.

That account does not show that access depended on team participation, or that the shared changing was itself a covered athletic activity. A room’s connection to sports does not establish the condition this legal argument needs. This response does not address the separate point that a person excluded from female competition would no longer have that competition as a reason to use its changing area.
Idaho’s separate medical-testing rule does not establish that H.R.28 would expose girls to intrusive exams.

H.R.28 defines sex by “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” without ordering medical inspections. The House member managing the bill described the intended method: “There is no requirement for inspections, and there is no necessary effort other than going to a person's birth certificate.”

The Idaho court tied intrusive checks to that state’s separate “sex dispute verification provision” . It also reported: “Most states that have instituted categorical bans on transgender participation in student athletics have verified sex via a student’s birth certificate.”

The argument’s own court source gives a working alternative to intrusive exams under comparable restrictions. Idaho shows that a legislature can choose exams, but it does not show that schools under H.R.28 would choose them over records. The claims of exam-related abuse and trauma depend on that step. This response does not address questions based on records, or fear and withdrawal caused by the possibility of challenges.

exceptions.text: The bill allows males to practice with a female team only if “no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport” . A roster spot is a place on a team.

Being on a team can give people an organized way to remove pollution. Fordham University rower Caitlin Boyle reported: “In the cleanup, 50 of my teammates on Fordham Rowing assisted me with picking up trash along the shores and streets of City Island in bags and then disposing of the waste properly.”
These projects can also teach people. Boyle wrote: “Additionally, I held a presentation for the team educating them on basic environmental knowledge and the importance of proper waste management.”

Teammates can help start larger efforts. University of Wisconsin rower Grace Latz said: “I started all of this because my teammates were taking similar classes to me and shared the same values, so it made it easier.”

The recycling group Latz helped start, called REthink, later reached other parts of the university: “Since then, REthink has expanded beyond the UW athletic department to work with the UW campus, the hospital, the Wisconsin unions, dining services and UW housing.”

Protecting female athletes’ places on teams that do this work also protects their access to cleanups, environmental teaching and larger recycling projects. [NAME] wants to defend nature, and keeping these ways of doing so gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.
The bill’s condition for male practice also protects a female athlete’s “opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” .

Rowing, a sport of racing boats with oars, lets athletes see the waters they use. University of Wisconsin rower Alexandra Bogner said: “I’ve rowed on both Lake Mendota and Lake Monona and have been able to see the ecological challenges that they face” .

Seeing litter while rowing helped lead Boyle to study waste management in schools: “Rowing on Long Island further inspired this thesis due to the plethora of trash that is floating around in the ocean.”
Practice also gave Boyle chances to act: “For the past four years, I have tried to grab every piece of waste out of the ocean at practice that I can reach.”

Protecting female rowers from losing practice time keeps open a path from seeing pollution to removing litter and studying ways to reduce waste. That serves [NAME]’s wish to care for nature and protect it from pollution.
The bill allows males to train or practice with a female team only if no female loses a “scholarship” . A scholarship is money that helps pay for college.

Money for athletes can support students doing environmental work. The University of Notre Dame described rower Anna Kottkamp as “an environmental science major” who “went on to earn a full athletic scholarship.”
Kottkamp was “an undergraduate research assistant for Jennifer Tank” , studying “the impact of cover crops on agricultural streams.” Cover crops are plants grown between main farm crops.

Tank’s research tests ways to protect water from pollution: “Her research combines the wide-scale planting of cover crops in winter with innovative drainage strategies that can reduce fertilizer runoff to streams and rivers.”

Protecting athletic scholarships for female students doing this work protects money for learning how to prevent water pollution. Supporting that way to protect nature gives [NAME] a further reason to favor the bill.

Women’s school teams compete in natural places. At a cleanup of the Malden River with the Tufts University women’s rowing team, an athletics coordinator explained that “our rowing athletes train and compete on it almost every day.”

On January 14, 2025, rules of the NCAA, the main college sports organization, could allow transgender women onto women’s teams: “Between January 19, 2022, and February 6, 2025, the NCAA called for the participation of transgender athletes to be regulated on a sport-by-sport basis.” Transgender women are people classified male at birth who identify as women.

Outdoor activities can strengthen concern for the environment. A study followed teenagers at a 15-day outdoor camp. Affective beliefs are feelings about the environment. The study reported: “Pairwise comparisons for affective beliefs revealed that scores for the experimental group increased after the intervention (p < .01), whereas scores for the control group underwent no significant change.”

College sailing gives a real example. Harvard University describes one sailor’s wish to protect the environment: “It's that time in the water with her teammates that has driven Hogan-Lopez to learn more about the environment and how to protect it.”

The ban would remove women’s outdoor competition from the choices open to transgender students who were otherwise eligible. It would end competition’s time in nature and shared experiences as a way for them to build that care.
The exception that lets students “train or practice” does not give back access to competition.
[NAME]’s concern for nature gives [NAME] a reason to keep this way of developing care for it, and therefore to oppose the bill.

Yale University places environmental leaders inside individual teams: “each participating varsity and club team has a sustainability captain. That person leads the efforts within their team and tailors the certification program to the schedule and structure of their team.” A varsity team is a school’s top team.

These positions include a “sustainability captain of the varsity women’s swimming and diving team” . That captain described practical care for nature: “We volunteered together at a New Haven Land Trust garden last year and performed manual labor to prepare for spring planting.”

On January 14, 2025, rules of the NCAA, the main college sports organization, could allow transgender women onto such teams: “Between January 19, 2022, and February 6, 2025, the NCAA called for the participation of transgender athletes to be regulated on a sport-by-sport basis.”

Team service also removes pollution and leads people to sign up for more conservation work. At the Tufts University cleanup, “Participants collected 33 bags of trash, which included 16 bags of sorted single use plastic bottles (over 1500 bottles)!” and “many students signed up to continue to be involved with the Friends of the Malden River.”
A position leading a women’s team’s environmental work is an opportunity tied to being on that team. It is also a way to bring teammates into practical care for nature.
The bill expressly covers “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” Conditional upon participation means open only to people on the team.
The bill's exception lets students “train or practice” . It does not protect a separate environmental leadership position inside a women’s program.
The bill would restrict access to these positions for otherwise eligible students it excludes from women’s programs. That ends a way for those students to organize practical care for nature.
[NAME] values taking part in defending nature. Keeping these chances to lead environmental work open gives [NAME] a separate reason to oppose the bill.
Male puberty builds strength. Testosterone is a hormone, and a review of research explains that “increases in testosterone due to puberty promote muscular strength” .

The review looked at 24 studies of transgender women who were not athletes. Here, transgender women are people classified male at birth who identify as women. After 12 to 36 months of hormone treatment, the review said: “transwomen likely retain a strength advantage over cisgender women.” Cisgender women are women whose gender identity matches their sex at birth.

Strength matters in speed and power events: “In sports demanding speed and power, muscular strength and the ability to generate high rates of force are recognised as key determinant in athletic success.”

In events that depend on strength, the bill would keep strength advantages retained from male puberty out of the female category. Giving women a real chance to earn sports rewards serves [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunity and just treatment.

Former college swimmer Paula Scanlan told a House committee that places were actually lost: “I know women who have lost roster spots and spots on the podium.” A roster spot is a place on a team. A podium spot is a top finish in a race.

The bill allows male training or practice only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.”

Where places or sports money are limited, the competition ban and the practice condition protect female athletes from losing them to male participants. For a girl who needs sports money to attend college, protecting that money keeps open a way into education.

A 2024 survey of U.S. adults who had played girls’ or women’s sports found reported gains in leadership skills: “Half of women (48.6%) credit the skills acquired through sports for their leadership development.”

Keeping a girl’s place in a good program keeps her chance to gain these benefits. Protecting these ways into education, well-being and adult leadership serves [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities in life.

World Rugby, the international body for the contact sport of rugby, links risk in that sport to “the size, force- and power-producing advantages conferred by testosterone during puberty and adolescence, and the resultant player welfare risks this creates” .

World Rugby's review explains the danger to a smaller player: “Forces and inertia faced by a smaller and slower player during frequent collisions are significantly greater when in contact with a much larger, faster player.”

World Rugby’s review of 12 months of lowering testosterone, a hormone, concludes that “this comparatively small effect of testosterone reduction allows substantial and meaningful differences to remain.”

In school contact competition such as rugby, excluding male competitors who have gone through male puberty removes this source of size and force mismatch. That protects athletes who are less able to withstand those forces.

Safety concerns have also cost whole teams games. After Payton McNabb was injured playing volleyball in 2022, her school board voted “to forfeit the remaining varsity and junior varsity volleyball games against Highlands School” , which the report describes as “attended by the transgender player.” To forfeit means to give up a game. The report says: “The board cited safety concerns for players.” That player’s status is not confirmed: “It is not possible to verify this athlete was trans.”

Where covered competition would otherwise include male competitors, the bill also removes that reason for a school to pull out its girls’ team. Protecting athletes from added collision risks and removing that ground for giving up games serves [NAME]’s concern for the weak and vulnerable, including girls [NAME] does not know.

Being on a team also brings educational chances. The bill itself names “scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.”

The ban reaches beyond games to “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” Conditional upon participation means open only to people on the team.

The same birth-based rule also restricts nonbinary students it classifies as male. Nonbinary students do not identify only as girls or boys. The Congressional Equality Caucus, a group of members of Congress, explains: “It would also limit the ability of non-binary and intersex students to participate in these programs as well.”

Girls born with variations in sex traits, called intersex variations, also face uncertain eligibility. The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn: “There is no principled way to apply the bill's unclear language to the many girls and young women born with intersex variations” . They describe the result: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.”

Blocking team competition and the activities tied to it takes away chances to learn and advance. [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities includes transgender, nonbinary and intersex students, which gives a reason to oppose these barriers.

Permission for “males to train or practice” gives back neither eligibility to compete nor equal access to team places and benefits. Even practice is conditional: it is allowed only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport” , among other protected opportunities.
The rule does not change by age or sport. One House member said: “this bill is a blanket ban that treats every age student in every sport the same.”

On January 14, 2025, the law of the Fourth Circuit, a federal appeals court, protected one individual girl’s participation in the states that court covers. Across the country, “Courts have reached different conclusions” . In its April 2024 B.P.J. decision, that court noted that puberty-blocking treatment meant “B.P.J. has never experienced elevated levels of circulating testosterone.” Testosterone is a hormone.

The court held that applying West Virginia’s ban would “treat her worse than people to whom she is similarly situated, deprive her of any meaningful athletic opportunities, and do so on the basis of sex.” Similarly situated means in a comparable position.

H.R.28 would make birth sex decide the question even in cases where a court had held, under the law then in force, that exclusion treated an individual girl worse than comparable students. Replacing that protection under Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education, with a duty to exclude conflicts with treating everyone justly. That gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.

The CDC, the federal public-health agency, did a national survey of high school students in 2023. Compared with other students, transgender students and those unsure whether they are transgender had more distress and less belonging: “Transgender and questioning students experienced a higher prevalence of violence, poor mental health, suicidal thoughts and behaviors, and unstable housing, and a lower prevalence of school connectedness than their cisgender peers.” Cisgender peers are students whose gender matches their sex at birth.

School sports offer health and belonging: “Sports participation is linked to increased academic achievement and fosters in students increased emotional, mental, and physical well-being and a sense of community.”

Denying team membership also marks students as outsiders. The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights describes that exclusion as “further isolating and stigmatizing these youth.” Stigma means shame or disapproval attached to a group.
Taking away this source of support while adding stigma burdens students who already need protection. [NAME]’s concern for vulnerable people gives a reason to oppose that harm.

A boys’ team is not a safe replacement for every excluded girl. In B.P.J.’s case, a federal appeals court explained: “By participating on boys teams, B.P.J. would be sharing the field with boys who are larger, stronger, and faster than her because of the elevated levels of circulating testosterone she lacks.” Testosterone is a hormone, and B.P.J. had taken puberty-blocking treatment.

The court named the resulting risk: “It also would expose B.P.J. to the same risk of unfair competition—and, in some sports, physical danger—from which the defendants claim to be shielding cisgender girls.” Cisgender girls are girls whose gender matches their sex at birth.

H.R.28 removes eligibility for girls’ teams even in these circumstances. For girls who want to keep competing on a sex-separated school team, the other choice brings this added danger. Protecting vulnerable students gives [NAME] a reason to oppose moving that risk onto them.

Schools must apply the rule without a set way to check it. Representative Hayes says: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.”

A comparable ban in Florida led to questions about a child’s private history. The Associated Press (AP) reported: “They interviewed officials at Monarch and at the daughter's middle and elementary schools, seeking to find out who knew the girl was transgender and when and how her records were changed.”

The investigation also asked teammates about her body: “When investigators interviewed the Monarch volleyball players, they said the team did not change clothes or shower together, so they were never disrobed with Norton's daughter.” Disrobed means undressed.
After the investigation began, the girl left the school. AP reported: “That all ended when the investigation began and the girl left Monarch.” It added: “The girl now attends school online.”

Women’s rights organizations warn that checking sex may involve “forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” . They name a further danger: “These procedures make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” .

A nationwide duty to enforce birth-sex eligibility creates grounds for the same kind of intrusive questions, with risks of exposure, humiliation and disrupted schooling and, as those organizations warn, abuse. Protecting children from these harms gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the rule.

A supporter replies: “There is no requirement for inspections” . That does not answer the risk. The documented records checks and interviews already invaded privacy, and they did not need an exam requirement.

Enforcing birth-sex eligibility invites suspicion of girls who do not fit stereotypes. Women’s rights organizations warn that checking practices “are especially likely to be used to target Black and brown women and girls who do not conform to white ideals of femininity, other women and girls who do not conform to sexist stereotypes, and nonbinary and gender nonconforming students.”

Such accusations have harmed girls who are not transgender. The same letter describes a Utah basketball player targeted for short hair and baggy clothes: “As a result, the student was subjected to harassment, bullying, and threats of violence, necessitating police protection for her and her family.”

Utah’s state school board, in its own official record, confirmed harm from the public accusation, recording “harassment, intimidation, humiliation” . Public accusations themselves expose children to abuse.

Extending this eligibility rule nationwide exposes students to harassment for their appearance and, as those organizations warn, to unequal checking tied to race and gender stereotypes. That conflicts with treating everyone justly and protecting vulnerable children.

Facing accusations, threats or humiliating checks also makes it harder to play for girls who remain eligible. [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities gives a further reason to oppose this effect of enforcing the rule.

The bill makes inclusion a new violation of Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education: “It shall be a violation of subsection (a) for a recipient of Federal financial assistance” to allow the participation it bars. A recipient is a school or college that receives federal money.

Existing enforcement law allows “the termination of or refusal to grant or to continue assistance under such program or activity” after an “express finding on the record, after opportunity for hearing, of a failure to comply with such requirement” . It also requires a finding “that compliance cannot be secured by voluntary means.” So money can be stopped only after a hearing, a formal finding and a failed attempt to get voluntary compliance.

That money supports education beyond the individual athlete. The Congressional Research Service (CRS), Congress’s research office, explains: “The Department of Education (ED) distributes substantial funding to elementary, secondary, and postsecondary institutions” .

Schools that keep including these students would put money for the affected program at risk, which could also harm other students. [NAME]’s concern for students’ equal opportunities gives a reason to oppose making inclusion grounds for withdrawing that support.

This kind of objection has led a team to give up a game: “A Vermont Christian high school forfeited a girls basketball game because the opposing team had a transgender player, the head of school said.” To forfeit means to give up a game.

The school’s court complaint explains the religious basis of its objection: “sex is immutable.” Immutable means it cannot change. The complaint says that playing that game would affirm the opposite, “in violation of its beliefs.”
In covered girls’ competitions, the bill removes the matchup that causes this objection. Girls with that belief can compete without giving it up.
Accepting people despite disagreement includes accepting girls whose religious or other beliefs differ from [NAME]’s. Keeping a way for them to play puts that acceptance into practice.
[NAME] has a reason grounded in tolerance to favor removing this cost of disagreement.

There is also room to cooperate across the competition rule. The bill allows “males to train or practice with an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls” if no female loses a place, opportunity, scholarship, admission or other sports benefit. Shared training remains a way to work together across differences.

The competition rule prevents male competitors from taking female team places. Even shared training is allowed only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” , among other protected benefits. A roster spot is a place on a team.

Girls’ teams can offer a setting for learning to work with different people. A player in a study of two high school teams with players of many ethnic backgrounds described her own learning: “I’m learning—I learn from my team—cooperation, tolerance, and patience.”
Protecting girls from this loss of places and practice keeps their access to those shared learning experiences.
[NAME]’s wish for people to listen to, understand and accept others gives a reason to protect girls’ chances to practice those habits with teammates.

On January 14, 2025, Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education, protected participation in at least some cases. In a 2024 case, “The Fourth Circuit ruled that application of the West Virginia law to the plaintiff violated Title IX, because it treated her worse than those similarly situated based on her sex and caused her harm.” The Fourth Circuit is a federal appeals court. Similarly situated means in a comparable position.

Differences between individuals mattered to that ruling. The court criticized a ban that applied “regardless of whether a particular student has any genuine athletic advantages” . H.R.28 would instead make birth biology and genetics decide the question for every student it classifies as male.

[NAME] values accepting people even when they disagree. That gives weight to including a classmate despite disagreement about that classmate’s gender, and to hearing the student’s situation before ruling the student out.

The bill would close a path to acceptance that the law then in force protected. Hearing individual students, or choosing inclusion as a school community, could no longer change eligibility under its birth-based rule.
The restriction also reaches activities tied to team membership. The bill includes “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.”
Shared sports offer chances to know people. Researchers describe “regular social interaction; opportunities to build positive relationships with teammates and coaches” .

Exclusion also marks students as outsiders. The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights warns that “denying transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth the chance to participate only serves to deny them an opportunity to be part of that community, further isolating and stigmatizing these youth.” Stigma means shame or disapproval attached to a group.
The limited permission for “males to train or practice” does not give back eligibility to compete on girls’ and women’s teams.

Required exclusion takes away shared competition and team-linked chances to build understanding, while adding to stigma against these classmates. [NAME]’s wish to accept and understand different people gives a reason to keep those chances and resist that treatment.

Intersex variations are differences in sex traits. The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn: “There is no principled way to apply the bill's unclear language to the many girls and young women born with intersex variations” .

These groups report exclusion under comparable rules: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” Chilled means made people afraid to take part.
Accepting all kinds of people includes accepting people born with different bodies. Their sex traits give [NAME] a reason to make room for them in shared school life.
Exposing these girls to exclusion because their bodies do not fit a simple birth-based test conflicts with that acceptance. [NAME] has a reason to oppose this risk.

Schools would have to follow a rule that makes birth sex decide eligibility. The bill applies to “a recipient of Federal financial assistance who operates, sponsors, or facilitates athletic programs or activities” . A recipient is a school or college that receives federal money.
Where schools have included transgender girls, the bill would make a claim that a girl was born male a basis to challenge her eligibility. This gives such accusations a path to exclusion.

That path has already been used under Utah’s rules for school sports eligibility. The Associated Press (AP) reported that Utah’s athletics association “secretly investigated a female athlete — without telling her or her parents — after receiving complaints from the parents of two girls she had defeated in competition questioning whether the girl was transgender.” The complaint was “among several the association had looked into in its efforts to comply with the Utah law” .

Public accusations can also bring harassment. In a separate 2024 case, Utah’s state school board found that a member’s post suggested “that one of the female students in the picture may not be female” . The board recorded “harassment, intimidation, humiliation” resulting from the post and comments.

Girls who look different face a particular risk. Women’s rights and sports groups warn that sex checks are “especially likely to be used to target Black and brown women and girls who do not conform to white ideals of femininity” .
The House member managing the bill says: “There is no requirement for inspections” . Sex challenges and public accusations do not require physical exams.

The bill creates grounds for exclusion that can turn differences in bodies, appearance and gender expression into reasons for suspicion and harassment. [NAME]’s tolerance toward different people gives a reason to oppose that risk, including, as those groups warn, an added risk for girls of color.

Rules based on hormones allowed these matchups in U.S. college sports. Testosterone is a hormone. May 2024 rules of the NCAA, the main college sports organization, included women’s rugby and stated: “Total serum testosterone thresholds apply to any transgender woman competing on an NCAA women’s team.” A threshold is a limit. Transgender women are people classified male at birth who identify as women.

A review of studies of transgender women who were not athletes found higher strength and muscle measures than in women who were female at birth, after hormone treatment: “values remain above that observed in cisgender women, even after 36 months.” Cisgender women are women whose gender identity matches their sex at birth.

World Rugby, the international body for the contact sport of rugby, links size and speed differences to injury: “When two opponents in a tackle are significantly different with respects to mass or speed, these risk factors increase significantly.” This passage is about risks of head and neck injury. A tackle is when one player stops another by force.
World Rugby's review of lowering testosterone concluded that “safety and fairness cannot presently be assured for women competing against transwomen in contact rugby.”

That conclusion was the basis for guidance about “the international level of the game” . World Rugby’s guidance does “not preclude national unions from flexibility in their application of the guidelines at the domestic/community level of the game” .
Where hormone-based rules allowed these matchups, H.R.28 would prevent them in covered female competitions. This removes the collision danger from those matchups.
Safer conditions for an ordinary way to exercise serve [NAME]’s wish to avoid injury and danger.

Limited team places can mean lost participation. ABC7 News reported that Taylor Starling was moved to the junior varsity (lower) team when a transgender runner joined a seven-place varsity (top) team, “causing Starling to miss a varsity cross-country meet.” After a complaint under Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education, she “was moved back up to the varsity cross-country team, only missing that one meet.”
The bill keeps female competition for those female at birth. It also makes male practice depend on protecting each female’s “opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” .
The bill prevents that source of exclusion from female competition and practice. Where a girl has no other team place, this keeps her chance to exercise on a team open.
The federal health department explains that sports “participation is one way for youth to get the physical activity they need to be fit and healthy.”
A U.S. study compared girls with boys during Title IX’s expansion of girls’ sports. It reported that the expansion “resulted in greater physical activity and improved weight and body mass.”
The CDC, the federal public-health agency, states that “regular physical activity prevents risk factors for various health conditions like heart disease, obesity, and type 2 diabetes.”
The CDC also reports that active young people have “stronger bones and muscles.” The brain-health benefits it lists include “reduced symptoms of depression.”
Keeping sports opportunities open protects a way to get exercise and its physical and mental health benefits. Protecting that way serves [NAME]’s wish to protect health and avoid disease.
The bill’s reach includes “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” Conditional upon participation means open only to people on the team.
A changing activity for women or girls that is open only because of team participation falls under the bill’s female-only rule.

Undressing with others against one’s wishes can damage a sense of security. Representative Walberg quoted swimmer Riley Gaines: “We did not give our consent to be exploited and exposed to a 6-foot-4 fully naked man.” She added: “You allowed college women to be traumatized” .
Applying the rule to those changing activities removes that path to unwanted shared undressing. Privacy in intimate settings supports feeling personally secure, which [NAME] values.
The bill sets a birth-sex rule but does not say how to check it. Representative Hayes noted that it provides “neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources” .

Idaho passed an intrusive rule for checking sex. The Ninth Circuit, a federal appeals court, described it as allowing “intrusive medical procedures to verify her sex, including gynecological exams” . A gynecological exam is a medical exam of female sex organs.
The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn that H.R.28 invites “invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” that “make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” .

Such checks also threaten mental health. The court explained: “The psychological burden of these searches falls not only on transgender women like Lindsay but also on all women and girls who play female athletics.”

Fear of checks also threatens participation. Representative Randall warned that intrusive questions and examinations would be “dissuading girls' participation in sports” . Dissuading means persuading people not to do something.

The new federal eligibility rule creates risks of bodily intrusion, abuse and distress in an ordinary school activity. By discouraging girls from playing, it also threatens the health benefits of exercise. Avoiding these dangers serves [NAME]’s aim to stay safe and healthy.
The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights warns that H.R.28 “will invite scrutiny and harassment of any other student perceived by anyone as not conforming to sex stereotypes” .

This kind of accusation has already put a girl in danger. After a Utah state school board member questioned a basketball player’s sex, the board found that her post “created a substantial risk of harm” .
The girl was not transgender. The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation report that the resulting threats required “police protection for her and her family” .

Making birth sex a federal condition for playing gives these accusations a new role in decisions about who can play. Threats against girls who are not transgender, and against their families, make this a safety concern in ordinary school sports. That gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
The ban reaches ordinary school sports as well as top-level competition. As Representative Bonamici explained: “this bill applies to every student of every age in every sport the same way” .
Federal health guidance links youth sports with “Increased physical activity levels” and physical activity with “Reduced risk of cancer and diabetes” .
A Colorado survey linked playing on three or more sports teams, compared with none, to “reduced likelihood of depression” among transgender students.

Sports also provide supportive relationships. The study cites research showing that “increased social support in adolescence, including that provided by team sports participation, protects against depression” .
The bill’s conditional permission “to train or practice” leaves the competition ban in place.

Boys’ teams do not keep every excluded girl in sports. Transgender girls in a survey reported avoiding sports because they feared being “forced to play on a team or use a facility that does not align with their gender identity” .

Leaving sports also risks losing a reason to see a doctor. In a study of health care providers who treat transgender youth, one warned that patients who no longer need sports exams “may miss health issues and immunizations due to not coming in” .

Closing access to competition removes a way to keep exercising and to have supportive relationships. For students pushed out of sports, it also puts sports-linked checkups at risk. Protecting physical and mental health gives [NAME] a reason to oppose these losses.

Denying students a place in school sports marks them as outsiders. The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights describes this as “further isolating and stigmatizing these youth” . Stigma means shame or disapproval attached to a group.

The effects may also reach teammates. A suggested advocacy letter from the American Psychological Association warns that “excluding any subset of girls from sports can encourage divisiveness and compromise group cohesion, undermining the benefits all youth deserve from team sports” .

Supportive school relationships matter for health. A research review by the CDC, the federal public-health agency, describes school communities “lessening emotional distress, anxiety, and depression” .

The law’s rejection of some students threatens the supportive school ties that protect mental health, even when no one leaves a sport. Protecting health in everyday school life gives [NAME] another reason to oppose the bill.

The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights warns that H.R.28 “will invite scrutiny and harassment of any other student perceived by anyone as not conforming to sex stereotypes” . The risk reaches girls whose bodies or appearance cause suspicion, whether they are transgender or not.

Such accusations already threaten school safety. The Salt Lake Tribune newspaper reported: “A Utah high school student needs police protection after a state school board member publicly singled out and suggested the student was transgender — without evidence — inciting threats from her followers on social media.”

Hostility aimed at a group can frighten a whole community. The U.S. Justice Department explains this wider harm when discussing hate crimes: “They represent an attack not just on the individual victim, but on the victim's community.”

Extending birth-sex eligibility rules to federally funded schools nationwide creates more occasions for this kind of intimidation. Protecting citizens and their communities from threats gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.

Requiring transgender students to play on teams based on sex at birth drives some out of sports. A 2025 study summarizes earlier research: “policies requiring youth to play on teams with their assigned sex, dissuade youth from participating” . To dissuade means to persuade people not to do something.

The loss also reaches girls born with variations in sex traits, often called intersex variations. Women’s sports organizations report: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” Chilled means made people afraid to take part.
The conditional practice exception allows “males to train or practice” . It guarantees no place in practice and leaves the competition ban in place.
Where schools now include them, the bill cuts off a way into sports for students it excludes or discourages.

Sports also provide a setting linked to less use of illegal drugs. A review of 17 studies that followed young people over time reports: “Sport participation was associated with reduced illicit drug use during adolescence.” Associated means the two happen together. It does not by itself prove cause.
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) describes organized sports as a tool for preventing violence: “Research shows that organized sport participation can reduce youth violence” .

School sports build community ties. The civil rights coalition explains that “School athletics are very often the centerpiece of communities across the country” and that exclusion means “further isolating and stigmatizing these youth.” HHS links sports with “Improved teamwork, social skills, and social responsibility” .
Community ties are connected with public safety. The U.S. Surgeon General, a top federal health official, links stronger community ties with “lower levels of community violence” .

Exclusion closes a way to cooperation, community ties, less illegal drug use and, as HHS describes it, violence prevention. Keeping those forms of protection helps the United States protect its people. That serves [NAME]’s goal of a secure, stable country.
The bill uses that distinction for female sports eligibility: “sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.”
The bill makes a public sports rule follow the understanding of sex [NAME] wants to maintain.
The same faith statement says: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” .
The Family Research Council, a Christian advocacy group, tells Christian parents to teach that “God created each of us either male or female” .

Using birth sex for sports eligibility makes that public practice follow the male-and-female understanding parents are told to pass down. The bill does not control classroom teaching. The connection claimed is that the sports rule is consistent with that particular inherited belief.

Separate school sports have a long legal history: “Long-standing Title IX regulations permit separation of the sexes in school sports programs provided schools offer equal athletic opportunities.” Title IX is the federal law against sex discrimination in education.

The Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission, a Southern Baptist agency, names the cultural practice it wants to keep: “Maintaining separate categories for males and females is essential to preserve the integrity and essence of women’s sports.”
Keeping female competition and its titles for female athletes preserves this form of women’s sports. [NAME]’s wish to honor cultural practices supports keeping it.

The January court ruling did not create the bill’s national requirement. The Congressional Research Service (CRS), Congress’s research office, says of the 2024 Title IX regulations that “a federal district court vacated them in January 2025.” Vacated means canceled. That removed the 2024 regulations. The older sports rule quoted above permitted separate teams. H.R.28 would add an express requirement to exclude male competitors from female sports.

The Southern Baptist Convention, a large Christian denomination, teaches that “parents are the primary stewards of and decision-makers for their children, rather than teachers, doctors, or the state” . A steward is someone responsible for caring for something.
Catholic teaching protects work that smaller groups can do themselves. It calls it an injustice to “assign to a greater and higher association what lesser and subordinate organizations can do.”

Sports rules are already partly a local responsibility: “Currently, schools, parents, and communities manage youth sports leagues and write rules about who can participate in different sports at different levels.”

Existing reviews of individual students already consider safety and fairness. The Congressional Research Service describes Illinois’s 2024–25 rules as “requiring approval to participate based on consideration of individual circumstances” and as considering whether “allowing eligibility would be inconsistent with concepts of fairness in competition or present a risk of injury to the participants” .

H.R.28 would remove that choice at covered schools. As Representative Norcross explained: “It inflicts blanket bans without the ability of states, local governments, schools, and parents to make reasonable exceptions.”

Even when parents and a willing school approve a child’s participation after an individual review, the federal rule would bar girls’ competition if it classifies that child as male. Keeping the family and local roles taught by [NAME]’s tradition gives a reason to oppose that loss of authority.

Schools would have to apply the bill’s definition of sex, but it gives no way to check disputed eligibility. Representative Hayes says: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.”
Women’s sports organizations warn that resulting checks “may include forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” .

Questions about intimate matters have occurred under a comparable state ban. The National Women’s Law Center reports that a Florida investigation included “interviews with her teammates on if they saw her undressed.”

Applying the rule in schools that now allow participation would require them to settle disputes about sex eligibility. The Florida account documents intimate questions, and the organizations also warn of invasive checks. For [NAME], keeping the particular religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy supplies the Tradition connection. General safety and dignity are separate reasons.
