In its study of 2021 networks, KFF, a health research group, found: “On average, 27% of actively practicing physicians who submitted Medicare claims were not included in any Marketplace plan network offered to enrollees that year.”

This creates a problem for people changing coverage: “This means that people transitioning to a Marketplace plan from another coverage source may not have been able to find any plan that included their doctor.”

KFF’s 2023 survey found “adults with Marketplace coverage were more likely than those with employer-sponsored health insurance to report that a particular doctor or hospital they needed was not covered by their insurance (20% vs. 13%)” .

Those gaps affected care and health: “Among Marketplace enrollees who experienced this problem, 34% said that needed care was delayed, 34% said they were unable to get needed care, and 25% experienced a decline in health status.”
Replacing employer coverage with Marketplace coverage risks losing an established doctor and missing needed care. [NAME]’s wish to protect their health gives a reason to oppose that risk.
The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, projects for 2028: “2.1 million fewer people would have employment-based coverage.”

Standard Marketplace bronze and silver plans, which are lower and middle plan levels, leave patients paying a larger share of treatment costs than typical employer plans: “Plans typically cover between 60 percent and 70 percent of an enrollee’s health care expenses — less generous than most ESI plans, which usually cover 80 percent or more.” ESI means insurance through an employer.

The ACA’s extra help with deductibles and copayments ends above 250 percent of the federal poverty level: “However, CSR benefits disappear once income rises above 250 percent of FPL.” CSR means this extra help with treatment costs, and FPL means the federal poverty level. ACA means the Affordable Care Act.

Among plans studied in five regions, the cheapest bronze and silver plans “typically impose substantial financial barriers through high deductibles” . A deductible is the amount a patient pays before insurance starts paying for services subject to it.

Higher deductibles can lead patients to use less useful care. A study followed a firm “which required all of its employees to switch from an insurance plan that provided free health care to a non-linear, high deductible plan.” It found: “Consumers reduce quantities across the spectrum of health care services, including potentially valuable care (e.g. preventive services) and potentially wasteful care (e.g. imaging services).”
For workers moving into these plans without extra help with treatment costs, the bill’s coverage shift risks making illness harder to treat or prevent. [NAME] has a health reason to oppose that risk.
The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, projects for 2028: “2.1 million fewer people would have employment-based coverage.”

Employer benefits commonly include access to dental insurance. KFF, a health research group, reports: “According to the 2023 KFF Employer Health Benefits Survey, 90% of small firms and 94% of large firms offer dental insurance programs to their employees.”

As of the vote, adult dental care was outside the ACA’s required medical benefits: “adult dental care is currently prohibited by agency regulation from being considered an EHB in individual and small group plans.” EHB means a benefit those plans must cover. ACA means the Affordable Care Act.

Replacing lost dental benefits from an employer generally requires a separate payment that the restored credits do not cover: “adult enrollees must typically cover the full cost of premiums without subsidies.”

Cost blocks dental care. KFF reports: “37% of Marketplace Enrollees Reported Delaying or Forgoing Dental Care Due To Cost Barriers” . It explains: “Delaying needed dental care could lead to more serious health problems down the road.”

For people leaving employer dental benefits, subsidized Marketplace medical coverage leaves a separate bill to maintain dental protection. The bill’s shift away from employer coverage therefore creates a risk of gaps in dental care. Avoiding those gaps serves [NAME]’s wish to avoid disease.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, estimates that if the bill became law in January 2026, more people would be insured: “0.1 million in 2026, 3.0 million in 2027, 4.0 million in 2028, and 1.1 million in 2029, relative to current law.”

Coverage helps people get care. A study of previously uninsured adults eligible for Marketplace subsidies found “decreased barriers to medical care, increased the use of outpatient services and prescription drugs”.
Cost can make it harder to control the spread of disease. A computer-model study of COVID-19 states that “financial barriers to COVID-19 care delayed diagnosis and exacerbated transmission.”
Finding cases helps protect others: “COVID-19 testing allows case identification, initiation of isolation, contact tracing, and prompt treatment.”

By making coverage affordable for more people, the bill reduces a barrier to diagnosis and care. That strengthens outbreak control and protects people beyond those receiving the credits, advancing [NAME]’s concern for national protection against threats.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, estimates that if the bill became law in January 2026, more people would be insured: “0.1 million in 2026, 3.0 million in 2027, 4.0 million in 2028, and 1.1 million in 2029, relative to current law.”

A comparison of keeping and losing the larger credits links their loss to “lower revenue for health care providers and fewer services rendered” and an “increase in uncompensated care sought by the uninsured”. Uncompensated care means care for which providers are not paid.
Revenue losses at rural hospitals “could force hospitals to reduce costs by eliminating services that would affect all members of their community.”

Small rural hospitals “are called upon to respond to a wide range of emergency situations in their communities”. Their emergency plans cover natural disasters and “Terrorism and bioterrorism events – bombings, use of biological agents such as anthrax”.

Supporting payments for care helps preserve hospitals and services that emergency responders need. That protects the country’s response capacity during disasters and attacks, including care for residents with other insurance.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, estimates that if the bill became law in January 2026, more people would be insured: “0.1 million in 2026, 3.0 million in 2027, 4.0 million in 2028, and 1.1 million in 2029, relative to current law.”
Marketplace plans must “offer substance use disorders benefits at parity with medical and surgical benefits”, meaning comparable insurance protections for addiction treatment.

Insurance helps people reach treatment. A study identifies “Financial barriers such as lack of insurance coverage” as an obstacle. In its long-term study of Baltimore residents who injected drugs, private insurance “was associated with receipt of buprenorphine and having a regular source of medical care.” Buprenorphine is a medicine for opioid addiction.
Medicines for opioid addiction, including buprenorphine, have “proven effectiveness at reducing mortality risks.”

An earlier ACA study, covering states with and without Medicaid expansion (Medicaid is public insurance for people with low incomes), found: “Areas with higher uninsurance rates prior to the ACA saw larger reductions in opioid-related ED visits after the ACA took effect.” These are emergency department visits; the study found the effect emerged over several years. ACA means the Affordable Care Act.

The national health-security strategy says drug and alcohol addiction makes it harder for communities to withstand crises. Resilience means the ability to recover. It states: “Community resilience plays a significant role in national health security.”

Making treatment coverage more affordable strengthens the response to a deadly drug threat and supports communities’ ability to withstand further emergencies. Both serve [NAME]’s concern for a secure country.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, estimates that if the bill became law in January 2026, more people would be insured: “0.1 million in 2026, 3.0 million in 2027, 4.0 million in 2028, and 1.1 million in 2029, relative to current law.”

Research on the larger credits describes improved access to care, including “primary and preventive care visits”, which “can both help prevent and manage costly chronic diseases.” Chronic diseases are long-lasting illnesses.
These illnesses affect the wider economy. CDC researchers identify “lost productivity in the workforce” among their burdens. CDC is the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Supporting care that prevents and manages illness helps preserve people’s ability to work. That supports the country’s ability to produce goods and provide services, strengthening its stability.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, estimates that if the bill became law in January 2026, more people would be insured: “0.1 million in 2026, 3.0 million in 2027, 4.0 million in 2028, and 1.1 million in 2029, relative to current law.”
Coverage losses cut provider income: “Health care providers that lose revenue must reduce how much they can spend on their staff and goods purchased from vendors”.
The effects spread beyond health care: “Reductions in labor expenses mean that some jobs are lost and some staff may be paid less. Thus, staff must restrict their purchases of consumer goods”.
Restoring the credits supports payments to providers, workers, and suppliers, reducing a source of economic disruption across the country.
Falling incomes also weaken public finances: “The combined reductions in individual and business incomes inevitably lead to lower state and local tax revenues.”

The resulting budget pressure hinders public services: “This means that state and local governments will have more difficulties balancing their budgets and paying for health, human service, and other government functions.”
Supporting employment and incomes also protects the revenue governments use to serve residents. This chain supports both national stability and the state’s capacity to protect its people.

An analysis of the credits’ expiration links higher insurance bills for people who stay covered to less spending elsewhere: “This reduces their ability to purchase other goods and services, further dampening state economies.”

By lowering premiums for eligible policyholders, the bill preserves money for other purchases. That supports households and the businesses that depend on their spending, strengthening economic stability across the country.
Connecticut committed its own money to replace lost federal help before the January vote: “Connecticut allocated an additional $51 million after a November 2025 special legislative session”.

Filling that gap uses money that could go to other health protection. California and Colorado shifted state subsidies away from reducing deductibles and copayments to reducing premiums: “switching from a program that lowered out-of-pocket cost sharing (by reducing or eliminating deductibles and copayments) to one that lowers monthly premiums to help people purchase and maintain comprehensive coverage.”

Restoring federal help meets more of that premium need and reduces pressure on states to fund replacements. That protects states’ ability to use limited health funds for other needs, serving [NAME]’s concern for a capable state.

Job losses can remove health protection (a downturn is a period when the economy shrinks): “Because insurance coverage in the U.S. is closely tied to employment, economic downturns pose a serious threat to Americans’ access to affordable health care.”

People losing job-based coverage can use the Marketplace outside its yearly enrollment window. CMS, the agency running the federal Marketplace, explains: “You’ll have 60 days to enroll in a Marketplace plan from the time your coverage ends, which may or may not be the last day of employment.”

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, projects lower prices before tax credits for the plans used to set subsidy amounts in 2027–2029 because “on average, the people who enroll in the marketplaces would be healthier than would be the case” without the extension.

This wider sharing of medical costs benefits people without subsidies too: “Even those not eligible for PTCs see lower premiums with enhanced PTCs because the additional enrollment has improved the nongroup market risk pool.” PTCs are premium tax credits; a risk pool is the group whose medical costs insurance shares.

The bill makes an available route to coverage outside work more affordable, through larger credits and lower insurance prices. That helps the country absorb job losses without also losing as much health protection, strengthening its ability to withstand economic shocks.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, estimates the bill would add about $80.6 billion to deficits over 2026–2035; its table reports “80,582” in millions of dollars . A deficit is the gap between government spending and revenue. Deficits mean more federal borrowing.
More debt makes the government more exposed to interest costs. Debt-service costs are payments on debt: “the larger debt is, the more an increase in interest rates raises debt-service costs.”

CBO connects debt to limits on national protection: “Lawmakers might feel constrained from using federal tax and spending policies to respond to unforeseen events or for other purposes, such as to promote economic activity or strengthen national defense.”
CBO also warns of harm to the U.S. role abroad if lawmakers become “reluctant to increase spending to prepare for or respond to an international crisis” .

The bill adds debt and interest demands that put defense and crisis response under greater budget pressure. Preserving the state's ability to prepare for threats and defend citizens gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added pressure.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, estimates the bill would add about $80.6 billion to deficits over 2026–2035; its table reports “80,582” in millions of dollars . A deficit is the gap between government spending and revenue. Deficits mean more federal borrowing.

An August 2025 budget update from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a budget policy group, included the July budget law and new tariffs. It projected debt growing faster than national output: “Debt held by the public will rise from about 100 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) ($30 trillion) today to 120 percent of GDP ($53 trillion) by 2035.”

CBO explains the risk of that path: “The likelihood of a fiscal crisis would increase if federal debt continued to grow faster than GDP, because mounting debt could erode investors’ confidence in the U.S. government’s fiscal position.”

A loss of confidence would raise interest rates and lower the value of existing government bonds. CBO says losses to banks and other investors “could be large enough to cause some financial institutions to fail.”

The damage could spread as money becomes harder to borrow and banks lend less: “such a crisis could spread globally as liquidity declined and financial institutions reduced their lending, leading to an economic contraction.”
The bill adds to the debt burden behind this crisis risk. Protecting the country against financial breakdown and economic disruption gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added exposure.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, estimates the bill would add about $80.6 billion to deficits over 2026–2035; its table reports “80,582” in millions of dollars . A deficit is the gap between government spending and revenue. Deficits mean more federal borrowing.

Growing debt creates risks beyond a sudden crisis. Treasury securities are US government bonds. CBO identifies “a gradual decline in the value of Treasury securities and other domestic assets, heightened expectations of inflation, and a loss of confidence in the U.S. dollar as the dominant international reserve currency.” This includes the dollar's role as the main currency other countries hold in reserve.
CBO explains the funding consequence: “Such developments would make it more difficult to finance public and private activity.”
Adding debt adds risks to stable funding and financial influence that support U.S. security. [NAME]'s concern for a strong, secure country gives a reason to oppose those risks.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, estimates the bill would add about $80.6 billion to deficits over 2026–2035; its table reports “80,582” in millions of dollars . A deficit is the gap between government spending and revenue. Deficits mean more federal borrowing.
CBO explains the mechanism: “The increased federal borrowing associated with larger amounts of debt reduces the resources available for private investment.”
Less investment weakens production over time: “That reduction in private investment would slow economic growth.”
The bill's borrowing puts pressure on investment and production that sustain national defense. Protecting that economic foundation gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.

The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's budget office, estimates the bill would add about $80.6 billion to deficits over 2026–2035; its table reports “80,582” in millions of dollars . A deficit is the gap between government spending and revenue. Deficits mean more federal borrowing.

CBO identifies a separate cost of growing debt: “Rising interest costs associated with federal debt would drive up interest payments to foreign holders of that debt and thus decrease national income.”
The national security strategy identifies the economy as a source of resources for security: it “generates wealth we can invest in strategic interests” .

Added borrowing carries an income cost through interest paid abroad, beyond its effect on domestic investment. Retaining national resources that support the country's strength gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that cost.

The enhanced credits expand fully paid coverage for eligible low-income households: “The reduction in applicable percentages allows households with incomes between 100% and 150% of FPL to receive full subsidies, reducing consumers' premium contributions to zero dollars.” FPL means the federal poverty level.

CMS, the agency running the federal Marketplace, links this feature to abuse: “the widespread availability of $0 premium plans created the incentive and opportunity for fraudulent and improper enrollments at scale” .

Gaps in checks of people's income remained in the rules for 2026. CMS explained that a planned check was paused: “Income DMIs will not be opened for applicants when the Marketplace attempts to verify an applicant’s attested projected annual household income with the IRS, but the IRS returns no tax data.” A DMI (data matching issue) asks a person for more information when records do not match. The IRS is the US tax agency. That means missing tax records would not trigger this extra income check.

A November 2025 conviction shows an actual loss from organized enrollment fraud. The Justice Department reported a scheme seeking “over $233 million in fraudulent ACA plan subsidies for which the federal government paid at least $180 million.” ACA means the Affordable Care Act.

Restoring larger subsidies expands the money and incentives exposed to a proven fraud mechanism. A strong state must keep public resources from financing crime. [NAME] therefore has a reason to oppose this added exposure.

CMS, the agency running the federal Marketplace, explains how fully paid plans hide unauthorized signups: “Because these enrollees do not receive a monthly premium bill requiring action on their part, they may not be aware they are enrolled.”

A planned $5 charge on automatic renewal had been paused before the January vote. CMS stated: “Qualifying consumers will continue to be automatically re-enrolled with no premium responsibility following application of Advance Payments of the Premium Tax Credit (APTC).”

The Government Accountability Office (GAO), Congress's audit agency, reported how many unauthorized signups and switches were reported: CMS received “approximately 275,000 complaints between January and August 2024 that consumers were enrolled in a plan or had their plan changed without their consent.”

GAO explains that these practices can cause “loss of access to medical providers and medications” . The November 2025 conviction also established harm (Medicaid is public insurance for people with low incomes): “some of these consumers experienced serious disruptions in their medical care and often lost their prior insurance coverage under Medicaid or other programs.”

By expanding plans that hide unauthorized enrollment, the bill increases exposure to organized abuse that can interrupt care. Protecting citizens from that threat through a reliable national insurance system gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
Insurance costs compete with household needs. An enrollee warned that losing the larger credits would mean “digging into basic necessities, like, food, car, gas, rent.”

Caring for children at home is a practice valued by the religious right, meaning politically conservative Christians: The group Focus on the Family says: “Focus on the Family has always taken pains to express and provide support for mothers who choose to stay home with their young children.”
Focus on the Family connects that role to passing on faith: “God created us to have relationship with Him. The most effective place for us to learn that is not at church — it’s at home!”
For eligible families using ACA insurance on one wage, the bill lowers the cost of keeping a mother at home to care for children and teach the faith. ACA means the Affordable Care Act.

The income cutoff can penalize two people who qualify separately but cross the married cutoff when their incomes combine. The Heritage Foundation explains that “the FPL for a couple is less than twice that for a single person” . FPL means the poverty line used to set the cutoff.
The bill extends the “Rule To Allow Credit to Taxpayers Whose Household Income Exceeds 400 Percent of Poverty Line” .
For otherwise eligible couples whose insurance costs qualify for help above that limit, marrying no longer causes all aid to disappear merely because their combined income crosses it.

The comparison must also count what the couple would receive unmarried. Consider two childless adults, each with $46,950 in annual income counted for the credit: 300% of the “$15,650” one-person amount. Married, their $93,900 is 443% of the “$21,150” two-person amount, above the cutoff. Assume their plans stay the same, with benchmark premiums (the prices used to set the credit) totaling $20,000 a year. Under ordinary 2026 credits, the table reads “At least 300% but not more than 400% 9.96% 9.96%” , so they pay about $9,352 unmarried and the full $20,000 married: a $10,648 cost of marrying. Under the restored schedule, “300 | 0.0600” means about $5,634 unmarried, and “400 or more | 0.0850” means about $7,982 married: a $2,348 cost. For this couple the bill lowers the cost of marrying by about $8,300.
Reducing this financial obstacle for such couples supports the traditional practice of marriage.

Small churches use ACA coverage for staff: “Among the most affected are small congregations that usually can’t afford group plans and instead provide salary stipends to staff members for use in the ACA Marketplace” . ACA means the Affordable Care Act.

A Christian fund that helps clergy (religious leaders) said its planned emergency aid depended on the larger credits: “If Congress renews the subsidies at the 2025 levels, the program will not move forward.”
Restoring those credits eases the strain on pastoral families and churches that help pay their insurance costs.

The Southern Baptist confession, a statement of belief, makes regular giving a religious duty: “According to the Scriptures, Christians should contribute of their means cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally for the advancement of the Redeemer’s cause on earth.”

Higher insurance bills also leave less money for giving. Tithing means giving part of one's income to a church. A pastor reported: “Riverside Church is projecting 20% attendance growth but flat giving for 2026 as more dollars go to health insurance instead of tithing” .
Lower bills leave members more room to continue customary giving and support their congregation.
The Southern Baptist confession says Sunday observance should include “exercises of worship and spiritual devotion, both public and private.”
Easing these pressures on church budgets helps sustain the clergy, worship, and teaching through which congregations practice and pass on their faith.

The Catholic Health Association links lost coverage to unpaid care: “the loss of coverage would put additional stress on local health care providers as they face more uncompensated care and bad debt.” These are bills providers do not collect.

Church clinics also face added demand for free care. Reporting from Bread of Healing at Cross Lutheran Church explains: “They are bracing for higher demand as more residents are expected to forgo insurance as a crucial tax credit is set to expire and premiums spike.”

Catholic providers identify care for those in need as their religious mission: “Our health ministry is especially committed to serving those most in need, recognizing that our mission is not complete until quality, affordable, and accessible health care is a reality for all.”
Keeping more patients insured eases unpaid bills and the added demand for free care, helping Christian institutions carry on an established ministry.

In a 2003 statement on agriculture, U.S. Catholic bishops identify the threatened inheritance: “They are about a way of life for farm families in the United States who are unable to meet debt payments and face selling a farm that has been in the family for generations.” Here, “They” means food and agriculture.

The bishops defend preserving this life: “We stand with farmers, particularly those who own small and family farms here and abroad, in their struggle to live with dignity, to preserve a way of life, and to strengthen rural communities.”
Lower insurance costs leave farm families more money to meet farm debts, helping them keep the land and work through which they pass on family and rural customs.
Some states have “laws that require all fully-insured group plans and individual plans (including Marketplace plans) to include abortion coverage.”
The Southern Baptist confession, a statement of belief, directs believers to “speak on behalf of the unborn and contend for the sanctity of all human life from conception to natural death” .

Larger credits lower the price of entering plans with abortion benefits. For [NAME], continuing the particular religious rule against abortion supplies a reason to oppose making coverage of that practice easier to obtain. This justification concerns that religious observance, rather than a general appeal to protect vulnerable life.

Federal credits cannot pay the abortion portion of the premium beyond the rape, incest, and life-endangerment exceptions: “this coverage cannot be paid with federal dollars.” The objection concerns cheaper entry into plans that include those benefits.

The Catholic bishops object to paying for the plan itself: “federal taxpayer dollars are still paying for the plans that cover abortion” . Their October 2025 letter asks Congress to pair extension with a limit: “We urge Congress to extend the enhanced PTCs while amending all PTCs to disallow their being used for plans that cover elective abortion.” H.R.1834 contains no such limit. PTC means premium tax credit.

Larger credits increase public support for the plans these religious bodies reject. Preserving their rule against indirect support gives [NAME] a reason to oppose those added payments, regardless of whether abortion numbers rise.

Plans covering abortions beyond the federal exceptions for rape, incest or danger to life must collect an abortion-coverage payment of “at least $1 per enrollee per month” and keep these payments apart: “deposit these separate payments into segregated accounts” .

Where state law requires Marketplace plans to cover abortion, buying one includes that payment. KFF, a health research group, describes the mandate as covering “individual plans (including Marketplace plans)” .
Christian health-sharing ministries state the religious concern as getting care “without being forced to fund procedures or drugs that violate their conscience.”

Where every Marketplace option includes this charge, refusing it means giving up Marketplace aid. The bill increases the aid a believer must give up. Preserving the practice of refusing payments that violate religious teaching gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that pressure.

Washington’s required benefits still include this care: its benchmark plan, the model plan that sets required benefits, “requires individual and small group health plans to cover gender-affirming treatment.”
Southern Baptists teach that “gender identity is determined by biological sex and not by one’s self-perception” and declare that “we oppose efforts to alter one’s bodily identity” .
Cheaper enrollment opens access to these plans’ transition benefits. Maintaining this religious understanding of sex gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.

The 2026 federal rule makes the state pay the cost of the excluded benefit (defray means pay): “the state is required to defray the cost of the benefit.” Washington appropriated money “so that the benefit can continue to be offered.” Larger federal credits still make the plan carrying that state-funded benefit easier to buy.

Illinois includes in vitro fertilization (IVF), fertilizing eggs outside the body, in its required individual-plan benefits: “IVF and other fertility treatments are covered on individual and small-group plans” .
The Catholic bishops describe IVF as “joining egg and sperm in a glass dish, not in the mother’s body” .

The bishops' teaching draws the moral line at replacing the marital act: “procedures that assist the marital act in being procreative are morally acceptable, while those that substitute for it are not.”
Cheaper access to IVF expands access to a substitute for marital intercourse. Preserving this Catholic teaching on how spouses should conceive children gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.

Most private plans must “cover, without any cost sharing, the full range of FDA-approved contraceptives and services” . Covered birth control therefore comes without a separate patient charge under the rule.

Larger credits expand access to plans with these benefits. Within Catholic traditionalism, maintaining this teaching about married sex gives [NAME] a reason to oppose widening access to contraception for preventing pregnancy.

The credits pay for “health insurance obtained through the marketplaces established by the Affordable Care Act.” Health care sharing ministries (HCSMs) fall outside that insurance system: “HCSMs are not health insurance” .
For eligible buyers, subsidies can make Marketplace coverage “significantly less expensive than an HCSM membership” .

These ministries practice religious mutual aid: “Members affirm shared faith commitments and contribute to each other’s medical bills, supported by prayer and mutual encouragement.” Christian Healthcare Ministries links this practice to a Bible verse, “the command of Galatians 6:2” .

For households receiving larger credits, the bill cuts Marketplace payments while payments to a ministry receive no credit. This gives them a stronger financial reason to choose insurance instead of contributing through a ministry. Preserving the religious practice of sharing medical bills, giving, and prayer gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that added incentive.

Marriage combines the couple’s incomes for the credit. A joint return is one tax form for both spouses. The law requires that “the taxpayer and the taxpayer's spouse file a joint return for the taxable year.”

For 2026 coverage in the 48 contiguous states, the poverty-line amounts used for credits are “$15,650” for one person and “$21,150” for two. Two married adults therefore face a lower poverty-line amount than two separate one-person tax households.

The ordinary 2026 premium-share table reads: “At least 250% but less than 300% 8.44% 9.96% At least 300% but not more than 400% 9.96% 9.96%” . Thus the share is 8.44% at 250% of poverty and 9.96% at 369%.

The bill restores the enhanced schedule. Its table from the US tax agency (IRS) gives “250 | 0.0400” and “369 | 0.0773” : shares of 4% and 7.73%. To find the income percentage, IRS instructions say to “drop any numbers after the decimal point.”

Consider two childless adults, each with $39,125 in annual income counted for the credit. Compare being unmarried throughout 2026 with being married throughout 2026. They are otherwise eligible all year. Assume their plans and full premiums stay the same, with premiums high enough to receive credits. Separately, each is at 250% of poverty; married, their $78,250 is counted at 369%. Under ordinary 2026 credits, their combined annual premium share rises from about $6,604 to $7,794 when married—a $1,190 cost. Under the restored schedule, it rises from $3,130 to about $6,049—a $2,919 cost. The bill adds about $1,729 to this couple’s annual cost of being married rather than unmarried.

The Southern Baptist confession calls marriage “the uniting of one man and one woman in covenant commitment for a lifetime” and “the framework for intimate companionship, the channel of sexual expression according to biblical standards” .
Maintaining this marriage tradition gives [NAME] a reason to oppose increasing the money such couples lose by marrying.

Other Chinese charges would remain on U.S. farm goods: “certain U.S. agricultural products are also subject to Section 301 retaliatory tariffs” .

The DW article reports an EU Commission spokesperson saying the deal would have no impact on EU decarbonization targets. CNBC reports analysts doubt the $750 billion pledge is feasible. Sources: , , .

Replacement plans were announced before the vote. In a May interview transcribed in a June 2 court filing, trade adviser Peter Navarro said: “So you can assume that even if we lose we will do it another way.” Here, “lose” means lose in court. This was a stated plan to keep the tariff policy after losing its emergency-law basis.

An October 2025 analysis described a possible temporary step toward other tariff powers: “Five months of Section 122 tariffs would provide time for the Commerce Department to do the investigation required by Section 232 of the Trade Act of 1962 for a president to impose tariffs for national security reasons.” Using Section 122 would still have to meet the conditions in that law.

This Point adds a rule that the burden is unjust because the country contributes little to the total deficit. [NAME]’s concern for just treatment of people does not by itself establish that national trade shares determine the burdens individuals should bear.
The bill ends the emergency “declared on April 2, 2025, by the President in Executive Order 14257” . The bill's text does not end other tariff powers.

Commerce Secretary Lutnick had announced replacement action if the emergency tariff power were blocked: “we just bring on another or another or another.” In September 2025, Treasury Secretary Bessent again said, “And there are lots of other authorities that can be used - not as efficient, not as powerful,” . The stated plan to replace blocked tariffs gives firms a concrete policy to consider.
A seller's claim that a doll teaches Bible verses does not establish that the doll helps [NAME] pass on an accepted Christian tradition.

This Point supplies the maker's purpose, but no basis for placing this aid within the tradition [NAME] seeks to keep. Lower import costs for the doll do not supply that missing link between the product and following [NAME]'s religion.

Officials said the policy would continue another way. Trade adviser Navarro said: “So you can assume that even if we lose we will do it another way.” [UNC 13] Commerce Secretary Lutnick said: “we just bring on another or another or another.” [SES 11] An October 2025 analysis says other laws “could result in similar ends” [UNC 14] . So firms and markets could still face uncertainty about rates under other laws.

It says prices of goods like fruit and vegetables may be less sticky (less likely to stay high), and prices likely decline if demand had fallen. Sources: .
