exceptions.text: By September 2025, the basic import tax under this emergency had raised solar costs: “the baseline tariffs remained in effect and contributed to price increases across solar market segments” .

In April 2025, before the higher rate on China was suspended, an energy consultant listed imported storage and power equipment among the goods most affected: “Grid-scale batteries and solar panels, as well as power transformers, are among the hardest hit by price increases on imports” .

The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a research group, warned in April 2025 that the taxes would also raise the cost of building clean energy factories, because the taxes apply to imported materials and equipment such as “cement, construction equipment” .
Ending these extra taxes reduces a cost barrier to installing clean power and to building clean energy factories.
Making it easier to replace fossil fuels with clean power supports [NAME]'s goal of protecting nature from air pollution and warming.
Denver manufacturer Geotech makes tools for cleaning contaminated water: “So we make a product to remediate or get oil, gas and diesel out of groundwater.”

Geotech’s president, speaking about the tariffs, reports higher costs for imported parts: “It’s been reciprocal. So we're paying more for the components used to manufacture the product.” He uses “reciprocal” to mean tariffs raise costs in both directions: on parts Geotech imports and on products it exports.

Managing changing tariffs also takes time away from improving Geotech’s tools: “The time involved in managing the uncertainty is keeping us from focusing on creating innovative products for our customers and offering better service to our customers.”

Ending this emergency removes the emergency’s taxes and rate changes from the work of making these tools. Supporting the supply and improvement of tools that remove pollution gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.

An April water-industry report said utilities (the organizations that supply water) import pumps, membranes and treatment supplies: “The tariffs will make importing these items more expensive for utilities.”

Higher costs can delay treatment work. In May 2025, when Chinese goods faced a 145% rate that was later suspended, the city of Decatur, Arkansas, had received part of its water treatment supplies and was postponing the purchase of the rest: “it will wait as long as possible for the rest, until the tariff issue is resolved” .

An April 2025 industry warning said water reuse projects also depend on equipment exposed to these taxes: “Membrane-based reuse and desalination systems—already under pressure in California, Texas, Florida—are particularly exposed.”
Removing these extra taxes from treatment equipment leaves more project money for cleaning water and sustaining habitats. Both serve [NAME]'s aim of protecting nature.
Recycling relies on imported machinery: “Most of the sectors’ equipment comes from overseas, and high tariffs could hinder domestic recycling infrastructure buildout and rattle commodities markets.”

A July 2025 industry report identified a tax on recycling equipment from Europe: “Today they are subject to a 10 percent duty” . Here, “they” means equipment imported from the European Union, and a duty is an import tax.
The later tariff framework between the United States and the European Union (EU) still included “a reciprocal tariff” . “Reciprocal tariff” is the name for the taxes under this emergency.
Ending the emergency tax on recycling machinery covered by that tax lowers a barrier to expanding this work. Conserving resources and preventing waste give [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.

China imposed an extra tax in response to the April policy: “in response to the United States' 34% IEEPA "reciprocal tariff" on imports from China, China announced an additional 34% tariff on all U.S. goods” . IEEPA is the emergency powers law used for these taxes.

That April retaliation still applied when the Senate voted. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) records an extension “for another 90 days from August 12, 2025, while retaining the 10 percent tariff” .
China's charge has moved with U.S.-China talks. After negotiations in Geneva, it “suspended 24 percent of the 34 percent” charge.

The emergency also allows further U.S. tariff increases in response to retaliation: “Should any trading partner retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties on U.S. exports or other measures, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase or expand in scope the duties imposed under this order” . The HTSUS is the official U.S. list of import tax rates.

After the May 2025 tariff reductions, the research group Trase still identified a threat to Brazilian habitats: “there remains a risk that the surge in demand for Brazilian soy from China, resulting from the ongoing tensions, could increase deforestation and carbon emissions in Brazil.”

Ending the U.S. taxes behind that retaliation, and their possible increase under this emergency, removes one source of a trade conflict that puts habitats at risk. Ending those taxes also makes a matching tariff cut by China more plausible, though that remains China's choice. Protecting those habitats gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.
The September 2025 order tied tariff relief to “the scope and economic value of a trading partner’s commitments to the United States in its agreement on reciprocal trade” .

The EU tariff framework called for changes to companies' climate obligations: “to propose changes to the requirement for a harmonised civil liability regime for due diligence failures and to climate-transition-related obligations.” A civil liability regime is a set of rules that lets people bring legal claims against companies. Due diligence means checking for harm in a company's supply chain.

In October, a further U.S. negotiating proposal “would commit Brussels to dropping rules requiring American firms to produce plans to fight climate change and end environmental and human rights violations in their supply chains.” “Brussels” here means the EU government. The same report says “the Commission does not intend to act on the criticism in the document” . So this example shows pressure applied, not a change the EU agreed to make.
Ending the emergency takes away its import taxes as a tool for these demands. Defending rules against climate pollution and damage in supply chains serves [NAME]'s commitment to defend nature.
The EU tariff framework includes an energy purchase plan: “the European Union intends to procure US liquified natural gas, oil, and nuclear energy products” .

In August 2025, a trade analyst explained the continuing tariff pressure: “The key to keeping the EU-US trade deal on track will be demonstrating rising EU energy purchases and investments in the US” .

The gas purchases have a pollution cost even when they replace gas delivered by pipeline. Chatham House researcher Chris Aylett explained: “Swapping pipeline gas for American LNG would further increase Europe's emissions” . LNG means gas cooled into liquid for shipping.
The source explains why: “That's because LNG production and transport emits more methane — a greenhouse gas far more potent than CO2, though it doesn't stay as long in the atmosphere.”

Ending this emergency removes its tariff pressure to expand purchases with those pollution costs. Resisting that pressure gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill as a way to defend nature from climate harm.

These promises support care for forests through checks on cutting trees and stronger enforcement. Ending the tariffs behind these promises weakens an incentive for those protections. That gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
[NAME]’s care for wild animals and plants supports these protections. The bill removes a tariff incentive for carrying them out.
These promises protect fish and marine animals. Ending the tariffs behind these promises weakens pressure for those protections, which [NAME] has a reason to preserve.
[NAME]’s care for nature supports using natural resources carefully and recovering materials from discarded goods. The bill removes a tariff incentive for those steps.
If applied to environmental rules, this process gives people a way to argue for protecting nature and requires the government to consider their comments.
Taking part in defending nature matters to [NAME]. Removing a tariff incentive for this public involvement gives [NAME] another reason to oppose the bill.

The vice president of Bangladesh’s garment manufacturers’ association reported lower clothing demand after the new tax under this emergency, called the reciprocal tariff: “US consumer spending has slowed due to the high tariff. Clothing consumption is declining, and buyers are not placing new orders because of it.”

Clothing producers reported fewer orders because of the reciprocal tax itself. The president of Bangladesh’s knitwear producers’ association said: “Due to the reciprocal tariff, US buyers are delaying or reducing orders as they negotiate to shift part of the tariff burden onto Bangladeshi suppliers.”
Ending this extra import cost removes a restraint on orders for new clothing.

The bill gives up a tax that holds back purchases of new clothing. New clothing creates demand for production, materials, water, transport and waste disposal. [NAME]’s wish to protect nature from destruction and pollution gives a reason to oppose losing that restraint.

The taxes raise shoppers' costs. An October study of the reciprocal taxes on clothing from Bangladesh explains: “The more likely outcome is that U.S. importers, retailers, and consumers will shoulder much of the additional cost.”

Ending these taxes removes pressure on the price of necessities. This protects food and clothing budgets where money is tightest. Protecting those least able to pay serves [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people and fair treatment.
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, a business group, reports: “Small businesses, manufacturers, and ranchers are struggling with higher costs” .

Small firms have fewer ways to handle tariff costs than larger rivals. CNBC explains: “Their margins are slimmer, their supply chains less diverse and their negotiating power with vendors dampened by the smaller sizes of their orders.” Margins are the profit left after costs, and vendors are sellers.

These costs can take money away from jobs. At Reekon Tools, a small tool company, “The hundreds of thousands of dollars Reed planned to use to hire between three and five designers and engineers is now going to tariffs instead, he said.”

Ending the emergency's taxes frees money that affected firms need to operate and hire. It removes a burden that people running smaller firms are less able to absorb. That supports fair opportunities to earn a living for owners and workers.
The April 2 order allows further tax rises, including power to “increase duties under this order” .

Uncertainty about tariff rates holds back staffing. In its June 2025 survey of firms in the Fourth Federal Reserve District (a region served by the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland), the Cleveland Fed found that “19 percent of contacts said that tariff-related uncertainty had led their firm to scale back staffing plans” .

Uncertainty also threatens workers' protection abroad. Asked about tariff uncertainty, Sara Park of the International Labour Organization (ILO) explained: “During periods of crisis or uncertainty, investment generally pauses. One concern is that factories stop investing in improving working conditions, which could affect occupational safety and health.”

Ending the emergency removes its power to change these tax rates again. That removes a source of pressure to hold back hiring and safety improvements. Protecting opportunities to find paid work and stay safe at work serves [NAME]'s concern for workers, including vulnerable workers abroad.

China directly answered the April taxes with taxes on U.S. exports. The Congressional Research Service (CRS), which writes reports for Congress, says that “in response to the United States' 34% IEEPA "reciprocal tariff" on imports from China, China announced an additional 34% tariff on all U.S. goods” .

Retaliation puts sellers at a disadvantage: “Foreign retaliatory tariffs on U.S. exports make U.S. goods less competitive in foreign markets compared to goods not subject to tariffs” . October reporting shows what this can mean for farm income: one Minnesota grower was selling soybeans “for less than what it cost to produce them.”

Reducing the U.S. taxes has already helped ease this conflict. The May 2025 joint agreement paired U.S. tariff cuts with China's commitment to “suspend or remove the non-tariff countermeasures taken against the United States since April 2, 2025.” Non-tariff countermeasures are responses other than taxes on goods.

Ending these taxes and their power to fuel new rounds of retaliation reduces an avoidable risk to export sales. Protecting people whose livelihoods are caught in that conflict gives [NAME] a reason to favor the bill.

The reciprocal taxes threaten demand for these workers' goods. The October clothing study warns that “the elevated tariffs are set to reduce demand, squeeze suppliers, and depress investment in future capacity” .

Lost sales and investment also threaten future opportunities. The U.N. report warns: “Higher levels of US protection on manufacturing, agriculture and food risk dampening LDCs’ hard-won progress in building productive capacities, reducing commodity dependence and promoting value addition.” That means building the ability to make more goods, sell a wider range of products and do more of the work that adds to their value.

Removing the added tax supports demand for workers' goods and investment in future production. That protects earnings for food, schooling and healthcare, women's ability to earn, and poorer countries' paths to better work. These are reasons for [NAME], who values protection and equal life chances for people worldwide.

Ending the reciprocal taxes removes a charge on people whose countries have little ability to buy U.S. goods and contribute little to the stated problem. Fair treatment calls for burdens to reflect people's circumstances and their part in the problem. Sparing poor people this disproportionate burden serves [NAME]'s concern for justice across borders.

People whose food budgets and jobs are at stake deserve public review of burdens placed on them. Ending this emergency enforces Congress's check on a way of taxing that does not require an investigation. That supports [NAME]'s concern that everyone be treated justly.

The president of Unionwear, a U.S. maker, explains the price protection: “Each tariff increase reduces the cost advantage of imports, making our domestic production more competitive without us having to change anything.” He also explains why taxes on the firm’s supplies do little to offset that benefit: “We source our raw materials domestically when possible, so tariffs on finished goods help us while tariffs on materials have minimal impact on our cost structure.”
U.S. makers have reported winning work. Royal Apparel said: “Several production programs that were initially set to go overseas have now been redirected to Royal Apparel” .

This demand reaches employers that open doors to people with disabilities. The cofounder of Stakes Manufacturing said its April garment partnership would “meet the rising demand driven by recent tariff changes” . Reporting on the firm found: “10% of the 225 employees at Stakes Manufacturing are people with an intellectual or developmental disability.”

Earlier import shocks (sudden rises in imports) from China trade do not measure the effect of this change. They do show how hard lost factory work can be to replace for people without degrees: “Almost all of the manufacturing job losses affected workers without a college degree, and this group saw almost no job gains in the next two decades.”

Removing this price protection puts vulnerable workers’ opportunities and their families’ security at risk. Protecting people who face barriers to work, and children who bear the costs of lost work, gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.

The bill removes these U.S. import taxes without requiring governments to agree to or carry out such changes. That removes an incentive to end discrimination that limits people’s chances to earn a living. Equal opportunities and just treatment give [NAME] a reason to oppose.

The bill removes this emergency’s tariffs as one option for backing that enforcement. Banning these goods closes a market for work obtained through force. [NAME]’s concern for people forced to work gives a reason to preserve pressure to carry out the ban.

Ending this emergency removes a tariff tool for pressing Cambodia to carry out those promises. Protecting children from the worst forms of labor, and workers from abuse over pay and hours, directly serves [NAME]’s concern for vulnerable people abroad.

Ending the tariffs behind these promises weakens a way to press for enforcement that protects these families’ food and work. Protecting vulnerable people who depend on shared fishing grounds gives [NAME] a reason to oppose.

The bill removes a tariff tool for enforcing the promise to keep this source open. Preserving that protection against export bans protects access to materials needed for medical tools. [NAME] has a reason to protect patients who depend on them.

Reuters reports a role for trade pressure in ending the July fighting: “Trump helped broker an end to the five-day conflict in July by calling the then-leaders of the two countries and urging them to end hostilities or risk their respective trade talks with Washington being put on hold.”

Reuters’ account of the July truce links talks to the tariff threat: “Washington would not move ahead with tariff negotiations with both until the conflict had ended.” The account also records the reward: “Mr Trump said tariff negotiations with both countries resumed after the ceasefire agreement.”

The incentive still concerned keeping peace at the October 26 expanded ceasefire signing: “The United States will have a robust commerce and cooperation, transactions, lots of them, with both nations, as long as they live in peace” . The official transcript records Trump’s purpose: “We have to use that business to make sure they—they don't get into wars.”

Ending this emergency’s tariff power removes an incentive already used to bring the two countries toward a truce and to keep trade tied to peace. Protecting border communities from renewed killing and displacement gives [NAME] a reason to oppose.

Tariff costs were still reaching cultural grocery stores in October 2025. At Chicago’s 88 Marketplace, the manager said “the recent 15% import tariffs on South Korean products will make it harder for the grocer to keep prices down.”

Customers were already paying some of those costs, according to Jan Zhu, the store manager: “While the store is absorbing some of the price increases, Zhu said it has still been forced to pass along some cost hikes to customers.”
Local replacements are hard to find: “And often, these items, like grains, spices or herbs, are not easily sourced in the U.S.”
Ending this added tax removes a cost that makes familiar foods harder to stock and afford. Helping neighbors keep their own food traditions puts acceptance of different ways of life into practice.

The same tax relief helps keep open shared spaces for meeting people and learning about their cultures. [NAME]’s wish to listen to and understand different people gives a further reason to protect these opportunities.

This tariff program allows higher taxes in response to another country’s retaliation: “Should any trading partner retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties on U.S. exports or other measures, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase or expand in scope the duties imposed under this order to ensure the efficacy of this action.”

Karen Umemoto, director of UCLA’s Asian American Studies Center, explains how conflict with a country can become hostility toward people: “When a top political leader blames another country for its woes, Americans often scapegoat those around them who ‘look like the enemy.’” To scapegoat means to wrongly blame someone.
Umemoto identifies renewed resentment in the 2025 tariff conflict: “And with the tariff war, we sense resentment rising again.”

Ending this tariff program and its power to raise taxes in retaliation removes one source of the conflict behind that warning. [NAME] has reason to remove a policy that feeds the risk of treating Asian Americans as enemies because of their ancestry.
Tariff pressure backs a promise to protect people at work despite differences in origin, faith or political views.
[NAME]'s commitment to accepting different people gives a reason to oppose removing that pressure.
The reform removes an extra permission requirement for foreign workers to become elected union representatives. This lets people from outside the country speak and lead.
[NAME]'s commitment to accepting different groups gives a reason to oppose removing tariff pressure for this inclusion.
These promises protect workers' ability to organize, challenge employers and have disputes heard without violence or harassment.
[NAME]'s wish to listen to different views and accept disagreement supports keeping tariff pressure behind those protections.

Malaysia makes the same promise: “Malaysia shall adopt and implement a prohibition on the importation of goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part by forced or compulsory labor.” Its deadline is “within two years of the date of entry into force of this Agreement.”
The promised bans, if enforced against such goods, would close the two countries' markets to goods made through the documented forced labor of Uyghurs and other Turkic Muslims.
[NAME]'s commitment to accepting different ethnic and religious groups gives a reason to oppose removing pressure for import bans that work against forcing members of these groups to work.
This requires officials to hear and consider the views of people from outside the country.
[NAME] values listening to people who are different. So losing tariff pressure for this practice gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
Repeal or permanent suspension protects against the return of this blanket blocking rule.
Hearing disputed political views and accepting gay people require room for their speech and social contact. This gives [NAME] a reason to oppose removing tariff pressure for that protection.
Tariff pressure helped bring Thailand to the July talks: “President Trump’s threat to halt tariff talks has forced Thailand’s hand.” To force someone’s hand means to push them to act.
The connection continued at the October 26 signing. Trump said: “We do transactions, lots of them, with both nations as long as they live in peace” .
Thailand's trade framework still offered relief under the same tariff order: “the reciprocal tariffs, as set forth in Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025, as amended” .
A final deal remained ahead: “In the coming weeks, the United States and Thailand will negotiate and finalize the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade” .

Continued tariff bargaining created pressure for the two rival countries to keep talking and to reduce hostility toward the other national group. The bill removes that pressure while the trade deal and these steps still require follow-through.
[NAME]'s wish to understand different people and accept disagreement gives a reason to preserve pressure for those practices.
Hospitals use imported essentials: “These imports include many low-margin, high-use essentials in hospital settings necessary for patient care.”
Replacing suppliers can take years: “Manufacturers cannot easily pivot to new suppliers, absent multi-year lead times” .
Taxes can make supplies harder to obtain: “Tariffs also may force hospitals to seek new vendors — often at higher cost or with lower reliability.” Vendors are sellers.
Missing devices threaten patients: “Disruption in the availability of these devices would curtail hospitals’ ability to perform life-saving surgeries and keep patients safe from contagion” .
Removing this added burden helps keep supplies available for surgery and infection control when [NAME] needs care.

Higher hospital costs can reach patients through insurance charges and bills: “This would result in downstream cost shifting to patients through increased premiums, deductibles, and other out-of-pocket expenses.” Premiums and deductibles are amounts people pay for health insurance and before insurance pays.
Cost already blocks care. The same article reports people “delaying or skipping care due to cost.”
Removing these taxes eases pressure on medical bills and insurance costs. This helps [NAME] obtain care that protects their health.
Supply costs compete with care budgets: “Rising supply costs force budget reallocation, limiting investment in staff, technology, and patient care.”
The hospital association cites a survey, taken in January 2025 before the April emergency, in which administrators expected to “delay equipment upgrades to manage financial strain.”

Equipment quality matters for finding illness. One surveyed administrator explains: “We do not want to misdiagnose a patient because we have decided to use lower quality equipment that cannot detect their issue.”

Ambulance services also depend on imports. In April 2025, their association warned about imported supplies and medicines. Medicines were exempt from these taxes. The association wrote: “Tariffs on any of these items will increase prices, and could result in product shortages, additional supply chain complexity, and other challenges that EMS simply cannot afford.” EMS means emergency medical services.
Removing taxes on covered supplies eases pressure to cut staff, services or equipment spending. That protects [NAME]’s access to emergency help and accurate diagnosis.

Disease research needs imports that a Johns Hopkins report described in April 2025 as taxed: “Biomedical labs rely heavily on imported equipment and materials, from microscopes to diagnostic tools, much of which is now subject to steep tariffs.”

Higher supply costs threaten that work, according to an expert named Dai in the same report: “Without affordable access to essential supplies, he warns, American biomedical research could slow down” .

Medical device makers also face pressure on research and development, meaning work on new or better products: “U.S. companies have been shifting resources to manage tariff costs, with R&D spending expected to be the most heavily impacted.”
That research serves patients. The industry describes its focus as “patient-centered diagnostics and treatments” , meaning ways to find and treat illness.
Removing these costs protects the research that better tests and treatments depend on. This advances [NAME]’s goal of avoiding and overcoming disease.

Nutritious imports remained taxed in late October. An October 24 report confirmed that major banana suppliers remained covered by the tax. An economist explained that “we absolutely should expect a 10% tax on banana imports to drive banana prices higher” .

Higher prices can worsen diets: “During periods of rising prices or uncertainty, households often shift from perishable nutritious foods towards cheaper, longer lasting processed items, reducing the overall quality of the diet.”
Ending these taxes lowers a barrier to nutritious food. This helps [NAME] protect their health.
Businesses absorbing higher import costs face options including “reduce headcount to offset costs or close shop and go out of business.” To reduce headcount means to employ fewer people.
Job threats affect health: “uncertainty and feelings of job insecurity can harm workers’ mental health, performance, and productivity at work.”
Ending these added costs reduces pressure on employers to cut jobs and the related threat to health. This is an ordinary risk [NAME] has reason to avoid.
Higher import costs reach household budgets: “Most of these costs are likely to be passed along to American consumers.”
A survey conducted in October found that some respondents “delayed or skipped buying doctor-prescribed medication in the past year due to their finances” .
Removing these added charges leaves more income available for medicine and medical visits. This helps [NAME] keep up needed treatment.
A May 2025 survey of reactions to tariffs found “most participants reporting emotions like stress, pessimism, frustration, or anxiety.”
Ending this source of higher prices removes a cause of financial worry and its health risks. This serves [NAME]’s concern for health.
The Security Industry Association, a trade group, warned in April that global tariffs “will directly increase the cost of essential security and life safety products” .
Removing taxes on covered safety products lowers a barrier to protection against break-ins and fire. This helps [NAME] stay personally safe.

Reporting on the April 2 tariffs explains the risk to imported treatment equipment: “If the new tariffs drive up costs, or cause supply shortages, water utilities may face delays in maintenance and critical infrastructure projects.” Water utilities are the organizations that supply water.
Removing taxes on covered equipment helps utilities pay for the treatment and maintenance that protect [NAME] from contaminated drinking water.

In May 2025, when much higher rates applied to goods from China, the cycling group PeopleForBikes warned that current and proposed helmet tariffs make protection “much less affordable, which could leave both adults and children unprotected from potential injury.”
Removing these added taxes lowers a barrier to wearing protection during an ordinary activity. This serves [NAME]’s wish to avoid injury.

A safety equipment industry report on tariffs enacted on and after April 2 warns about personal protective equipment, or PPE: “the current tariffs will drive up PPE costs across the board, leaving companies with few options: raise prices, cut labor, or reduce their investment in safety equipment.”
Cutting protection threatens personal safety. The report warns of “preventable injuries and fatalities” .
Ending these taxes removes pressure to cut workplace protection. This reduces an injury risk [NAME] has reason to avoid.

The taxes under this emergency cover medical gloves from suppliers beyond China. For rubber surgical gloves, an October 9 analysis records a “19% tariff on those from Malaysia” . The October 26 Malaysia agreement keeps “at 19 percent the reciprocal tariffs first set forth in Executive Order 14257 of April 2, 2025” .

U.S. medical-supply makers explain the link to emergency production: “Reciprocal tariffs aren’t just about fairness; they’re about ensuring that our nation can produce life-saving medical supplies when they matter most.”
Ending the tax removes a price advantage for U.S.-made gloves and removes support for keeping that production available when overseas supplies are disrupted.
[NAME] needs protection from infection and safe medical care. Keeping that backup supply gives [NAME] a personal health reason to oppose the bill.
Military supply chains use imported parts. Senator Shaheen identified sectors that “source a large part of their components from outside North America” .

The defense exemption from import taxes leaves out supplies shared between military and commercial work when tracking the two separately is too costly or impractical. The exemption’s exclusions cover supplies “identical in nature to supplies purchased by the Contractor or any subcontractor in connection with its commercial business” when “It is not economical or feasible to account for such supplies so as to ensure that the amount of the supplies for which duty-free entry is claimed does not exceed the amount purchased in connection with this contract.”

Costs that suppliers must pay themselves threaten the firms and workers that make military equipment. Shaheen warned in April that this “could drive more companies and jobs out of the defense industrial supply chain, stifling innovation.”

When suppliers pass higher costs to the military, the same budget buys less. The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a research group, explains: “As a result, the Department of Defense simply cannot buy as much with its budget.”
Ending these taxes on supplies outside the defense exemption removes a cost from military production.
Protecting suppliers and military buying power strengthens the state's ability to equip its forces and defend its citizens.

The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a research group, identifies tariffs on Australia as a threat to trust between the two allies: they have “the potential to significantly erode trust in the U.S.-Australia alliance.”

Trade friction also limits closer defense ties with New Zealand. CSIS reports that this friction is “shrinking the permission space for New Zealand leaders to align more closely with the United States on key policy issues, such as potentially joining AUKUS Pillar II.” “Permission space” means how much the public will accept.

The damage also blocks joint action on China's trade practices. The research group Brookings concludes: “This means a coalition focused on addressing the trade challenges with China cannot be built while the United States treats its allies as economic rivals.”
Ending these taxes removes a source of distrust and political resistance to cooperation. That helps the United States work with partners on shared defense and economic threats.

U.S. firms have moved production beyond China to protect supplies. CSIS, a research group, describes an effort to “diversify manufacturing supply chains and protect from shocks that were made apparent during the Covid-19 pandemic and from export controls, sanctions, and other punitive economic measures targeting China.”

The taxes under this emergency also apply to goods from these other production sites. The research group Brookings reports: “Southeast Asian countries like Vietnam, Thailand, and Cambodia—popular destinations for Taiwanese manufacturers as they diversify their supply chains away from China—face U.S. tariff rates similar to Taiwan’s, making diversification to Southeast Asia less cost-effective.”

Ending these taxes lowers the cost of importing covered goods from those other suppliers. Cheaper supply options make it easier to keep backups against disruptions and foreign pressure. This strengthens U.S. resilience, meaning its ability to withstand shocks.
Water utilities (the organizations that supply water) rely on foreign equipment: “U.S. water systems are deeply reliant on imported gear” .

Higher import costs squeeze utility budgets. WaterWorld's analysis of the April 2 order states: “The tariffs will make importing these items more expensive for utilities. These increased costs could translate into higher utility rates and budget constraints.”
Those costs threaten maintenance: “If the new tariffs drive up costs, or cause supply shortages, water utilities may face delays in maintenance and critical infrastructure projects.”
Ending these taxes on covered treatment equipment removes a cost obstacle to timely repairs and upgrades.
Keeping water and sewage systems working protects the public from disease and supports emergency response. This strengthens the country's ability to protect its citizens.
Hospitals depend on foreign supplies: “international sources supply a significant proportion of essential medical goods.”

These include devices that prevent infection: “Some of these devices are single-use, designed to protect patients from infection, such as single-use blood pressure cuffs, stethoscope covers and sterile drapes.”
The American Hospital Association warns that tariffs “may force hospitals to seek new vendors — often at higher cost or with lower reliability.” Vendors are sellers.
Supply disruptions “would curtail hospitals’ ability to perform life-saving surgeries and keep patients safe from contagion” .

Higher costs also threaten the continued provision of care: “Persistent expense growth threatens hospitals’ solvency and ability to sustain comprehensive services in their communities.” Solvency means having enough money to keep operating.

Ending these taxes on covered medical devices removes a cost and supply risk from hospitals. Ending the taxes helps preserve the country's ability to protect people from serious illness and infection.
Removing these taxes eases costs and trade disruption for U.S. firms and households. Reducing that nationwide strain supports the economic base of a strong, stable country.

The emergency lets the President raise these taxes by changing the official list of import tax rates (the HTSUS). The order says: “Should any trading partner retaliate against the United States in response to this action through import duties on U.S. exports or other measures, I may further modify the HTSUS to increase or expand in scope the duties imposed under this order to ensure the efficacy of this action.”

Uncertainty has its own cost. Researchers at the Federal Reserve, the U.S. central bank, explain that “trade policy uncertainty, including around tariffs, likely causes firms to delay investment, potentially slowing economic activity even without any actual tariff changes” .

Production capacity is needed for defense. The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), a research group, explains: “the United States needs people, materials, and production capacity to field military forces.”

Ending the emergency ends the power to change rates under the emergency. Removing that source of uncertainty helps firms plan investments in the production capacity the country needs to remain strong and withstand shocks.

Researchers at the Federal Reserve, the U.S. central bank, traced a specific disruption to news about these taxes: “On the morning of Monday, April 7th, a rumored tariff pause and its swift rebuttal within minutes triggered significant intraday volatility in US Treasury yields and precipitated a sharp decline in liquidity across US Treasury cash and futures markets.” Treasury securities are U.S. government debt. In plain words, a rumor about a tariff pause and its quick denial made the interest rates on this debt swing during one day, and made this debt harder to trade.

Liquidity means how easily an asset can be bought and sold. The Federal Reserve explains the danger: “In extreme cases, low liquidity can threaten continued market functioning, leading to a situation in which participants are unable to trade without incurring a significant cost.”
This concerns a core part of U.S. finance: “Treasury market liquidity is particularly important because of the key role these securities play in the financial system.”
Ending this tariff program removes a source of sudden policy news that has strained trading in U.S. government debt. Reducing that risk supports the country's financial stability.
Congress has a lawful way to end this use of power. An emergency ends when “there is enacted into law a joint resolution terminating the emergency” .

Enacting the resolution applies Congress's legal check to this emergency. Keeping executive power (the power of the President) under standing rules protects dependable self-government. This supports the secure and stable state [NAME] values.

The taxes under this emergency cover battery packs. In a September 10 ruling on a lithium-ion pack from China, U.S. Customs applied an “additional ad valorem rate of duty of 10 percent” . “Ad valorem” means a tax set as a percentage of the value.

Battery tariffs offer a way to shift purchases toward U.S. suppliers. Congress's research service explains: “Such a policy might pivot demand toward domestic producers of batteries and battery parts rather than imported sources” .
These are defense supplies. The Defense Department says: “More and more of our platforms, vehicles, and future capabilities rely on lithium-ion batteries.”

Building U.S. battery production addresses a current military supply risk. In July 2025, government auditors reported efforts “to reduce reliance on foreign sources that are located primarily in China.”

The bill removes an extra incentive to buy U.S.-made batteries and invest in their production. Keeping that incentive supports the supply base for current and future military equipment. That serves [NAME]'s goal of a state able to defend its citizens.

Tariff relief gives the United States something to offer in return for help stopping companies abroad from supplying restricted buyers. The bill removes that bargaining tool. Keeping it helps protect the country against adversaries gaining military technology.
U.S. tax terms are part of the bargain. The United States promises to “maintain at 19 percent the reciprocal tariffs” and names products “to receive a zero percent reciprocal tariff rate.”
Ending these taxes gives up a tool for securing and backing access to other mineral supplies. Protecting military production against foreign cutoffs gives [NAME] a reason to preserve that tool.
The bill removes an extra tool for getting foreign help closing these ways of moving money. Keeping that tool serves [NAME]'s concern that the United States protect itself against armed threats.

Sharing threat warnings and defenses helps protect these systems. Ending tariff pressure gives up a way to press for that help. Protecting vital services during a crisis serves [NAME]'s concern for a secure, stable country.
Tariffs raise the cost of imported instruments: “Now, tariffs are causing a big jump in costs for music stores.”

When churches buy or replace covered imported instruments, the bill removes an added cost of keeping their familiar worship music. Preserving that religious practice serves [NAME]'s value of tradition.
A Christmas-tree importer reported higher prices caused by tariffs: “it also had to raise prices by 10% as a result of the tariffs.”
Removing the added tax on covered Christmas goods cuts a continuing cost of buying or replacing what these customs use. This helps [NAME] preserve family ways of celebrating Christian faith.
Southern Baptist teaching states the inherited duty: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” .
A doll maker describes a tool for that teaching: “When you squeeze its hand, the Talking Jesus Doll speaks 10 of Jesus' phrases from the Bible – including the Lord's Prayer and John 3:16.”
CBS News documented the maker's exposure to the earlier, higher tariffs: “With sky-high tariffs in place, he had paused shipments from China, and had containers of goods waiting in limbo overseas.”

Ending the remaining reciprocal tax removes an added cost from these imported teaching aids. Helping parents carry out the religious duty of passing their faith to children directly serves [NAME]'s wish to preserve Christian beliefs across generations.

Southern Baptist teaching says “Christians should contribute of their means cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally for the advancement of the Redeemer’s cause on earth.”
An April 2025 report warned that price rises caused by tariffs put giving at risk: “At the same time, donors may give less as they face rising prices and a turbulent stock market.”
Reducing this pressure on household budgets helps protect families' ability to keep giving regular offerings and paying for church work.

Participants pack a “shoebox gift filled with fun toys, school supplies, and personal care items” . These goods include a heavily imported product: “Over 80% of toys sold in the U.S. are made in China, according to The Toy Association trade group.”

Removing the added tax on commercially imported toys bought for these gifts lowers a cost of continuing this outreach. Regular church offerings and this established Christmas gospel practice are the traditions at stake.

Tariffs make goods from other countries cost more, which helps U.S. makers compete: “by making foreign goods more expensive, tariffs make domestic products more competitive.” American Giant is one maker that produces in the United States: NPR reports that it “sources and manufactures almost all its products in the U.S., from cotton to the final stitch.”
A U.S. study of growing imports from China during 1990–2014 found harm to men's work and pay: “On average, trade shocks differentially reduce employment and earnings of young adult males.”
Those earnings losses affect family life: “shocks to males' relative earnings reduce marriage and fertility.”

Marriage and the husband's role as provider are religious commitments in [NAME]'s cultural tradition. The Southern Baptist faith statement says, “Marriage is the uniting of one man and one woman in covenant commitment for a lifetime.” Of a husband, it says, “He has the God-given responsibility to provide for, to protect, and to lead his family.”

By removing a defense against job and pay losses caused by imports, the bill puts marriage and the provider role at greater risk. Keeping those religious roles and passing them on gives [NAME] a reason to oppose it.

A study using U.S. church data for 1990–2010 found that import shocks from China “led to a reduction in the number of churches” . The study also found the shocks “caused an increase in the number of religious adherents” . Adherents are members.

Members' money supports church life. The Southern Baptist faith statement calls for regular giving: “Christians should contribute of their means cheerfully, regularly, systematically, proportionately, and liberally” . Losing income leaves less money for that duty.

Losing local work can pull younger generations away from their congregations. The account of the closing of the Ragsdale Church of Christ reports, “Young people have left the region seeking employment” .

Ending this price protection for U.S. makers puts the jobs and income that help keep local congregations going at risk. Keeping those congregations and their shared customs alive honors [NAME]'s religious heritage. This gives [NAME] another reason to oppose the bill.

The CRS warning and FinCEN's April 2026 proposal are in C18 . FinCEN's text is a proposal, open to comment. It is not the bill. CRS is the Congressional Research Service, which does research for Congress. FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency.
C18 is limited to payments involving an issuer's own account holders. The text does not show that criminal transfers fall in that group once coins have moved away.

The bankruptcy passages do not show that the bill's own bankruptcy rules add a loss of access compared with the law it changes. The detail is in C08 : ordinary bankruptcy already pauses claims, and the bill adds a faster release route.
The community-lending forecast relies on a mistaken reading of exposed deposits and skips how reserve purchases affect bank funding. The evidence is in C11 .
FinCEN's later proposal does not support the added monitoring on which this reason depends. The proposal and Section 9's unwritten rules are in C19 . FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency.

Tether announced in 2024 that it would monitor secondary markets with Chainalysis tools, and confirmed adoption in May 2025. Tether is a dollar-linked stablecoin and the company that issues it. Sources: , , , .

Research under Section 9 must consider the amount and sensitivity of information and privacy risks. FinCEN's guidance or rules are due within 3 years. FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency. Sources: , , , .

An issuer can see a transfer yet lack the facts needed to recognize a crime. FinCEN's proposal on this is in C18 . Secondary-market transactions are those not directly involving the issuer.
C18 is limited to payments involving an issuer's own account holders. The text does not show that ingredient purchases fall in that group.

exceptions.text: The bill gives approved stablecoin issuers a legal duty. They must have “technical capabilities, policies, and procedures to block, freeze, and reject specific or impermissible transactions that violate Federal or State laws, rules, or regulations” . See C13 . To block or freeze means to stop coins from moving.

Foreign coins sold through U.S. trading services also depend on obeying lawful orders. See C14 . Treasury can bar U.S. service providers from trading a foreign issuer's coins after that issuer defies an order.

For environmental-crime payments covered by lawful U.S. orders, the bill strengthens the means to interrupt payments and seize proceeds. Giving authorities stronger tools against activities that destroy forests and wildlife serves [NAME]'s wish to defend nature.
The bill requires full backing for approved coins. Issuers must hold at least one dollar of reserves for each dollar of coins. See C04 .
If an issuer fails, coin holders come first for repayment from required reserves. See C05 .

The lower fees and tracking already existed. The bill adds protection for gifts while they are held as approved stablecoins. These rules reduce the risk that issuer failure or other debts divert those gifts. Protecting this way of giving preserves money for forest defense and helps [NAME] take part in defending nature.
Section 16 gives firms under federal banking regulators clear permission to handle stablecoins. See C01 .
Solar projects already use this payment method. Fortune reports: “Owners of each farm receive the stablecoin USDC for the production of Glow carbon credits” .

The bill's clear rules help institutions use faster payments in renewable-energy markets. Releasing money sooner modestly improves the finances of participants in those markets, including developers. The solar example shows that some projects operate near the edge of viability (they can only barely get built). This reasoning does not specify an amount of new renewable power. Making this finance easier to use serves [NAME]'s wish to protect nature from pollution.
This argument depends on the bill leading to more Bitcoin mining. See C03 . Mining is computer work that earns new Bitcoin and uses a lot of electricity.
The bill encourages an activity whose added power demand worsens climate risks. Protecting forests and ecosystems gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
This argument depends on the bill leading to more Bitcoin mining. See C03 .
Mining's air pollution threatens nature beyond its climate effects. [NAME] has a reason to oppose expanding this source of damage to forests and lakes.

Some plants that supply mines use once-through cooling. They take water from rivers or lakes and return it heated, with cleaning chemicals. The withdrawal and discharge “can harm fish and wildlife, and can negatively impact recreation and water quality” .
Expanding mining increases exposure to damage from taking and returning cooling water. Protecting wildlife and waterways gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
