More noisy mining sites add a risk to wildlife in surrounding habitats. [NAME]'s wish to defend nature gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
Issuers licensed under the bill must keep reserves worth at least the full amount they owe users. See C04 .

Enforceable backing rules protect against coins issued without enough money to repay users. That protects small savings and aid payments, including money vulnerable people abroad need for food, shelter, and care.

Issuers lose the freedom to impose their own discretionary cash-out limits or change fees without warning. This protects people whose essential spending leaves little room for delays or surprise charges.

Public reports, outside checks, and marketing rules make accurate safety information less dependent on a customer's expertise or wealth. That gives people [NAME] does not know fairer treatment when deciding whom to trust with their money.
Firms holding stablecoin assets for customers must treat them as the customer's property and generally keep them separate. See C07 .
If an issuer fails, holders have first claim to required reserves, shared in proportion to their claims. See C05 .
If required reserves are missing, unpaid coin claims also come first against the issuer's remaining assets, up to the missing amount. See C06 .

Users gain protection against unrelated business debts, a proportionate share of reserves, and a public voice in the issuer's failure. These rules support just treatment of customers who lack the power to bargain for protection themselves.

Requiring issuers to manage these risks adds protection against theft and disrupted payments. That matters especially for people with few resources to replace lost money or wait for a failed payment system to recover.
Public officials must check managers and gain powers to correct misconduct. Customers receive protection that does not depend on their own money or skill in investigating and challenging a firm.
A major crypto failure, including a stablecoin issuer's collapse, can reach people who never used stablecoins. See C10 .

The bill directs oversight at routes through which issuer trouble can spread to other financial firms. Protecting pensions, savings, and credit from those risks extends [NAME]'s concern to strangers who never chose to use stablecoins.

Section 4 requires suspicious-transaction reporting. See C27 . Section 4 also requires the ability to block, freeze and reject impermissible transactions. See C13 . Section 5 requires compliance programs aimed in particular at “cartels and organizations designated as foreign terrorist organizations” .
Section 8 conditions U.S. trading of foreign coins on the issuer being able to comply and complying with lawful orders. See C14 .

Requiring issuers to detect and block criminal transfers makes it harder to move stolen funds beyond recovery or use them to finance further harm. This serves justice for victims across borders, including people [NAME] will never meet.

Customers gain protection against unwanted extra costs and pressure to give up other providers. That is fairer treatment of people with limited money and gives competing businesses a fairer chance to serve them.
For public companies mainly engaged outside finance, approval to issue coins requires limits on using customers' private transaction data without their consent. See C20 .

Requiring permission stops these firms from taking those commercial benefits from private payment histories without customers' agreement. Giving customers a say in that bargain supports just treatment.
People seeking to start a qualified provider gain stated criteria, reasons for rejection, and a way to challenge mistakes. This supports [NAME]'s concern for just treatment by public officials.
Section 4 bars issuers from paying holders interest or other returns just for holding or using a coin. Such interest could otherwise draw money from bank deposits that fund loans. See C12 .

The ban prevents issuers from using direct interest payments to draw those deposits. Blocking that incentive protects a source of loans for households and small firms in communities where limited credit already restricts opportunity.
This argument needs some household money to move into stablecoins. See C02 .
Expanding this substitute for bank savings exposes people to losing money needed for daily life. Protecting households that cannot replace those losses gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that expansion.
This argument needs people to rely on these coins for necessities. See C02 .
In a nonbank issuer's bankruptcy, withdrawals from reserves can be paused until a court acts, and the 14-day target is only a best-efforts target from a hearing. See C08 .

Having assets available is different from having money available to pay for food or rent. Promoting payment money that can remain frozen, even for a shortened period, exposes people without a cash cushion to missed necessities, giving [NAME] a reason to protect them.
This argument needs more people to use these coins for payments. See C02 .
The stablecoin law adds “no protection for unauthorized transfers” . It also has no required process for handling errors. See C25 .

People who cannot replace stolen or missing payment money need clear refund duties and a way to enforce them. Expanding stablecoin payments without establishing those rights gives [NAME] a reason to protect the people least able to absorb the loss.

Removing this route for pursuing dishonest sales takes away a protection already used for stablecoin customers. [NAME]'s concern for protecting weaker customers from powerful firms gives a reason to oppose that loss.

Such an issuer can gain nationwide access through official silence, while states lose the power to require another license before it serves their residents. Protecting residents from entry without a completed safety decision gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this rule.
This argument needs wider use to reach small holders. See C02 .

Widening use without equal, affordable access to redemption leaves small holders dependent on fees, middlemen, and terms they cannot meet. Fair treatment gives [NAME] a reason to oppose expanding payments on those terms.

Users supply the money and bear its uninsured risk, yet the law blocks them from bargaining for interest solely for holding it. This preference for firms over their direct customers gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the rule as unfair.
If required reserves are missing, coin holders' remaining claims come first, up to the missing amount. See C06 .
The claims pushed behind include “priority wage and tax claims” .

When the remaining assets run out, paying token holders first leaves less for workers already owed wages. Protecting those workers and treating their claims justly gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this change.
This argument needs added stablecoin use. See C01 . It also needs that use to reduce funding for local lending. See C11 .

Shifting funding away from community banks threatens a source of home, farm, and small-business loans in those places. Protecting people's chances to build a livelihood gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this expansion.
This argument needs added stablecoin use. See C01 .
The bill permits bank deposits as backing, so a rush to cash out tokens can pull funds from banks. See C09 . Breaking the buck means falling below the promised dollar value.
A major issuer's collapse can reach people who never used stablecoins. See C10 .

Expanding these links exposes uninvolved workers, retirees, borrowers, and taxpayers to private firms' risks. [NAME] has reason to protect vulnerable people from the spillover and resist making strangers pay for it.

The bill does not bar commercial issuers whose shares are not publicly traded. The bill does not create the combination of commerce and payments. But by removing regulatory uncertainty, the bill makes this route more usable. See C21 .

A platform can use its existing business to make other payment products costly to switch to. See C22 . Public Citizen gives the example of a retailer that “might disfavor a subcontractor if it failed to use the aggregator's stablecoin.” .

Expanding this business model exposes small sellers and workers to payment terms they cannot readily refuse without risking income. Equal opportunity gives [NAME] a reason to resist making this power easier to use.
The bill leaves commercial companies a more usable route to issue coins. See C21 .

Giving sellers more financial information gives them another tool for steering people toward more expensive choices based on their needs. Protecting customers from that unequal power gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the expansion.
The President's family has a stablecoin business that stands to benefit from wider use, and legal experts say the bill's stated ethics safeguard does not cover the President. See C24 .

Enlarging a business through which interested parties can enrich the President gives wealthy interests another route to seek favor. Just treatment of everyone, including people without that financial access, gives [NAME] a reason to oppose expanding this channel.
This argument needs added use of dollar stablecoins. See C01 .

Promoting dollar tokens exposes people in weaker economies to faster financial outflows and weaker tools for stabilizing their economies. [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people everywhere gives a reason to oppose imposing those risks on strangers abroad.
This argument needs added stablecoin use. See C01 .

Even without a financial crisis, this shift reduces public income available for shared services and opportunities. Taking resources from governments already short of funds gives [NAME] a reason to protect the people who depend on those resources.

The public supplies part of the cost of running this private payment system, including people who never use it. Fair treatment gives [NAME] a reason to oppose placing those costs on the public instead of the firms earning the income.
[NAME] has a reason to support a system that judges applicants by safety and hears their reasons when they disagree with a refusal.

The bill would add reserve duties ( C04 ) and bankruptcy priority ( C05 ) to regulated tokens while preserving open networks, lawful direct payments and wallets people control themselves. That protects funds sent through an alternative to ordinary payment gatekeepers.
Accepting people despite disagreement gives [NAME] a reason to protect the means they use to speak, organize and support one another.
[NAME] has a reason to favor protections for a payment route that supports lawful voices and ties beyond the approval of ordinary payment companies or authoritarian banks.

Reserve duties ( C04 ) and bankruptcy priority ( C05 ) would protect regulated tokens used in these payments, while clear issuer fees would help users choose how to pay. These protections support ways of helping relatives and receiving aid that fit life across borders or without a bank account.
Accepting people whose lives differ includes making room for their cross-border family ties and their own choices about receiving help.
[NAME] has a reason to favor protections that accommodate those choices and circumstances.

For covered public companies mainly outside finance, section 4(a)(12) restricts commercial uses of private personal information from stablecoin transactions without the consumer's consent. The restricted uses are targeted advertising or content, sale, and sharing with non-affiliates. See C20 .

Users could refuse these covered issuers permission to turn their private payment records into advertising profiles or pass them to commercial outsiders. This restricts a route through which beliefs and group ties become information used to sort and exclude people.
Tolerance gives [NAME] a reason to protect people's ability to keep different beliefs and associations without those differences becoming grounds for unfair treatment.
[NAME] has a reason to favor these limits on commercial exposure of people's differences.

Section 4 requires closer customer checks. See C17 . Steptoe identifies a change for some issuers in these know-your-customer (KYC) checks: “Therefore, these more granular KYC obligations will be an important change for some issuers.” Steptoe is a law firm.
Adding more detailed checks to stablecoin issuance strengthens a known incentive to reject customers whose ordinary religious giving or family payments abroad appear risky.
Accepting people across religious and cultural differences gives [NAME] a reason to resist treating those differences as grounds for blanket rejection.
[NAME] has a reason to oppose extending this risk of group-based exclusion to more stablecoin issuers and their customers.

Section 4 requires issuers to identify and verify account holders. See C17 . This adds formal rules for some issuers operating as money-transfer firms. Steptoe explains their current freedom over customer checks: “MSBs are not subject to CIP or CDD rules, meaning they have additional flexibility with respect to how they KYC users.” MSBs are money-services businesses, including money-transfer firms. CIP, CDD and KYC refer to identity and customer-risk checks. Steptoe is a law firm.

The bill extends more detailed verification duties to issuers serving people whom existing financial checks already struggle to recognize. Where issuers do not adopt such alternatives, that raises the risk of rejection from direct accounts for people with these backgrounds and identities.
Accepting people across different backgrounds and identities gives [NAME] a reason to resist excluding them when their documents differ or are hard to replace.
[NAME] has a reason to oppose extending this barrier to participation.

Section 9(d) requires new guidance and rules for how issuers monitor transfers on blockchains, which are shared digital records of transfers. This could cover more transfers than issuers' current duties. See C19 . Issuers must also identify their account holders. See C17 .
[NAME]'s wish to listen to and understand different people gives [NAME] a reason to protect the private support and contact that let unpopular groups speak and be heard.

By opening more transfers to monitoring, the bill increases the risk of deterring the support and contact that let different groups be heard and understood. That gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill.
The bill's freezing requirement adds a legal condition, including for issuers that did not build this power into their tokens. See C13 .
Foreign issuers also need this capability to reach U.S. customers through digital-asset services. See C14 .
Requiring issuers to build and use freezing powers strengthens the means to enforce existing financial penalties against people for judicial work the U.S. government rejects.
Holding tokens in one's own wallet does not remove issuer control. See C13 .
Accepting people despite disagreement gives [NAME] a reason to resist cutting them off from ordinary payments over disputed legal judgments, across national and political differences.
[NAME] has a reason to oppose making that financial exclusion easier to enforce.
The bill requires issuers to monitor and report suspicious transactions. See C27 .
Such reporting helps investigators stop the suppliers. See C18 .
The bill also makes obeying federal blocking orders a legal duty, for permitted issuers ( C13 ) and for foreign issuers on U.S. services ( C14 ). This is separate from finding the payments.

Required reporting, yearly accountability, and enforceable blocking duties strengthen investigators' means to interrupt ingredient purchases and the production they support. Cutting this supply of poisonous drugs serves [NAME]'s interest in protecting health and avoiding danger.

An actual freeze shows that stablecoins on this route can be blocked: “Stablecoin issuer Tether has frozen $28 million worth of USDT on Russian crypto exchange Garantex.” The bill makes obeying federal blocking orders a legal duty ( C13 , C14 ). USDT is the stablecoin issued by Tether.
Section 9 requires FinCEN to write tracing standards. See C19 . FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency.

Required tracing standards and enforceable freezes strengthen the means to find and deny ransomware profits. Attacking this source of funding and profit helps protect the medical care and emergency response [NAME] relies on.
The bill makes foreign issuers' access through U.S. providers depend on blocking capability and compliance. See C14 . Permitted issuers have a similar duty. See C13 .

The bill adds pressure to carry out freezes against terrorist funds. Denying these resources restricts support for violence and the promotion of attacks on Americans. That advances [NAME]'s personal safety at home.

The bill's required tracing standards ( C19 ) and blocking duties ( C13 , C14 ) strengthen tools for finding these networks and cutting off their funds. Disrupting scams before they take more from victims helps prevent the severe distress they cause. Protecting mental health gives [NAME] a personal security reason to favor those controls.

Suspicious-activity reports help investigators act. FinCEN says they “may aid law enforcement in disrupting these actors and prevent further victimization.” The written duty is in C27 , and whether it helps identify payments is in C18 . FinCEN is Treasury's financial-crime agency.

The bill's tracing standards ( C19 ) and enforceable freezing duties ( C13 , C14 ) strengthen this route for finding blackmailers and obstructing their money flows. Stopping coercion that drives victims to despair and suicide serves [NAME]'s interest in health and personal safety.
This argument needs some everyday household money to move into stablecoins. See C02 .
Stablecoins issued under this framework “are not federally insured.”
If an issuer fails, money can be frozen by a bankruptcy pause on exchanging tokens for money. See C08 .
Wider use would expose more household payment funds to losses or freezes when people need money for medicine and treatment.
Protecting access to care gives [NAME] a health reason to oppose this shift.
This argument needs household funds to be on these networks. See C02 .
Network problems can block access even when an issuer holds its reserves. See C23 .
Growth can also make attacks more rewarding on Ethereum, one public network used by stablecoins. See C28 .
Wider adoption would put more household funds on these networks and increase the rewards for attacking them.

Cost is already a barrier to care: “Twenty-eight percent of adults went without some form of medical care in 2024 because they could not afford it” . So losing access to payment money threatens treatment. Avoiding this added source of interruption gives [NAME] a health reason to oppose the bill.

A consumer advocate warns that the bill would “create a regulatory imprimatur for stablecoins without removing the dangers associated with them” . An imprimatur is an official approval. The new approval system can encourage trust while payment risks remain. This trust draws in household money. See C02 .
The bill itself does not require a process for investigating customers' transfer complaints. See C25 .
The new credibility would draw household money into a market used by scammers, without requiring issuers to investigate customers' missing funds.
Fraud losses that leave users struggling to pay bills carry a documented mental-health concern. Protecting mental health gives [NAME] a reason to oppose promoting this exposure.
This argument needs added stablecoin use. See C01 .
The bill permits reserves in uninsured bank deposits, so a rush to exchange tokens for dollars can drain otherwise sound banks. New York Fed researchers report this link already operates. See C09 .
Expanding stablecoin use would enlarge a route from token runs to banking stress, beyond the people who own tokens.

Financial crises reach ordinary households' incomes and savings, including people who took no such risk. See C10 . The 2008 example in that claim shows how a crisis can reach households, not the expected size of a stablecoin-related shock.

Expanding this route for financial shocks puts household money for care at risk and exposes nonusers to the financial strain linked to depression. A review of U.S. studies finds “a consistent, positive association between financial strain and depression in the United States.” Those health stakes give [NAME] a reason to oppose the bill even without owning stablecoins.

Permitted issuers must check their account holders and report suspicious transactions: “identification and verification of account holders with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer” . The reporting duty is in C27 , and whether it helps identify payments is in C18 .
The bill makes the ability and willingness to obey federal blocking orders a condition of issuance. See C13 .
Treasury can act against foreign issuers that defy those orders, after notice. See C14 .

Treasury must research better detection methods, and its financial-crime agency must issue guidance and rules on monitoring blockchain transfers. See C19 . Some services can hide who sends or receives money.
The bill requires full backing with cash or other assets readily sold or withdrawn. See C04 .

Full backing, limits on reserve risks and use, and enforceable oversight address the conditions that cause runs and forced sales. Reducing those routes to a financial crisis protects the stable U.S. economy [NAME] values.

Covered custodians—firms safeguarding stablecoin reserves, coins used as collateral, or keys used to issue coins—must protect customer property from their own creditors and generally keep it separate. See C07 .
In an issuer's failure, coin holders have first claims on required reserves. See C05 .
If reserves fall short, holders' unpaid claims also get priority on the issuer's other assets to cover missing required reserves. See C06 .
Protecting payment assets and giving holders a route to recover them limits the disruption a failed firm causes to households, businesses, and commerce. That protects national economic stability.
Regulators must establish “appropriate operational, compliance, and information technology risk management principles-based requirements and standards” .

A safety gate for these commercial groups, together with limits on issuer activities, restricts routes through which payment troubles spread across the economy. That serves [NAME]'s concern for a stable country.
Such barriers threaten economic stability. Brookings warns about firms that use private data or raise the costs of switching to other payment products. See C22 . Brookings is a policy research group.
The bill forbids both permitted and foreign issuers to pay interest or yield solely for holding or using their coins, and such interest could otherwise draw money away from bank deposits. See C12 .
Removing this incentive protects bank funding for lending and a channel through which the central bank steadies the economy. Both support the national stability [NAME] values.
A workable U.S. route for firms and expertise strengthens the country's capacity to build and oversee technology central to its financial power. That supports a state able to defend its citizens.
The bill supports wider use of digital dollars. See C01 .
The bill is expected to increase stablecoin use. See C01 . The bill allows “short-dated Treasury bills” among required reserves.

Supporting this demand helps the state borrow at lower short-term rates. Money saved on interest is available to defend citizens and meet national emergencies, giving [NAME] a security-based reason to favor the framework.
This argument needs added stablecoin use. See C01 .
This argument needs added stablecoin use. See C01 .
Regulating an issuer does not put that whole network under its control. Network failure can stop payments even when backing assets remain safe. See C23 .
On Ethereum, one public blockchain, growth increases the reward for attacks. See C28 .

Expanding everyday payments ( C02 ) on such networks raises both the rewards for attackers and the economic stakes of an outage. Keeping essential transactions working is part of keeping the country secure and stable.
Bank trouble and coin withdrawals can reinforce each other. See C09 .
A larger, more connected stablecoin market ( C01 ) gives mass withdrawals more scope to drain banks and put upward pressure on federal borrowing costs.

Failure can also freeze payment funds, because a bankruptcy pause can stop cashing out, and the faster process still requires a court decision. See C08 . This gives holders no promise of cash when a payment falls due.

Reliable access matters beyond investors: “Producers and consumers need to be able to reliably send and receive payments for goods and services bought and sold.” This route needs ordinary payments to rely on these coins. See C02 .

Promoting this money puts more ordinary economic activity behind private promises whose failure can spread through banks and markets. That leaves the U.S. government facing payment disruption and pressure for emergency support, threatening national stability and the government's ability to manage crises.
Wider use ( C01 ) can reduce banks' deposit base, and this loss undermines local loan funding. Stablecoin reserves cannot simply replace those loans, and stablecoins carry no lending duty. See C11 .

The bill does not bar commercial ownership of issuers. The bill does not create this combination of commerce and payments, but its framework makes the route more usable. The bill's special approval test for publicly traded commercial companies leaves a gap for privately held firms, which still need an issuer license but do not face that test. See C21 .
Payment networks become more useful as more people join them, favoring a few large providers, and a commercial platform can use its other businesses to strengthen that control. See C22 .
The president's family already has a stake in this market through World Liberty Financial and its USD1 coin, and the bill's ethics clause leaves ownership conflicts open. See C24 .

A 2023 international fundraiser for churches in the Philippines also offered stablecoin gifts: “Donors can send Tether (USDT), USD Coin (USDC)” . The bill's protection depends on the coin: Tether is “licensed in El Salvador” , so the rules below for approved issuers reach Tether only if it becomes an approved issuer. USDT is the stablecoin issued by Tether.
The bill requires full backing ( C04 ). It also requires issuers to set out “procedures for timely redemption of outstanding payment stablecoins” . Redemption means exchanging a token for money.
If an approved issuer fails, holders have priority over other creditors for required reserves. See C05 .
Firms holding stablecoin reserves for customers must take steps to protect customer property from their own creditors. See C07 .

For gifts made and held in approved issuers' coins, full backing and stronger rights to recover assets reduce the risk that an issuer's or asset holder's failure takes money intended for Christian work. The sources do not report how long churches hold such gifts as coins.
Protecting these gifts helps congregations sustain worship, teaching and missions. That supports the religious practices [NAME] wants to continue.

This argument needs added stablecoin use. See C01 . The bill also requires issuers to identify account holders. See C17 . It also requires “monitoring and reporting of any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation” .

Moving gifts from private cash into tokens that can be traced back to identified accounts exposes religious giving to wider scrutiny. Preserving this inherited way of giving gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that shift.
Helping betting businesses overcome payment barriers, even with those hurdles, works against preserving this religious rule in public life and family habits.
Giving that trade a clearer, more reliable payment route strengthens a business that [NAME]'s tradition teaches families and churches to oppose.
This argument needs added stablecoin use. See C01 .
Stablecoin purchases can draw money away from lenders, who must replace departing deposits to keep funding new loans. See C11 .
The bill directs token backing into specified reserves, including “short-dated Treasury bills” . Nonbank issuers cannot simply use those reserves for church loans. See C11 .

Drawing deposits away from such lenders threatens funding for churches and ministries. Protecting the institutions through which families practice and pass on their faith gives [NAME] a reason to oppose that pressure.

exceptions.text: These local gains do not show that S.2's added patrols would reduce this traffic instead of moving it somewhere else.
Interior reported gains in some places: “CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.”

The Forest Service reported that stronger controls beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” “Funneled” means pushed into one place.
Enforcement can reduce traffic in one place and push it into wild land in another. So one step is missing: that added patrols would reduce the traffic near wildlife water, and not only move it.
Catching someone faster does not show that there is less damage to trails, plants or fences.
The tower report describes a narrower result: “The response time from target identification to suspect apprehension dramatically decreased,”

The Forest Service reported that stronger controls beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” “Funneled” means pushed into one place.

Speed of response does not measure total travel through habitat or fence damage avoided. Enforcement can also push traffic into wild areas. So this argument does not connect faster catching to less damaging traffic overall.
This argument treats immigration enforcement as a way to control invasive species, but does not show how stopping people would keep species out.
Interior lists “invasive species introductions” among the harms, but it does not explain how these species arrive.
Seeds can travel on people. The National Park Service explains: “Seeds can readily become lodged in our boots and stuck to our clothing.”

The missing step is keeping species from reaching habitat. A person caught after walking through the land may already have carried the seeds there. The list of harms and the general report of reduced border activity do not show that S.2 would reduce this spread.
The sources do not connect S.2's added arrests to fewer abandoned campfires in these forests.
The Forest Service names “warming and cooking fires built and abandoned by cross-border violators” as a cause of wildfires.

The same testimony says that enforcement beside Coronado National Forest “funneled growing amounts of illegal vehicle and foot traffic through the valleys and mountains of the Forest.” “Funneled” means pushed into one place.

This argument relies on Interior's general report of reductions in some areas. But the fire evidence comes from a forest where enforcement pushed traffic into the backcountry (remote land). So added patrols may not mean fewer people camping there. One step is missing: that patrols would reduce crossings in fire-prone wild land, and not only move them.
A division of duties inside a joint patrol does not show that S.2's money protects land officers' time for conservation.

Interior describes patrols that use officers from both agencies: “Border Patrol agents frequently conduct joint patrols with Interior law enforcement personnel on Interior-managed lands, including national parks, wildlife refuges, and public lands.”
Its account of one operation says: “Interior law enforcement officers focused on resource mission-related violations during this operation.”

This shows who did what inside joint operations, and those operations also use land officers. The Forest Service's 2006 complaint does not show that S.2's added money for Customs and Border Protection (CBP) would reduce the enforcement work those officers now do. So this argument has not shown that the bill would free their time for conservation.
The testimony does not separate help with fighting fires from help with planned burns.

The testimony describes clearing fire areas and guarding firefighters: “The Coronado National Forest must now send armed officers to clear wildland fire areas or provide security for firefighters.” It adds: “Agents of the Border Patrol have been used to help in these efforts.”
The discussion covers both kinds of fire work: “during prescribed fires or fire suppression operations” . Prescribed fires are planned burns. Fire suppression means fighting fires.

General security help at fires does not show that Border Patrol support made planned burns possible. Without that step, the claimed support for plant care rests on a guess about which fire work agents helped with.
This sewage argument leaves out limits on these warehouse plans that existed before June 9, 2026.

Social Circle had locked the water meter at the planned detention center. Its city manager described the condition: “The lock is there until ICE indicates how water and sewer will be served without exceeding our limited infrastructure capacity.”

An April 15 court order stopped work at the Williamsport warehouse while the case continues: “Defendants are enjoined during the pendency of this lawsuit from construction and renovation at the warehouse located at 16220 Wright Road, Williamsport, Maryland 21795 (the “Williamsport Warehouse”) for the purposes of operating the warehouse as a detention and processing facility;”

Maryland's warning concerns going beyond sewer capacity: “Exceeding the capacity of the sewer lines would likely result in sewage backups and overflows” . Maryland also requires a fix: “Any necessary upgrades must comply with applicable State permitting requirements and be funded by DHS.”

S.2's operating money does not remove the water lock, the court order or the permit rules. So the warnings do not show that the bill makes operation beyond sewer limits more likely at these sites. These limits could change later, and this response does not cover other sites.
More border-patrol staff does not by itself mean more damaging off-road driving at Organ Pipe.
Section 201 pays for several uses of staff: “hiring, paying, training, and equipping U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents” .
The agreement behind this example allows agents to patrol “on foot or on horseback” .

The Park Service later described more staff aimed at reducing vehicle use: “The U.S. Border Patrol Ajo Station has increased its Horse Patrol Unit (HPU) with the recent graduation of agents through the class. The Ajo Station HPU patrols at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument in an effort to reduce mechanized equipment in the wilderness.”

Paying for staff and damaging vehicle use are separate steps. The 2012 report of more damage does not show that S.2 adds such driving or keeps it going. The horse patrols at this same site show why more staff alone does not establish that link.
The forestry examples do not show that S.2 raises the risk that needed forest work is left without crews.
Later reporting on the 2025 case found that crews kept working: “Both of the private crews have active agreements with the Forest Service and have been assigned to new fires.”
The 2007 report describes efforts to replace arrested workers: “For now, Olson said his office is working with the company to get replacement workers as soon as possible.”

The forestry association's warning is about temporary work visas (H-2B visas). Its proposed solutions include: “An exemption for forestry workers from the H-2B visa cap to address the reforestation backlog.” It is not a warning about arrests.

Arrests alone do not show that forest work would lack crews, because crews continued to get work and replacements were sought. A warning about late planting does not show that S.2 raises the chance of those delays. So one step is missing: from the added enforcement money to more unfilled forest work.
This argument does not connect general staff money for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) to more teaching for children and families.
Project iGuardian uses “special agents and subject matter experts” to give presentations. More presentations therefore need their time, not only a larger agency budget.

November 2025 reporting described agents being moved to immigration work, “dramatically slowing investigations into child exploitation and sex trafficking” . So other work was competing for agents' time.

Section 102 pays for agents and support staff for “mission support and operations and maintenance” . Its child-protection training rule concerns “such personnel and State and local law enforcement” , not presentations to families.

This teaching program depends on agents' time, and training investigators to identify victims does not add that time. So the step from general money to more teaching is uncertain. This does not show that general money could not reach this work.
This argument's examples do not show that S.2 would add trafficking investigations or survivor-support staff while agents were reportedly being moved to immigration work.

November 2025 reporting described agents being moved to immigration work, “dramatically slowing investigations into child exploitation and sex trafficking” . This is evidence that staff assignments can reduce trafficking work even when the agency has more money.

The earlier growth of the Victim Assistance Program came from money set aside for it: “From FY 2020 to FY 2023, the VAP received congressional enhancement funds” . So this example shows what targeted money did, not what general HSI money would do.
This weakens the step from HSI's budget to this work under those reported staff moves. It does not show that general money could not help.
The fraud totals do not show more protection against scams from S.2 now that agents at Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) were reportedly being moved to immigration work.
These are past results: “In FY 2024, HSI conducted 61 romance fraud” cases and “258 elder fraud cases” . They describe how investigators' work was divided at an earlier time.

Those reports give a reason to question whether added investigators' time would reach these scams. The 2024 totals do not answer that question. This does not show that the money cannot reach this work.
Cheap replacement weakens the step from a seized shipment to less drug use overall.

Drug-policy researchers Jonathan Caulkins and Peter Reuter explain: “But traffickers can easily replace what is seized.” They say fentanyl is cheap to make and easy to move: “It is absurdly cheap for high-level traffickers to replace seizures.”

A 2026 review of many studies (search through April 2025) treated some seizures as disruptions by police. The results point in different directions. Local or regional studies linked seizures to more overdoses nearby or the next year, while a study in a Florida county linked fewer seizures to more deaths. These are associations (things found together), not estimates for S.2's border resources.

Replacement challenges the step from seized shipments to fewer drugs reaching people and less overdose risk. It does not deny that the seized drugs themselves stay off the street. Neither the review nor cheap replacement proves that more seizures have no benefit.
This argument's earlier counterterrorism results do not show that new money would bring back or grow investigators' work on these threats.

The report places the “70 criminal indictments” in fiscal year 2024. In January 2026, senators cited reporting that “a major joint FBI-HSI investigation into illicit Iranian oil shipments” had “suffered from the redeployment” of investigators.

The missing step is investigators' time on these threats under the reported practice of moving agents to immigration work at the time of Congress's June 9 vote. An earlier total of criminal cases does not show that added agency money would supply this time. This does not show that added money could not reach this work.
The cyberattack count does not show more protection for essential services from S.2.

The report says, “In FY 2024, OCC disrupted 195” break-ins and attacks. OCC is Operation Cyber Centurion, and FY means fiscal year. This measures the existing operation's work, not the effect of added money under the later reported practice of moving agents to immigration work.
The January 2026 letter reported that “entire HSI units have reportedly been reassigned en masse to immigration enforcement” .

An earlier work pattern cannot simply be carried forward when assignments have reportedly changed. This count does not show that new money would reach cyber investigations. This does not show that added money could not reach this work.
The safety report's training problem comes from unclear rules, which this money does not change.

The report found unclear training rules: “ICE does not clearly define requirements for refresher training” . It recommended that ICE “Mandate that law enforcement officers complete refresher” training quarterly.
S.2 pays agencies to “hire, pay, train, and equip” staff, but it does not set that schedule or fix the guidance.

So money alone may not improve the training that the report says is missing. This response does not cover equipment. The same report says “Seventy percent of ICE personnel we interviewed believed additional equipment is needed” .
The lack of a public safety threat does not by itself show that this custody is needless or unjust.

Custody can have a purpose other than preventing violence. For people already ordered removed, the Supreme Court tests detention against a period “reasonably necessary to secure removal” . It names the purpose of “assuring the alien’s presence at the moment of removal” . This case does not cover every kind of immigration custody.

Section 202(9)'s limit covers “funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph” and allows releases “required by existing law” . It does not stop all spending on monitored release, and it does not end a right to release.

Keeping a person from running away before a timely removal can justify custody even when the person is not dangerous. This argument does not show that monitoring would serve that purpose in the cases it objects to. So its step from “no safety threat” to “unjust confinement” leaves out that question.
The Los Angeles findings do not show that the added staff and local agreements would spread race-based stops under the approach reported before Congress's June 9 vote.

On May 5, CBS reported the account of Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy, that “Border Patrol agents have not been making seemingly random immigration stops at parking lots and public places.”
The same report says ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) had prioritized “operations focused on arresting people who have criminal records” .

Evidence about the earlier operation does not show that the added money would carry race-based stops forward under this reported change. The CBS report is an official's account, and it does not discuss the local agreements. This does not show that such stops have ended.
This argument carries the effects of particular past operations forward without accounting for the change in approach before Congress's June 9 vote.

CBS reported that Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy, had been told to work on “winding down the Minneapolis operation” . It also described a shift by ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) toward “operations focused on arresting people who have criminal records” .

Those reports weaken the use of the Minnesota food, medicine and school harms to predict what added money would do. This does not answer the research on school harm after enforcement actions, and it does not show that such operations have ended.
The lack of a new warrant rule does not show that S.2 makes it more likely that the paused home entries start again.
On May 8, the secretary wrote: “I have paused the practice of entering an illegal alien’s residence who is subject to a final order of removal with an I-205” .
The secretary described the pause as lasting “while I assess the policy.” So it was an announced pause during a review.

The June 9 comparison includes this pause. Leaving out a new rule tied to this money does not itself restart the practice. This does not answer the separate point that the money would also pay for these operations if the pause ended.
This argument predicts more violent encounters from the earlier record without looking at the change in command and tactics before Congress's June 9 vote.
By May, CBS reported that the commander who led the wider sweeps had been removed: “Bovino was relieved of his command following Pretti's killing and retired from Border Patrol in March.”
The same report describes a move by ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) toward “operations focused on arresting people who have criminal records” .

These changes bear directly on how agents meet people during operations. This argument does not explain why added money under this approach would increase the violent encounters or the punishment of peaceful advocates in its examples. This does not show that such incidents have ended.
This argument treats more surveillance capacity as indiscriminate collection without showing what makes the funded collection indiscriminate.

Section 103 pays for surveillance “along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” Section 202 pays for “information technology maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations, including improvements to fee collections and body-worn cameras.”

The Brennan Center predicts tools that “facilitate indiscriminate collection of information about Americans as well as immigrants.” Its account does not trace these spending lines to collection without a fair purpose or limit.

The quoted provisions state what the money is for. They do not show unfair selection or use of people's information. So the step from this money to the unfair intrusion behind this justice argument is missing.

This argument does not connect the added staff to more ethnic profiling under the conditions in place at Congress's June 9 vote. Ethnic profiling means treating people as suspects because of their ethnic group.
The investigation describes a particular campaign “throughout the summer of 2025 in Los Angeles” . The relevant question is about added work after June 9, 2026.

Before Congress's June 9 vote, CBS reported a change in Border Patrol's street operations, according to Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy: “He noted that, since the Minneapolis operation was scaled back, Border Patrol agents have not been making seemingly random immigration stops at parking lots and public places.”

This argument projects the earlier campaign's methods onto added staff without addressing this later change. So more enforcement capacity alone does not establish more use of that particular way of choosing people. This is an official's account, and it does not show that such stops have ended.

The transport provision pays for “alien departure or removal operations.” Removal is a civil process tied to immigration status, not a criminal punishment: “deportation is classified as a civil rather than a criminal sanction” .

The arrest fund includes an adult who, “following an arrest, charge, booking, or conviction for a criminal offense under Federal, State, or local law, other than a minor traffic offense, is the subject of an immigration detainer, notice request, or custody-transfer request issued by the Department of Homeland Security” . These conditions concern criminal process and immigration custody. They are not tests of ethnicity, faith or opinion.

The limit on release spending applies to “funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph” and keeps the exception “except as required by existing law” . It does not cancel release rights or stop other money from paying for release.

This argument identifies family disruption and a preference for custody. Neither one makes acceptance of a person's background or beliefs depend on that person staying. The missing value step is why enforcing these civil rules rejects difference. Having no conviction does not supply that step.
The evidence does not connect the added withdrawal to the local police roles that these agreements create.
The survey is about police involvement in general, in 2012. Its measure includes the statement “I feel more isolated because local law enforcement is more involved in immigration enforcement” .

These agreements cover different kinds of work. ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) describes its Warrant Service Officer model as allowing local officers “to execute civil immigration warrants on behalf of ERO.” ERO is ICE's enforcement branch. This model concerns warrants for people already in custody, not new street questioning.

The recent article concerns federal raids and rumors, including times when “volunteers show up to a report of a raid, only to find the rumors were prank calls.” It also reports: “The sheriff has previously insisted in a video message that his office does not enforce federal immigration law.”

The recent article describes fear in a place where the sheriff says he does not do this work. So the article does not show the effect of these agreements. This argument does not say which added police contacts would create the barrier. This response does not answer the survey's general finding about police involvement.
Paying for government lawyers does not by itself show a choice against hearing immigrants' circumstances.
Listening to someone's circumstances does not require agreeing that the person should win a legal case.

The report places immigrants' communication barriers in detention: “Attorneys must adhere to strict visitation rules, making it difficult for lawyers to communicate with their clients.” This does not describe an effect of hiring government lawyers.
The government's lawyer does not decide whose story wins. The same report explains: “If the Notice to Appear does not state a valid ground for removal, the judge must terminate the case.”

This argument shows that immigrants need legal help. It does not show that paying for the other side rejects their account or blocks it. The unequal spending becomes an argument about tolerance only by assuming that support for the government's case works against listening to immigrants.

This argument joins a broad prediction about collection to encounters whose data source is unknown. It does not show which added capability supports the intimidation.
A successful seizure does not show the drop in fentanyl exposure that this argument gives to more scanners.

Section 103 pays for “Procurement and integration of new nonintrusive inspection equipment” . Buying equipment and being able to use it are different. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) reported in January 2026: “Some factors have limited the use of the systems, such as limited staff and system outages.”
Seized fentanyl can be replaced. Jonathan Caulkins explains that synthetic opioids “permit seizures to be replaced in days” . The amount seized does not show how much less fentanyl buyers can get.

Two steps lack support: how this money adds scanning that can really be used, and how added seizures reduce what people are exposed to after suppliers respond. The seized-pill example does not establish the added health protection.
This argument does not connect its pharmacy case to work that Section 102's limited money may pay for.

The money must support “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” Not every activity of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) is an allowed use of this money. Customs concerns goods crossing the border.

The case concerns an international drug operation: “Lopez Reyes led the enterprise, orchestrating and controlling every facet of the scheme from the Dominican Republic.” The report also says “the defendants shipped counterfeit pharmaceuticals to victims across the United States and around the world” .

Finding pill factories in U.S. basements does not place the investigation outside customs work. This argument names no part of this international case that the limited money would expand outside the excluded missions.
One detention does not show that S.2's broader removal money reduces residents' exposure to violence.

Research on a similar detention and deportation program found, “The results show that the Secure Communities program has had no observable effect on the overall crime rate.” Secure Communities shared local arrest fingerprints with immigration officials.

A separate study of violent victimization (being a victim of violent crime) in 2005–2014 reports, “The activation of 287(g) jail enforcement agreements and anti-detainer policies had no significant impact on violent victimization risk during the period.”

The example shows one person kept apart from the public. These studies weigh against assuming that more of this enforcement means less violence. They cover older programs and wider crime measures, so they do not settle what would happen with people who have violent convictions.
Expanding 287(g) agreements does not show that jail transfers would replace public arrests.

These agreements give local officers some immigration powers outside jails too. ICE's February 2026 description says, “The Task Force Model allows your officers to enforce limited immigration authority while performing routine police duties or as an active participant in an ICE-led task force.”

Section 202 pays for agreements in general. It also pays for “release monitoring, transportation, and arrests of covered unlawful aliens encountered in jurisdictions that are not qualified cooperating jurisdictions” .

More authority to make immigration arrests is different from moving the same arrests into jails. This example shows that one transfer was safe. It does not show a change in where arrests happen because of S.2.
The reported end of releases narrows this argument's example about screening before release.
The inspector general found that agents finished record checks before releasing migrants in its sample. That 2022 audit describes how the check worked then.

The older release audit does not show how much checks before release matter under the policy reported at the comparison date. This response is partial. It does not answer the case for keeping checks at the first encounter or before entry, and it does not show that added staff cannot support those checks.

Reported practices had changed in some places before Congress's June 9 vote. May reporting from Chicago found: “Community leaders and rapid responders say they are seeing more targeted arrests rather than the large, highly visible sweeps seen last fall.”
The commander of the Minneapolis operation had also left: “Bovino was relieved of his command following Pretti's killing and retired from Border Patrol in March.”

This argument projects earlier tactics onto the added money without accounting for the reported changes. This response does not answer its point about yearly funding, and it does not show that these tactics have ended.
The mask and identification rules do not change under S.2, and the public-profile part of the FBI's link rests on 2025 conditions.

The FBI account ties impersonation to the “recent increase in ICE enforcement actions” and ICE's “heightened profile” , citing “five 2025 incidents” . It documents crimes under the existing enforcement campaign, not a change in identification caused by S.2.

The report separates existing rules from its advice. Officers must identify themselves “as soon as it is practical and safe to do so.” The FBI also recommends that officers “cooperate with individuals who request further verification” . The bill does not change the identification rule.

May 2026 reports describe less public operations. Chicago-area community leaders reported “more targeted arrests rather than the large, highly visible sweeps seen last fall” , and Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy, said “fewer viral videos of ICE agents making arrests” came from targeted operations. Neither report says that enforcement stopped.

Having no mask ban does not show added confusion compared with existing law, and a 2025 public profile may not fully carry over to less visible operations. This narrows the argument to the link with the number of enforcement actions. It does not show that added operations would create no more opening for impersonators.
This argument does not show that S.2 worsens the staff shortage behind the reported diversion of investigators.
Section 202 pays for “Hiring, paying, training, and equipping” immigration staff. So more immigration work can use new staff. This is not evidence of more transfers from other cases.

Section 102 adds $7.45 billion for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI): “$7,450,000,000” . Its money “shall be used for functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.”

Within that amount, “$108,500,000 shall be used to hire, pay, and equip additional child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts” . This pays for additional people for the work that this argument says lacks staff.

The protected investigation money matters to the claimed staff loss, even though other money can pay for immigration assignments. This argument has not shown that the new hiring money leaves a larger staff gap or causes more investigators to leave other protective work.
The observer example does not show that S.2 expands the monitoring used to discourage people from watching.
The quoted lawyer says threats can scare observers “regardless of whether such databases even exist.” The report shows a threat. It does not show the database or technology behind it.

S.2 pays for technology maintenance for “enforcement and removal operations” . Its additional DHS money is also tied to listed uses: “for the purposes provided in this title or in paragraph (3) or (7) of section 100051 of Public Law 119-21.” These spending permissions do not name an added project to track peaceful observers.
This argument does not connect added monitoring from S.2 to more intimidation or less effective watching. A threat that can work without the claimed database does not supply this link.
The Minneapolis evidence may not carry over to added operations, and the survey came before the reported change in tactics.

Before Congress's June 9 vote, the president had ordered the Minneapolis operation wound down (gradually ended). He gave this job to Tom Homan, a top administration official on border policy: “Earlier this year, Mr. Trump charged Homan with winding down the Minneapolis operation” . KFF's evidence about avoided activities came from the “KFF/New York Times 2025 Survey of Immigrants (August 28-October 20, 2025).” It measured fears before the changes above.

Continued immigration enforcement does not show continued use of the particular surge tactics, so the Minneapolis disruption is weak evidence about added operations. This does not show that fear has gone down, and the survey still supports a link between enforcement fears and avoided activities.
The Social Circle evidence does not show that S.2 increases the risk to water and sewer systems from that project.

In March, the city blocked the water connection and explained: “The lock is there until ICE indicates how water and sewer will be served without exceeding our limited infrastructure capacity” . So there was a limit on the project before S.2.
S.2 pays for “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” It does not change the project's water access or review rules.

The warnings concern one project's design and operation. This argument has not shown that S.2 changes how that project gets water or disposes of waste. This limit could change later, and this response does not cover other sites.
This argument does not establish its chain from more drug detection to less opioid abuse and protected family teaching.

Finding drugs does not show a lasting loss of supply. Drug-policy researcher Jonathan Caulkins explains the problem: “There is little point in working hard to seize drugs that can be replaced at a very low cost.”
GAO also says that the Department of Homeland Security's “ability to fully assess the effectiveness of its efforts is limited.”
The family practice at the end of the chain is teaching faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values” .

This argument needs a reason to expect that added detection reduces abuse even though seized drugs can be replaced cheaply. A scanner's ability to reveal hidden items does not supply that step. Without it, this spending is not connected to protecting the family practice of passing on faith.
The sources limit how far this warning about closing churches can go.
The bishop's instruction was a plan to keep leadership: “The bishop has instructed each congregation with endangered pastors to prepare three laypeople to take over, should their leader be deported.”

The report makes closure depend on more conditions: “In some cases, if the pastor is deported, the congregation may be unable to find a new leader. Documented fixes limit the prediction from earlier bans, while access elsewhere stays uncertain.

An interim agreement at Broadview led to visits before Congress's June 9 vote: “Faith leaders began daily visits Friday, May 15, 2026” . It allowed spiritual care once a day, including “bringing the Sacraments and other religious items approved beforehand.”

Added custody cannot simply be assigned the former bans at sites where access improved. This response is partial: it does not answer added custody at sites without such measures, or where access depends on special help. The persecution evidence does not connect S.2's transport money to more unsafe returns, because the law and other decisions control where people are sent.

The BBC reports that Ali's wife was returned to Iran and summoned by Iranian intelligence. Her lawyer said sensitive information about her change of religion and other reasons for asking for protection “was not removed before deportation.” This account concerns how protection, destinations and religious information were handled.

Existing law bars removal to a country when the official finds this kind of threat, with listed exceptions: “the Attorney General may not remove an alien to a country if the Attorney General decides that the alien's life or freedom would be threatened in that country because of the alien's race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.”

The family report's warning about relatives depends on the destination: “abandoning the religious freedom that is guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution but is not respected by all countries.” Section 202's transport money does not choose destinations or replace decisions about protection.

More removal money alone does not show more returns to religious persecution, including for relatives who move with a deported family member. This does not show that unsafe returns will not happen; the BBC case shows that one did.

GAO reported: “Some factors have limited the use of the systems, such as limited staff and system outages.” Officials at four field offices “did not always have sufficient staff to fully use the systems.” The inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), its internal auditor, found that CBP “did not have a well-defined maintenance and sustainment plan” . Researchers Jonathan Caulkins and Peter Reuter write: “But traffickers can easily replace what is seized.” Caulkins also says synthetic opioids “permit seizures to be replaced in days” . A 2026 review found results in different directions and these were associations, not estimates for S.2. The Government Accountability Office (GAO), a federal audit agency, said DHS’s “ability to fully assess the effectiveness of its efforts is limited.” This does not show that seizures have no benefit.

Studies of similar programs did not find less crime. One found that Secure Communities “has had no observable effect on the overall crime rate.” Another found that “The activation of 287(g) jail enforcement agreements and anti-detainer policies had no significant impact on violent victimization risk during the period.” A third, using 2005–2010 data, found “no evidence that these 287(g) arrangements had meaningful crime reduction benefits.” Secure Communities shared local arrest fingerprints with immigration officials. 287(g) agreements let trained local police do some immigration work. These studies cover older programs and broad crime measures, not only people with violent convictions, so they do not settle the question.

exceptions.text: The Department of the Interior manages many federal lands. It reported that border staff and equipment reduced damaging traffic: “By deploying personnel, equipment, and infrastructure, CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” CBP is Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency.
The Forest Service said that people crossing the border leave trash behind: “Perhaps one of the most well known of the impacts of illegal immigration is the litter left behind” .
This trash can ruin water that wild animals drink: “Water sources near this contamination are often so fouled by pollution that wildlife can no longer use them.”

Section 201 pays for staff, and Section 103 pays for surveillance. Both support patrols like the ones Interior describes. Where added patrols reduce crossings through wild areas, they can reduce this pollution. Protecting water that wildlife uses serves [NAME]'s care for nature.

Section 103 pays for towers on the southwest and northern borders only if CBP (Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency) has tested and accepted them “to deliver autonomous capabilities.” “Autonomous” means the system works without constant human control.
CBP reported that people were caught faster with autonomous towers: “The response time from target identification to suspect apprehension dramatically decreased,”

The Forest Service reported that “unauthorized trails and roads have been created on the Forest by illegal foot and vehicle traffic.” It said that when these trails spread, this “damages and destroys cactus and other sensitive vegetation; disrupts or prohibits revegetation; disturbs wildlife, their security and travel routes; causes soil compaction and erosion” .

Crossing traffic also broke a fence that protected the habitat (home area) of endangered species. The fence became “ineffective in restricting livestock use” . As a result, “This fence damage has allowed the destruction of endangered species habitat to continue” .
Paying for staff and faster detection makes it easier to stop damaging traffic and fence damage. That protects plants, wildlife habitat and soil from destruction, which [NAME] values.

In March 2025, the Department of the Interior described harm from unlawful border activity: “national parks, wildlife refuges and the species they protect are adversely impacted by land degradation and destruction from trail cutting, trash accumulation, invasive species introductions” . “Invasive species” are plants or animals that come from elsewhere and harm local nature.

Border operations have reduced the activity that carries these risks: “CBP operations have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.” CBP is Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency.

Added staff and surveillance help stop this traffic. Less unlawful travel through parks and refuges can reduce one way that harmful species spread there. Reducing this spread is a way to protect nature.

The Forest Service documented the link: “Large numbers of warming and cooking fires built and abandoned by cross-border violators have caused wildfires that have destroyed valuable natural and cultural resources.” “Cross-border violators” means people crossing the border illegally.

S.2 supports a way of reducing this activity that has worked in some areas. The Department of the Interior reported that border operations “have reduced cross-border illegal activity and the environmental impacts of this illegal activity in a number of areas.”
Stopping people before they travel and camp in natural areas makes it easier to prevent these fires. Avoiding fires that destroy nature gives [NAME] another reason to favor S.2.
Section 101 pays to “hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and Border Patrol support personnel to conduct functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions.”
These agents give fire warnings. In April 2025, agents saw smoke near the border. “They promptly contacted fire crews from the Forest Service and Mexico.”

U.S. crews put out the small fires that followed: “U.S. fire services swiftly put out spot fires caused by embers that blew across the border, while Mexican crews battled the main blaze to the south.”

Agents also called for help during a 2021 fire in the Jacumba Wilderness: “El Centro Station notified the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) of the situation.” This response worked: “The combined resources and firefighting efforts were able to control the fires.”
S.2 supports staff who notice fires and bring in the crews needed to control them. This helps protect natural areas from spreading fire.

The Forest Service reported that border enforcement took its officers away from conservation: “The law enforcement efforts in response to cross-border violators and smugglers of controlled substances diverts our officers from other management and resource protection activities.”

The Department of the Interior described “intelligence-supported joint patrols on Interior and USFS managed lands.” (Joint patrols use officers from more than one agency. USFS is the Forest Service.) Interior reported that duties were divided: “Interior law enforcement officers focused on resource mission-related violations during this operation.” These are violations that harm the land and its resources.

Together with the immigration staff in Section 201, Section 103 pays for “Enhancing border security by combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals, at the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.”
S.2 supports the border-enforcement side of this division of work. Keeping land officers' time for protecting natural resources serves [NAME]'s care for nature.

The Forest Service uses fire to care for land, as well as fighting unwanted fires: “The Forest Service works to both fight wildland fires and to use prescribed fires as a tool to manage vegetative resources.” Prescribed fires are planned burns.

Security is part of this work: “The Coronado National Forest must now send armed officers to clear wildland fire areas or provide security for firefighters.” The same testimony says: “Agents of the Border Patrol have been used to help in these efforts.”

Section 101 pays for duties other than immigration and customs enforcement. That supports staff who help make these work areas safe. Helping people carry out this care for plants supports the active defense of nature that [NAME] values.
Section 103 pays for “Air and Marine operations' upgrading and procurement of new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities.” “Platforms” here means aircraft and boats.
Air and sea crews of Customs and Border Protection (CBP) joined a 2024 operation that “located and stopped a total of 19 Mexican fishermen engaged in illegal fishing” .
S.2 pays for equipment used in this work. Making it easier to stop illegal fishing protects sea life and serves [NAME]'s concern for nature.
Section 103 pays for “Air and Marine operations' upgrading and procurement of new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities.” “Platforms” here means aircraft and boats.

During the 2010 oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico, Customs and Border Protection (CBP) reported that its crews were “providing airspace de-confliction and flight advisories to the numerous government agencies that are participating in the clean up and containment efforts.” This means helping cleanup aircraft share the air safely.

S.2's money adds to the aircraft whose crews have been asked to give this help. This use is occasional and depends on which aircraft are bought. But it can add to the ability to coordinate pollution cleanup. Helping contain oil pollution serves [NAME]'s aim of protecting nature.
Section 202 pays for deportation transport: “Funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” “Removal” means deportation.

This transport includes flights: “ICE’s air transportation is being carried out through a network of chartered flights” . ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the agency that arrests, holds and removes noncitizens.
These flights release pollution that heats the planet: “US immigration enforcement flights are producing hundreds of thousands of metric tonnes of climate-damaging carbon emissions” .
They also pollute the air around airports: “planes frequently idling, taking off and landing in the same communities contributes to local air pollution” .
Added transport money supports flights with both kinds of pollution. [NAME]'s wish to protect the environment from pollution gives a reason to oppose that support.

Section 202 pays to keep enforcement facilities in use: “Funding for facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.” It also pays for “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.”

Dilley, Texas, has a detention center used by ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement), and it depends on ICE money. The site stopped operating in 2024 “when funding for the contract with ICE was terminated and the facility was idled” . In March 2025, the company that runs it announced that “it has agreed under an amended intergovernmental services agreement (IGSA) between the City of Dilley, Texas, and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to resume operations” .

ICE's own assessment found that the cleared site offered “limited natural habitat for native wildlife” but expected wildlife to stay away during use: “migratory birds and other wildlife will likely avoid the proposed project area during construction activities and during operations.”

S.2 gives ICE more resources to run facilities with this effect. The disturbance at this already-cleared site is small, but protecting wildlife still gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this added support.

Section 202 pays for “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions” and “Funding for fleet maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.” A fleet is a group of vehicles.
ICE's assessment of a detention center in Dilley, Texas, names sources of air pollution during operation: “vehicular use and emergency generators during the operation phase.”
Added money for these facilities and vehicles supports activities that release air pollution. [NAME]'s wish to prevent pollution gives a reason to oppose this money.
Section 202 pays to run enforcement facilities through “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions” .
The city government of Social Circle, Georgia, warns that running ICE's planned detention center would “risk sewage overflows into nearby land and water” . ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Maryland's assessment of a warehouse in Williamsport explains the same risk. Its agencies estimate sewage flow at “more than seven times the existing projected flow for the facility’s prior commercial use.”
Maryland's agencies explain the risk: “Exceeding the capacity of the sewer lines would likely result in sewage backups and overflows” .
These waters support wildlife: “A number of State-listed Endangered species, Species in Need of Conservation, and other Rare species rely on the waters in the vicinity of the Warehouse property.”

More operating money supports a detention network that is trying to change warehouses into detention centers, and those plans carry documented sewage risks. Protecting land, water and the wildlife that needs them gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this support.
Section 201 pays for “hiring, paying, training, and equipping U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents” for immigration enforcement.

At Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, an agreement between agencies allows off-road patrols in emergencies: “This agreement authorizes border enforcement agents to drive off-road in wilderness under exigent or emergency circumstances that involve threats to human health and safety.” “Exigent” means urgent.
In 2012, the National Park Service reported that, since the agreement began, “monitoring data have shown that off-road-vehicle impacts have increased” .
The Park Service explains the physical harm from these roads and trails: “These incursions damage soils, vegetation, and wildlife habitat.”
Extra money for these patrols supports off-road driving that damages soil, plants and habitat. Protecting wild places gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this money.
Sections 201 and 202 pay immigration enforcement staff “to carry out immigration enforcement activities.”

This work reaches forest workers. In 2025, Border Patrol arrested a firefighter whose work included “clearing fallen trees and other debris to prevent the Bear Gulch fire, a 9,000-acre blaze, from growing” . He was later “quietly deported to Mexico” .

ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) has also removed tree-planting crews. After a 2007 raid on a company replanting burned land in Boise National Forest, “Ten of the workers were deported to Mexico and four others were released pending an immigration hearing” .
This work had a short planting season. A Forest Service spokesperson explained: “You have to plant in cooler times, when the ground is moist” .
Late replanting threatens nature. In 2025, the Forest Resources Association warned that without timely reforestation (replanting), “these lands risk erosion, habitat loss” .
More ability to arrest and remove these workers puts time-sensitive forest care at risk. Protecting forests gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this added ability.

Section 103 pays for aircraft and related equipment of Customs and Border Protection (CBP): “Air and Marine operations' upgrading and procurement of new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities.”

This branch of CBP uses surveillance drones (aircraft with no pilot on board) to help other police agencies. A 2025 CBP statement reported that “MQ-9 Predators are supporting our federal law enforcement partners in the Greater Los Angeles area, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement, with aerial support of their operations.”
