CBP has used such tools at environmental protests: “Customs and Border Protection responded to the protests with its MQ-9 Reaper drone” . The Standing Rock movement wanted “to protect water, the climate, and Indigenous sovereignty” . During a 2020 pipeline dispute, “CBP flew drones over its planned pipeline route and over the homes of anti-pipeline activists” .

Researcher Nathan Goodman explains how this can keep people from taking part: “Surveilling protesters is a concerning use of drones, as it may chill or repress speech, association and assembly protected by the First Amendment.” To “chill” speech means to make people afraid to speak.

S.2's aircraft money can add to or upgrade the group of aircraft whose drones have been used to watch people defending the environment. The bill does not name drones. The added risk of discouraging these people gives [NAME], who values taking part in defending nature, a reason to oppose this money.
Section 102 sets aside money for more investigators and evidence analysts: “$108,500,000 shall be used to hire, pay, and equip additional child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts” .

Their job is “to support the identification and rescue of victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse” . The money also pays to train investigators and local police: “to train such personnel and State and local law enforcement regarding identifying victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse” .

Representative Lee described the need: “Today, more than 89,000 children depicted in child sex abuse material remain unidentified.” In fiscal year 2024, an international operation hosted by the victim-identification lab of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes) led to the “identification and assistance of over 140 victims.”

More investigators, analysts and trained police make it easier to find these children and help them escape abuse. Children cannot make themselves safe. Protecting them serves [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people and their chance of a safe childhood.

Section 102 adds money “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” and for the operations of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the part of ICE that investigates crimes.
HSI's Project iGuardian teaches children, parents and community groups through “in-person presentations” . Its wider campaign aims to “prevent and combat online child sexual exploitation and abuse” .

S.2's general HSI money can help keep or grow this teaching, although the bill does not direct money to it. The teaching gives families tools to see danger and ask for help before abuse takes hold. Helping children protect themselves serves [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people.

Section 102 pays for agents of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes) and “other necessary expenses for Homeland Security Investigations' mission support and operations and maintenance” .

This work includes criminal cases about forcing people into sex or work: “Homeland Security Investigations initiated 1,686 criminal investigations related to sex trafficking and forced labor, leading to 2,545 arrests.” These are fiscal year 2024 results.

One HSI-backed sex-trafficking case involved adults and children and brought an abuser to justice: “the defendant was found guilty at a jury trial and sentenced to 380 months” after using “violence, false imprisonment and the use of drugs.”
HSI's victim program also makes sure survivors “are informed of their rights” and “receive necessary assistance” . Earlier added money was used “to create 76 new full-time positions” .

More resources for investigations and victim support help people escape force and get help afterward. Freedom from forced sex and work, access to help, and justice against abusers serve [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people and equal opportunities.
Section 102's staff and operating money supports the criminal work of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), including “wire fraud, identity theft, bank fraud” .

ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which includes HSI) reported that in fiscal year 2024, “HSI also conducted 258 elder fraud cases” , producing “121 indictments, 52 convictions, and $12.6 million seized.” HSI also investigated romance scams: “HSI conducted 61 romance fraud” cases that year.

More ability to investigate these scams, win convictions and take criminals' money strengthens protection against financial harm. [NAME] has a reason to protect victims' money and seek justice for them, including strangers targeted because of age or trust.
Section 102 adds resources for staff of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes) and “mission support and operations and maintenance” .

HSI's human rights center helps prosecute people for “human rights violations and war crimes” committed before they came to the United States. In fiscal year 2024, it “supported more than 180 investigations” related to suspected war criminals.
Resources for investigating and prosecuting these crimes help hold abusers responsible. [NAME]'s concern for justice reaches victims abroad, including people [NAME] has never met.

Section 103 adds $3.45 billion for inspection equipment, air and sea response, surveillance and related work: “$3,450,000,000 for the following” . Its purposes include “to combat the entry or exit of illicit narcotics at ports of entry and along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders” .

The work includes “combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” . Precursor chemicals are the ingredients used to make drugs. ICE describes the danger as “the synthetic drugs that fuel overdose deaths” . An overdose means taking enough of a drug to cause serious harm or death.
Finding and stopping these drugs keeps seized drugs from reaching people. More resources for this work strengthen protection for people at risk of overdose, whose lives matter to [NAME].

Section 202 pays for staff “to carry out immigration enforcement activities” and “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” “Removal” means deportation.

This work includes taking custody of people convicted of attacks on children. ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) reported a January 2026 arrest of a man convicted of “first-degree rape of a child” : “upon his release from prison Jan. 2, ICE took him into custody for removal to Mexico.”

Added staff and transport support taking people with violent convictions into custody after prison. Custody keeps them away from possible victims in the community, which gives [NAME] a reason to support protection against more attacks.
Section 102 pays for agents and support staff of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes) and “mission support and operations and maintenance” .

HSI's National Security Unit “supports counterterrorism investigations within HSI.” HSI's fiscal year 2024 results in this work included “70 criminal indictments” . ICE said HSI helped produce “terrorism-related disruptions.”
Resources for investigating and stopping terrorist threats strengthen protection for people who could face violence. [NAME]'s concern includes possible victims who are strangers.

Section 102 adds resources for staff of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes) and “mission support and operations and maintenance” . HSI's criminal work includes protecting computer systems.

HSI's Operation Cyber Centurion fights attacks on “major utilities, healthcare, public education” , financial systems and emergency services. In fiscal year 2024, it “disrupted 195” computer break-ins and attacks.

Resources to stop attacks on hospitals, utilities and emergency services protect people who need these services for safety and care. This serves [NAME]'s concern for people least able to protect themselves during an emergency.

Section 103 pays for “new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities” , meaning aircraft and boats. Section 101 pays for Border Patrol staff for “functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions.”

These teams carry out rescues. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) reported that an April 2024 aircrew found lost migrants, landed, and treated a man who was not responding and was “severely dehydrated and suffering from heat exhaustion.” A Border Patrol emergency medical technician then took over his care.

CBP explained how this works: “The ability of our agents to rapidly transition from a law enforcement role to conduct rescue operations where they can deliver immediate medical aid is crucial to saving lives.”
More resources for air response and rescue staff strengthen lifesaving help for people stranded at the border. [NAME] has a reason to protect them whatever their immigration status.
Section 202(3) lists “body-worn cameras” among the uses of its added technology money. These are small cameras worn by officers.

The February 2025 camera policy of ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) makes wider use depend on “appropriated funding resources.” It tells officers to record “interactions with the public during Enforcement Activities” in areas where the camera program operates.
The policy allows review of recordings “to assess, evaluate, or address any officer action” , including “civil liberties, or any other issues.” Civil liberties are basic rights protected by law.

Added resources for camera use support evidence about how officers treat people. Evidence for reviewing disputed encounters serves [NAME]'s concern that people facing government power be treated justly.
Section 202 pays for ICE staff across its branches and “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

ICE's fiscal year 2026 budget names medical care as part of those operations: “Custody Operations program’s detainee healthcare activities” . These services include “medical, mental, and dental health services” .

More resources available for staff and custody health services support care for people who depend on the government for treatment. Protecting people in this dependent position serves [NAME]'s concern for vulnerable people of any nationality.
The bill pays for staff training and equipment, including money “to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and Border Patrol support personnel” and similar money for other agency staff.

A report by the inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) describes protective gear as “equipment to protect them while on duty.” It also describes defensive training “to mitigate and prevent assaults” .

Resources for protective equipment and safety training support safer work. Protecting workers against known job dangers is part of treating them justly, which gives [NAME] a reason to favor this money too.

The Brennan Center, a law and policy institute, says the money would let the Department of Homeland Security continue the Trump administration's mass deportation strategy. It says this strategy has included “locking up immigrants who pose no public safety threat” .
Section 202(9) sets aside an arrest and custody fund of “Not less than $350,000,000” .

For this fund, the bill rules out spending on release or on alternatives such as check-ins, except when existing law requires it: “None of the funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph may be used, except as required by existing law, to release, parole, place on alternatives to detention” . “Parole” here means letting a person out of custody for a time.

The bill adds capacity to take away people's freedom under a strategy that reaches people who pose no safety threat. It also rules out less restrictive uses of this fund. Just treatment gives [NAME] a reason to oppose paying for that loss of freedom.

Section 202 pays for more federal staff and for local police to take part through “expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” . These agreements “allow state and local law enforcement agencies to perform certain immigration enforcement functions” .

More staff and a wider enforcement network extend the reach of an operation with documented stops based on race. Being held because of one's background conflicts with equal opportunities and just treatment.

Section 202 pays for government lawyers “to represent the Department in immigration enforcement and removal proceedings.” A removal proceeding is the legal process that decides whether a person must leave the United States.
An inspection of Camp East Montana, a detention site, found violations including “no way for detainees to contact their families and lawyers.”

A person who cannot reach a lawyer has less chance to challenge the government's case. Adding removal capacity in a system with these barriers increases the risk of removal without a fair chance to defend oneself. Concern for just treatment reaches these strangers.
Section 202 pays for “facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.”
Human Rights Watch documented conditions in Florida in 2025, including “overcrowding, degrading treatment and denial of medical care” .
Before Congress's June 9 vote, Senator Kim described a very sick man he met in detention: “He should have been in a hospital, but, instead, he was isolated in that cramped room for 5 months.”
Children also face unsafe conditions: “In Dilley, families described receiving food with worms and mold, tainted water, and inadequate education.”

The new operating money lasts until September 2029, although these are “federal agencies that are typically funded through the annual appropriations process.” This means Congress usually decides their money each year.
The bill keeps a system with these dangers going and adds money it can use without new yearly approval. That makes refusing a future year's operating money a weaker way to demand safer conditions.

Human Rights Watch said on June 16 that Congress approved S.2 “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” Lawmakers and activists had proposed reforms such as requiring warrants from judges and stronger bans on racial profiling. Paying for more detention without those reforms exposes people who depend on their jailers to more harm. Protecting children and sick people gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this money.
Detaining parents has already harmed children who are U.S. citizens: “U.S. citizen children have experienced family separation as a result of a parent being detained.”
The harm includes losing care during a medical crisis. A father “was detained on his way to the hospital in Texas to deliver milk to his premature 12-day-old daughter.”

Paying for more arrests, detention and removals raises the risk of losing daily care from a parent, including for babies who need it urgently. Protecting children who depend on parents gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this expansion.

Senator Smith described help needed during Minnesota's enforcement operation: “Churches and neighbors organized mutual aid and delivered prescriptions to folks who couldn't leave their own homes.” She also described “food deliveries for people who were afraid to go to the grocery store.”
Children suffered lasting trauma and missed school: “Kids traumatized by these tactics and still not back in school.”

School harm also reaches children of U.S.-born parents. A research review reports that “negative academic impacts following immigration enforcement actions extended to U.S.-born students with U.S.-born parents.”
The same review describes lasting effects, with “one study finding notable reductions in 4-year college enrollment following a large-scale worksite raid in Texas in 2018.”

Paying for more such operations extends a threat to getting food and medicine, and to children's well-being and schooling. Protecting vulnerable people and equal chances in life gives [NAME] a reason to oppose these wider harms to communities.
Representative Thompson reported that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) used earlier money to “break into homes without warrants” . A warrant is official permission to enter or arrest.
S.2 adds enforcement money without the proposed requirement for warrants from judges: “It does not require officers to get judicial warrants.”

In May, the DHS secretary wrote that ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) “has not rescinded the memorandum; however, I have paused the practice of entering an illegal alien’s residence who is subject to a final order of removal with an I-205” , “while I assess the policy.” “Rescinded” means cancelled. An I-205 is ICE's removal warrant.

S.2's operating money would pay for operations in which such entries could start again after the review, and it adds no rule requiring a judge's approval. Protecting people from unchecked entry into their homes is part of treating strangers justly. So this risk gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the money.

Lives were at stake. The Brennan Center, a law and policy institute, says Democratic legislators blocked more funding for the Department of Homeland Security and demanded reforms after “the killing of U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.”

Representative McCollum reported: “Peaceful demonstrators were threatened and detained for exercising their First Amendment rights.” The First Amendment protects free speech and protest in the United States.

Human Rights Watch said on June 16 that Congress approved S.2 “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” Lawmakers and activists had proposed reforms such as requiring warrants from judges and stronger bans on racial profiling. More money without those reforms extends the risk of injury, death and unjust detention to people caught in these operations and to people peacefully helping others. Protecting them and treating peaceful advocacy justly gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this money.

Section 103 pays for “Upgrades and procurement of border surveillance technologies along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” Section 202 also pays for “information technology maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations” .

The Brennan Center, a law and policy institute, predicts a wider effect from the funding it describes, which includes S.2's money: “The funding will also allow DHS to continue to build surveillance capabilities that facilitate indiscriminate collection of information about Americans as well as immigrants.” “Indiscriminate” means without choosing carefully. DHS is the Department of Homeland Security.

This money adds capacity to collect people's information without separating people involved in wrongdoing from everyone else. Just treatment gives [NAME] a reason to oppose exposing strangers to this intrusion and checking.
Immigrant workers support other workers' jobs: “significant job losses among immigrant workers could mean less demand for other work done by U.S.-born workers.”

Such losses have already reached one local industry. Minnesota's enforcement operations harmed its restaurant industry, contributing to “about 4,600 lost jobs and $71 million in lost wages in the first three months of 2026” .

Paying for more removals threatens the jobs and earnings of people other than those removed. Lost pay makes basic needs harder to meet for families with little money. Protecting their livelihoods and chances in life gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the added removal money.
Section 202 pays for ICE staff across its branches, including investigators and lawyers, “to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

ICE's human rights center handles immigration cases involving “individuals who have persecuted others based on race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion” . To persecute means to harm or punish people because of who they are or what they believe.
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the part of ICE that investigates crimes, also investigates crimes including “torture, genocide, recruitment and use of child soldiers” .
HSI's work includes “Supporting efforts to return violators to their home countries to face justice for the crimes they committed there.”
Past money helped ICE's human rights center “increase staffing and, in turn, to generate more case leads.”
Section 102 adds resources for criminal human rights investigations; section 202 adds resources for immigration cases against persecutors.
Persecution attacks the differences [NAME] values accepting. Holding persecutors responsible gives [NAME] a reason to pay for this work.

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the part of ICE that investigates crimes, already investigates efforts by foreign governments to silence people abroad: “HSI already works to investigate allegations of transnational repression” . Transnational repression means a government threatening its critics in other countries.
These threats include “incidents targeting individuals critical of foreign authoritarian regimes, like the Iranian regime and the Communist Chinese Party” .

Section 102 adds resources for investigators whose work includes stopping these threats. Protecting critics from being forced into silence defends their ability to hold and express views that others reject. [NAME]'s acceptance of people despite disagreement gives a reason to support this protection.

The victim program of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes) uses support staff covered by Section 102's money: “forensic interviewers, victim assistance specialists” . Forensic interviewers are trained to question victims carefully for legal cases.
HSI provides “interpreters and translation services, allowing victims to fully understand and communicate their needs as they navigate legal, medical and support systems.”
Its victim support uses a “culturally sensitive approach” . Interview specialists “create neutral, safe spaces where victims are empowered to share information in their own words.”

Section 102 supports staff and services that help people explain their experiences across differences in language and culture. Paying for this work directly serves [NAME]'s wish to listen to and understand people who are different.
Victim specialists at Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes) “support and provide services to victims, regardless of their immigration status” .

Their work includes more than interviews: “HSI's special agents and Victim Assistance Program Specialists (VAPs) focus on removing victims from dangerous situations and ensuring their basic needs are met.”
HSI describes this support as “delivery of services in a nonjudgmental manner.”

Section 102 supports help for victims in HSI cases across differences in immigration status. Treating these people as worthy of care puts acceptance into practice, including when someone disagrees with their entry or stay. [NAME]'s tolerance gives a reason to pay for this help.
S.2 pays for staff and operations of Customs and Border Protection (CBP) “in order to carry out immigration enforcement activities.”

Human Rights Watch documented tactics by ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) and CBP in Los Angeles in summer 2025 that included “detaining people based on their perceived race, ethnicity, or national origin” .

Human Rights Watch said on June 16 that Congress approved S.2 “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” Lawmakers and activists had proposed reforms such as requiring warrants from judges and stronger bans on racial profiling. More capacity for these operations, without those reforms, increases the risk of this documented practice of treating groups as suspects.
Accepting different ethnic and national groups gives [NAME] a reason to oppose added support for treating people's background as a reason for suspicion.
S.2 pays for “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” “Removal” means deportation.

A report published before Congress's June 9 vote found: “Individuals who are not public safety threats and have deep ties to their communities have been indiscriminately targeted under this administration.” It also records children experiencing “family separation as a result of a parent being detained.”

The bill sets aside “Not less than $350,000,000” for certain immigration arrest and custody work, including “custodial transfer, release monitoring, transportation, and arrests of covered unlawful aliens” .

Some adults qualify without a conviction: “following an arrest, charge, booking, or conviction for a criminal offense under Federal, State, or local law, other than a minor traffic offense, is the subject of an immigration detainer, notice request, or custody-transfer request issued by the Department of Homeland Security” . A detainer is a government request to hold a person for immigration officers.

This arrest fund cannot pay for release or community alternatives unless existing law requires it: “None of the funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph may be used, except as required by existing law, to release, parole, place on alternatives to detention” .
The added deportation money and the arrest fund's preference for custody strengthen the means of separating people from community life, including parents and people without convictions.
Accepting different people as neighbors gives [NAME] a reason to oppose more ability to exclude the established community members described above, who are not threats.

S.2 pays for “expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” . These are “agreements that allow state and local law enforcement agencies to perform certain immigration enforcement functions” .

A 2012 survey of Latinos in four counties found that people were reluctant to contact police “specifically because they fear that police officers will inquire about the immigration status of themselves, their friends, or their family members.”
The same survey found: “Many Latinos feel isolated and admit to withdrawing from their community.”

Recent reporting also describes this withdrawal. In March 2025, CalMatters reported a volunteer's account that “some families have refused to leave the house for fear of apprehension by immigration enforcement agents.”
Expanding the immigration role of local police strengthens a reason residents give for avoiding contact. The harm reaches beyond people who are detained: fear keeps other neighbors apart.
[NAME]'s wish to listen to and understand different people gives a reason to oppose this added barrier to everyday contact.

S.2 pays for government lawyers “to represent the Department in immigration enforcement and removal proceedings.” A removal proceeding is the legal process that decides whether a person must leave the United States.

The American Immigration Council explains the existing imbalance: “Yet, in every immigration case, the government is represented by a trained attorney who can argue for deportation, regardless of whether the immigrant is represented.”

The same report explains why detention makes it harder for an immigrant to answer: “Attorneys must adhere to strict visitation rules, making it difficult for lawyers to communicate with their clients.”
A detention inspection described before Congress's June 9 vote found “no way for detainees to contact their families and lawyers.”
The bill directs added legal help toward the case for deportation in a system where people in custody face documented barriers to presenting their own case.
[NAME]'s wish to hear and understand those people gives a reason to oppose this spending priority.
S.2 pays for “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.” This is money for ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement).

In October 2025, Human Rights Watch documented “excessive force against peaceful protesters, legal observers, volunteer street medics, and journalists” outside a detention center in Broadview, Illinois.

Its findings rest on witnesses and video: “Witnesses and video confirm that DHS agents used tear gas and fired projectiles directly into groups of protesters, including from the detention facility roof, often without warning, and without protesters appearing to pose any risk to agents.” DHS is the Department of Homeland Security.

Human Rights Watch said on June 16 that Congress approved S.2 “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” Lawmakers and activists had proposed reforms such as requiring warrants from judges and stronger bans on racial profiling. Added operating money without those reforms supports enforcement with a documented pattern of frightening peaceful critics and people who help others hear their views.
Accepting people who disagree gives [NAME] a reason to oppose added support for this intimidation.
S.2 pays for “information technology maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations” .

The Brennan Center, a law and policy institute, predicts wider surveillance from the funding it describes, which includes S.2's money: “The funding will also allow DHS to continue to build surveillance capabilities that facilitate indiscriminate collection of information about Americans as well as immigrants.” DHS is the Department of Homeland Security.
NPR did not print one observer's last name because “she fears retaliation from the federal government for speaking out.”
The added capacity supports surveillance with a documented use against critics and a documented fear of punishment for speaking. That pressures people to hide their voices.
[NAME]'s acceptance of disagreement gives a reason to oppose extending this pressure on peaceful speech.
S.2 pays for “facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.”

Washington's Department of Health reported in April 2026: “DOH has seen an increase in complaints regarding lack of access to religious services, prayer, and religious diets during Ramadan 2026.” Ramadan is a Muslim holy month.

A March 2026 report describes a Muslim detainee's request to pray with others: “Vijandre has asked the facility’s chaplain for a quieter place and permission to pray with the dozens of other Muslim detainees in their housing unit. The chaplain tried to help, but Vijandre said he learned the warden denied the request.”

Human Rights Watch said on June 16 that Congress approved S.2 “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” Lawmakers and activists had proposed reforms such as requiring warrants from judges and stronger bans on racial profiling. Added support for detention without those reforms helps keep centers running with current, documented barriers to minority worship.
Accepting different religious groups gives [NAME] a reason to oppose added money for holding people under conditions that block their faith.

Section 103 pays for new scanners and for stopping drugs: “Procurement and integration of new nonintrusive inspection equipment” and “combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” . Nonintrusive inspection equipment scans vehicles without opening them. Precursor chemicals are the ingredients used to make drugs.

Scanners have helped find hidden fentanyl. In a 2024 vehicle inspection, “CBP officers used non-intrusive technology to screen the sedan revealing anomalies inside all four tires of the vehicle.” (CBP is Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency.) Officers found packages in the tires: “Four of the packages contained nearly 54,000 blue fentanyl pills” .
These drugs are a hidden, deadly health risk: “Drugs may contain deadly levels of fentanyl, and you wouldn't be able to see it, taste it, or smell it.”

Finding and seizing hidden drugs keeps those drugs out of circulation. Paying for more of this work strengthens protection against a poison in the U.S. drug supply, which serves [NAME]'s wish to protect their health.
Section 102 pays for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the criminal investigation branch of ICE: “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” .

HSI and its partners have investigated fake pharmacies selling pills made in U.S. drug factories. Their report describes taking pills from those factories: “Law enforcement raided at least three of these pill mills and two other narcotics storage locations, seizing approximately 625,000 counterfeit pills” .

This fraud reaches people seeking health care. The report describes victims “who were in need of medication — people suffering with legitimate ailments.” It reports, “At least nine of the victims later died of narcotics poisoning.”
Added money supports finding these sellers and removing their poisoned pills from sale. That protects people seeking medicine, which gives [NAME] a health reason to favor this added capacity.
Section 202 pays for enforcement staff and “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” “Removal” means deportation.

This work includes custody after a criminal sentence ends. ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) reported that it “apprehended an illegally present Dominican national convicted for murder in Massachusetts in 2007 when officers arrested Cesar Augusto Polanco, 59, January 24 at the Massachusetts Correctional Institution in Norfolk after he was released from state custody.”
ICE kept him in custody for the removal process: “Polanco remains in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.”

Holding people with violent convictions after prison, and removing them, keeps them away from people they could attack here. Added money for staff and transport supports this protection for U.S. residents such as [NAME].

Section 202 pays for partnerships with state and local police: “Supporting coordination with state and local authorities by expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act” .

One kind of agreement lets trained local officers identify people in jail for immigration proceedings. ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) explains that they “place them into immigration proceedings at the time of release from state or local custody.”

A transfer can avoid a dangerous arrest in public. In the Polanco case, ICE said cooperation let officers “make the arrest in the safety of a jail cell rather than sending a team of officers into the community to make a potentially dangerous arrest.”

Paying for these partnerships supports more arrests in controlled places. Keeping these confrontations out of public places protects people nearby, which gives [NAME] a separate reason based on personal safety.

Section 102 pays for staff of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes), including “other necessary expenses for Homeland Security Investigations' mission support and operations and maintenance” . The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) says HSI “conducts criminal human trafficking investigations worldwide.” Human trafficking means forcing or tricking people into work or sex.

Trafficking is a danger inside U.S. life: “many human traffickers and victims are U.S. citizens.” Contact can begin through ordinary relationships or job searches: “They can be relatives, romantic partners, or close family friends. Or they can be the people behind an employment ad or a new friend on social media or online gaming.”

Traffickers' control includes “actual physical assaults and sexual violence” . Finding victims also opens a way to help, including “medical and mental health care, safety planning, and legal services” .

Added money supports finding violent exploitation and bringing victims into protection and care. Protection against abuse through everyday work and relationships serves the personal safety [NAME] values.

Section 102 pays for agents of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes) “to hire, pay, train, and equip” . Section 203 also allows support for state and local crime prevention through “paragraph (3) or (7) of section 100051 of Public Law 119-21” ; paragraph (7) of that 2025 law includes “addressing crime and public safety threats” .

HSI has helped investigate gang violence that led to convictions. A Justice Department report says “the defendants were also convicted of conspiring with each other and committing acts of violence” , and names the investigators: “The ATF, HSI, DEA, U.S. Marshals Service, Metropolitan Nashville Police Department, Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, La Vergne Police Department, and Kentucky State Police investigated the case.”

The danger reaches ordinary residents: “Throughout the course of the conspiracy, the MS-13 members committed several armed carjackings of citizens near the Nashville, Tennessee, area.” MS-13 is a violent gang. A carjacking is stealing a car from a person by force.

Paying for federal investigators and local partners strengthens the ability to investigate and prosecute violent gangs. Stopping their attacks protects [NAME]'s safety when moving through the community.
Section 201 pays for border agents and support staff “in order to carry out immigration enforcement activities.”

The Border Patrol uses names, photographs and fingerprints in these checks. Its inspector general (an internal auditor) reports: “The e3 Portal captures biographical information, photos, and fingerprints and automatically compares them to a series of Federal law enforcement databases that provide real-time potential criminal history information, including wants, warrant data, and terrorist watchlist matches.”

The checks inform decisions to release people: “We determined that Border Patrol agents conducted required record checks and verified the checks did not contain derogatory information before releasing the migrants from our sample.”
Paying and equipping agents supports a check for security threats before people enter U.S. communities. That protection against terrorism serves [NAME]'s wish to avoid danger.
Section 101 pays for Border Patrol staff for “functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions.”

The Border Patrol had an “immediate requirement to assist the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in implementing its May 18, 2026 Order” , with guidance on “screening, processing, and expulsion procedures under Title 42 authority.” These are duties under public health law.

The May 18 order's stated term covered June 9: “This order will be in effect for 30 days, effective immediately.” The CDC described its goal as “preventing its introduction into the United States.” It explains the danger: “Ebola is a serious viral disease that spreads through direct contact with infected bodily fluids and can be fatal.”

The CDC issued a continuing order on June 21, effective at 5:00 p.m. that day through July 21, and asked the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to help enforce it. This later evidence shows that DHS's supporting role continued after the May order's stated term. It does not name the Border Patrol, show unbroken coverage between the orders, or settle whether Section 101 can pay for this work.

Paying staff who carry out these existing health protections supports efforts to keep infection from reaching U.S. communities while the health orders apply. [NAME]'s wish to avoid disease gives a reason to support this added help.
Section 103 pays for “Air and Marine operations' upgrading and procurement of new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities.” “Platforms” here means aircraft and boats.

These crews use their boats and aircraft to rescue people. A report describes a boat crew in Rochester finding a person in distress: “Agents rescued that person, observed signs of hypothermia, and provided medical attention.” Hypothermia means dangerously low body temperature.

Aircraft also reach stranded people. After finding people beside a capsized boat in Montana, a pilot “landed on a nearby sandbar, assessed the condition of two people, and loaded them into the helicopter.”
Better aircraft and boats add ways to reach people in emergencies and bring them to safety. That serves [NAME]'s interest in surviving accidents and getting help when in danger.

Section 202 pays for more enforcement staff: “Hiring, paying, training, and equipping U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel and the personnel for all its directorates, including officers, agents, investigators, attorneys and support staff, to carry out immigration enforcement activities.”
Citizens have been physically harmed: “Americans have been dragged, tackled, beaten, tased and shot by immigration agents.”
People can be caught up while doing ordinary things. ProPublica reports that “agents grabbed and handcuffed a woman on her way to work who was caught up in a chaotic raid on street vendors.”
More operations using these practices create more chances for dangerous encounters during work and travel. [NAME]'s wish to avoid injury or death gives a reason to oppose this added exposure.
S.2 supports custody as well as arrests: “Funding for facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.”
Being a citizen does not keep people out of this system: “We found more than 50 Americans who were held after agents questioned their citizenship.”
Neglect is a wider problem in custody. Human Rights Watch documented detention conditions in Florida in 2025 that included “overcrowding, degrading treatment and denial of medical care” .

Medical neglect has reached citizens. A detained car wash owner's lawyer said “he was held for 12 hours and wasn’t given medical attention despite having broken ribs in the incident and having recently had heart surgery.”

Paying for more arrests and custody adds to the risk from a system where even citizens have been denied urgent care. Avoiding this danger to health and personal safety gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the money.

S.2 pays for 287(g) agreements, which let local police do immigration enforcement: “Supporting coordination with state and local authorities by expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1357(g)).”
The program again includes a street-policing version, called the task force model: “Allows officers trained by ICE to enforce immigration law during routine police activity, like traffic stops.”

A study using national crime-victim survey data from 2005–2014 found a higher risk of being a victim of violent crime: “the activation of Secure Communities and 287(g) task force agreements significantly increased violent victimization risk among Latinos” .

The reporting problem also weakens police protection for the wider public. The president of the Major Cities Chiefs Association explained: “Whether we seek to stop child predators, drug dealers, rapists or robbers – we need the full cooperation of victims and witness. Cooperation is not forthcoming from persons who see their police as immigration agents.”

A February–March 2026 survey with a random sample of adults in Minneapolis and St. Paul asked about Operation Metro Surge, a large federal immigration deployment. In Minneapolis 49.4% and in St. Paul 46.1% agreed that they were less likely to seek help from police because of how ICE and Border Patrol agents carried it out. These are reported intentions about a federal operation, not measured crime results or an effect of local police working under 287(g).

Paying to expand this police role expands a barrier to reporting crime and helping investigations. [NAME] relies on police being able to find and stop dangerous offenders, so this loss of cooperation gives [NAME] a personal safety reason to oppose S.2.
The FBI has documented the danger: “Criminals posing as US immigration officers have carried out robberies, kidnappings, and sexual assaults in several states” .

Its bulletin connects this danger to how visible enforcement has become. WIRED reports that “criminals are using Immigration and Custom Enforcement’s heightened profile to target vulnerable communities, making it harder for Americans to distinguish between lawful officers and imposters while eroding trust in law enforcement.”
S.2 leaves masked operations in place: “The GOP bill does not restrict mask-wearing” GOP means the Republican Party..

More operations in this form give fake officers more of the cover (conditions that help them hide) they already use and make fake arrests harder to recognize. Avoiding robbery, kidnapping and assault gives [NAME] a safety reason to oppose this expansion.
S.2 pays for deportations: “Funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.”

Past enforcement reduced nursing care. A study comparing counties as Secure Communities began found that “the program reduced directcare staff hours per resident day” . These are hours of hands-on care in nursing homes. Secure Communities shared local arrest fingerprints with immigration officials.

Another study of that program's start in 2008–2013 found both fewer home care workers and less help for older adults: “We find that Secure Communities reduces the overall size of the home care workforce by 7.5%” ; “older adults needing assistance are 2.9 percentage points less likely to receive any help at home” .

Among Twin Cities survey respondents who missed work over enforcement concerns, about 28% reported a caregiver who could not come. This is a local self-report about disrupted care, not a drop in the national care workforce.

S.2 pays to expand local immigration checks, arrests and removals. The earlier program and recent reports support a risk to care being available. They do not estimate how much S.2 would add to this risk.
Long-term care is an ordinary health need over a lifetime: “Most Americans will need long-term care at some point in their lifetimes” .

Shortages also threaten hospital care. JAMA, a medical journal, explains: “The resulting shortages could reverberate through emergency departments and hospitals, leading to the inability to discharge patients and tying up nurses and other staff.”
[NAME] depends on timely care, whether at home, in a nursing home or in a hospital. Protecting access to this care gives [NAME] a health reason to oppose the added enforcement money.
Enforcement already reaches medical settings: “The Infectious Diseases Society of America is alarmed by reports of immigration enforcement activity occurring near health care settings.”
S.2 expands enforcement without adding protections for hospitals. Representative Thompson said of S.2: “It does not stop raids at daycares, churches, or even hospitals.”

Clinicians explain how this discourages care: “When patients fear that seeking care could expose them or their loved ones to immigration enforcement, they delay or avoid treatment, disengage from therapeutic care, decline crisis services, and withhold clinically relevant information.”

In the 2026 Twin Cities survey, 29.2% of Minneapolis respondents with scheduled appointments and 20.6% in St. Paul reported missing one because of enforcement concerns. This is a recent self-report, not an estimate of what S.2 would add.

Infectious disease specialists name the wider health risk: “Fear of seeking health care puts individual patients at risk and threatens the health of entire communities, including by delaying the timely identification and treatment of infectious diseases.”

Expanding enforcement around these services adds barriers to finding and treating infections. [NAME] shares the community's exposure to diseases that spread, so protecting disease control gives [NAME] a health reason to oppose S.2.
S.2 pays to keep enforcement facilities running: “Funding for facility maintenance and sustainment to support enforcement and removal operations.”

KFF, a health research group, reports “recent measles outbreaks in Arizona and Texas detention facilities” and explains: “Overcrowding as well as limited capacity and resources may also increase the risk of the spread of communicable diseases, such as measles.” Communicable diseases are diseases that spread between people.

Outbreaks have infected people outside the detained population. In its report on mumps outbreaks in 2018–2019 in migrant detention facilities, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recorded that “an additional 33 cases occurred among staff members.”

Staff connect detention facilities to daily community life: “ICE detention facilities are often located in small, isolated towns that employ local residents who move each day between facility and community.”

More arrests feeding this system, and money to keep it running, increase chances for infections to reach the public through staff. [NAME]'s interest in avoiding disease gives a reason to oppose this added exposure.

Psychiatrists describe the link from enforcement fears to illness: “Fear of detention, deportation, or family separation acts as a chronic psychological stressor, contributing to anxiety, depression, trauma-related symptoms, sleep disturbance, isolation from community support, and worsening of serious mental illness.” A stressor is something that causes long-term strain.

People do not need to be detained to suffer these effects: “Reports of violent encounters involving federal immigration agents, including recent fatal and non fatal shootings, intensify fear, psychological distress, and community-wide trauma.”
Paying for more of these operations exposes the wider community to fear and trauma. [NAME]'s wish to protect mental health and be personally secure gives a reason to oppose this expansion.

The April 2026 yearly funding law left out the Border Patrol and ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement): it “did not include funding for the U.S. Border Patrol or U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement” .

An April 3 presidential directive had already told the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to use funds with “a reasonable and logical nexus to the functions of DHS” to pay employees during this gap, “subject to the availability of appropriations.” A nexus is a link. So S.2 adds money set aside for these agencies on top of this instruction. It does not create the first possible way to pay them.

S.2 adds money available through September 2029 “to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and Border Patrol support personnel” . It also adds flexible money that the administration describes as “$5 billion in additional appropriations to DHS to account for any unforeseen costs that ICE and Border Patrol may incur in future years” .
Money that lasts across budget years, pays officers and covers unexpected costs supports a ready security workforce. That serves [NAME]'s concern for a strong state able to defend people.

S.2 pays for “Upgrades and procurement of border surveillance technologies along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” It also pays for new air and sea equipment for “rapid air and marine response capabilities.”

S.2 requires land-border towers to be tested for their ability to work on their own. It bars spending on towers that “have not been tested and accepted by U.S. Customs and Border Protection to deliver autonomous capabilities.”

Existing towers show how detecting people leads to action: “These towers have been instrumental in identifying and tracking border crossings, contributing significantly to successful apprehensions in the sector.” An apprehension is an arrest.
Customs and Border Protection (CBP) says technology and equipment investments “increase agent safety” and “improve CBP’s ability to respond to detected threats and other urgent situations” .
Better detection, response equipment and officer safety strengthen the ability to stop crossings and smuggling. Control over U.S. territory directly serves [NAME]'s concern for a secure country.

S.2 pays for identity checks based on physical traits, such as face images: “Necessary expenses, including the deployment of technology, relating to the biometric entry and exit system” . “Biometric” means based on the body, such as a face or fingerprint.
Customs and Border Protection (CBP) explains that its face-comparison service can “identify the traveler biometrically and to enable CBP to confirm and expedite the traveler’s arrival or departure.”

CBP reports that “facial comparison results in better security by reducing imposter threats.” It also uses departure checks for security: “CBP performs watchlist vetting of departing travelers.” A watchlist is a government list of people of security concern.

More reliable identity and departure checks make false identities harder to use and strengthen checks against security records. This supports the state's ability to control who crosses its borders and to find threats.

S.2 pays for inspection equipment “to combat the entry or exit of illicit narcotics at ports of entry and along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders.” Its purposes include fighting “fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” , the chemicals used to make it.

This equipment has stopped drugs. For fiscal year 2023, Customs and Border Protection (CBP) reported that large-scale scanning systems were “aiding in the interdiction of more than 127,000 pounds of narcotics” . Interdiction means stopping and seizing.

CBP explains the protective step: “Seizures remove dangerous drugs from illicit supply chains, keep them out of our communities, and deny TCOs valuable profits.” TCOs are criminal groups that work across countries.
More ways to detect and stop drugs strengthen protection against a deadly threat to U.S. communities, which gives [NAME] a security reason to favor the bill.
S.2 pays for ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) staff and “transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” “Removal” means deportation.

S.2 sets aside “Not less than $350,000,000” for work including “custodial transfer, release monitoring, transportation, and arrests of covered unlawful aliens encountered in jurisdictions that are not qualified cooperating jurisdictions” .

S.2 also pays for local cooperation: “Supporting coordination with state and local authorities by expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)” . Under the jail version of these agreements, local officers help “identify criminal aliens and immigration violators in state and local custody and place them into immigration proceedings at the time of release from state or local custody.”

These tools reach people with serious criminal records. ICE's 2024 arrests included charges and convictions for “sexual assault and sex offenses” and “homicides” . ICE explains the custody link: “When criminal noncitizens complete their sentences, ICE assumes custody and places them in the appropriate removal proceedings.”

More staff, custody transfers and transport give ICE more ways to keep removable violent offenders from returning to communities after prison and to carry out their removal. That strengthens public protection, which [NAME] values.
Section 102 pays “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” . Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) is the part of ICE that investigates crimes.
HSI builds criminal cases against “terrorist networks and facilitators” , including the people who help those networks operate.

HSI also pursues violent gangs. Its 2024 report describes gang cases involving “firearms trafficking and possession, violent crimes, terroristic acts” and reports that gang investigations produced “2,189 indictments and 1,106 convictions.”

Paying investigators who build these cases strengthens the state's ability to stop organized violence and terrorism. That directly serves [NAME]'s concern that the United States defend itself against threats.

Section 102 pays for investigators of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes) and “other necessary expenses for Homeland Security Investigations' mission support and operations and maintenance” .

HSI's work includes criminal cases against people who force adults into sex or work. In a 2025 Delaware case, a jury convicted a trafficker on “seven counts of sex trafficking seven adult victims, five counts of forced labor, and one count of interstate transportation for purposes of prostitution.” The Justice Department states: “Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.”
Supporting this work gives the state more ways to stop force and abuse inside U.S. communities. Protecting people from organized crime serves [NAME]'s concern for a secure country.
S.2 sets aside “$108,500,000” for staff who investigate abuse and examine evidence: “shall be used to hire, pay, and equip additional child exploitation investigators and forensics analysts” .

Their job is “to support the identification and rescue of victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse” . The money also trains federal, state and local staff: “to train such personnel and State and local law enforcement regarding identifying victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse” .

This work reaches children in the United States. In 2024 testimony about online sexual blackmail (“sextortion”), Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) reported that it “has identified and rescued over 675 domestic victims of West Africa-based sextortion schemes.”

More investigators, evidence analysts and training strengthen the country's ability to find abused children, rescue them and pursue their attackers. This is a direct gain in the state's ability to protect people.

Section 102 pays for agents and operations of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes): “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” .
HSI investigates money laundering, which hides money earned from crime. Its financial investigators “identify and seize illicit proceeds” .

These investigations have taken money away from criminals. In 2024, HSI reported that its El Dorado financial task forces had achieved, over ten years, “over 2,100 arrests and the seizure of more than $2.68 billion in illicit proceeds.”
Supporting investigations that seize criminal earnings removes resources that keep criminal networks going. That strengthens the state against organized threats to public safety.

Section 102 pays for ongoing investigations by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes), through money “for Homeland Security Investigations' mission support and operations and maintenance” .

This work includes fraud cases that lead to convictions and seizures: “HSI also conducted 258 elder fraud cases that resulted in 137 criminal arrests, 121 indictments, 52 convictions, and $12.6 million seized.” Elder fraud means scams against older people.

Supporting investigators who pursue scammers and seize their money strengthens protection against people who steal through fraud. That serves [NAME]'s concern for a state able to defend people and the country's financial security.

Section 102 pays for investigators, support staff and operations of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes): “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” .

HSI's Operation Cyber Centurion (OCC) fights hacking and attacks that lock computers until money is paid. Its targets include attacks on “major utilities, healthcare, public education, financial systems, emergency services and local government operations.”
This program has stopped attacks: “In FY 2024, OCC disrupted 195 intrusions and attacks.” FY means fiscal year.
Supporting this work strengthens defenses for services people need for power, medical care, emergency help and government. Keeping these services secure supports the national stability [NAME] values.

Section 102 pays for agents of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes) and criminal investigations outside its immigration and customs enforcement missions: “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” .

HSI and partner agencies investigated a supplier that sold unsafe helmets and body armor to government agencies. The official account states: “This case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations, the Defense Criminal Investigative Service, and the General Services Administration Office of Inspector General” . The supplier pleaded guilty to wire fraud (cheating people using phones or computers): “Meining was charged by criminal information with wire fraud, and, on March 23, 2023, he pleaded guilty to the single charge.”

A Defense Department investigator described the harm: the supplier's actions “put U.S. servicemembers at risk, degraded American warfighter readiness, and undermined the missions of our military services.”
More ways to investigate this fraud help protect the people and equipment the country relies on for defense. That directly serves [NAME]'s concern for a strong state able to defend its citizens.

Section 102 pays for staff and operations of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI, the part of ICE that investigates crimes): “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel” .

HSI gives staff to help the U.S. Secret Service with “National Special Security Events (NSSEs) and protective detail assignments.” Its 2024 report lists support for both parties' national conventions and the NATO summit in Washington: “the North Atlantic Treaty Organization in Washington, D.C.; the Republican National Convention in Milwaukee, Wisconsin; the Democratic National Convention in Chicago, Illinois” .
Supporting this group of trained officers strengthens protection at public gatherings and major government events. That serves [NAME]'s concern for public safety and stable national institutions.
S.2 pays for “Air and Marine operations' upgrading and procurement of new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities.” “Platforms” here means aircraft and boats.

Customs and Border Protection (CBP) describes aircraft that support emergency workers through “the rapid-response deployment of equipment, canines, and personnel.” It also describes helicopter abilities that include “essential aerial relocation, transport, tactical response, rescue, and investigative surveillance functions” .
Paying for more air and sea response gives the government more ways to bring help and rescue people in danger. That strengthens the country's ability to protect people during emergencies.
Human Rights Watch documented immigration agents “detaining people based on their perceived race, ethnicity, or national origin, and using excessive force.”

The harm reaches citizens. The Brennan Center, a law and policy institute, says Democratic legislators blocked more funding for the Department of Homeland Security and demanded reforms after “the killing of U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.”

Human Rights Watch said on June 16 that Congress approved S.2 “without adopting essential oversight and accountability reforms.” Lawmakers and activists had proposed reforms such as requiring warrants from judges and stronger bans on racial profiling.

S.2 also gives money outside the yearly funding decisions. The American Action Forum, a policy group, says S.2 “provides funding for federal agencies that are typically funded through the annual appropriations process.”

More operating money through 2029 gives these operations more resources and less need to ask for yearly approval. That weakens a practical way for Congress to demand safer conduct. Paying for more exposure to documented violence undermines the citizen protection [NAME] values.

S.2 pays for local immigration-enforcement agreements: “Supporting coordination with state and local authorities by expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act” .

The street-policing version was already allowed before Congress's June 9 vote. A February 2025 agreement with ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) lets local officers “interrogate any alien or person believed to be an alien as to his right to be or remain in the United States” .

A study of crime-victim surveys from 2005–2014 found that these street task forces raised Latinos' risk of being attacked: “287(g) task force programs significantly increased violent victimization among Latinos” .
Research on Secure Communities, another program linking local police to deportation, found that “Secure Communities reduced the likelihood that Hispanic victims reported crime to the police.”
Reporting helps police catch offenders: “When crime reporting declines, police are less able to identify, prevent, and solve crimes when they occur, making it harder to apprehend offenders.”

S.2 expands agreements that include a form of policing with documented costs to public safety. The reporting evidence also shows how linking police to deportation can weaken crime control. [NAME] has a reason to oppose weakening the state's ability to protect communities from offenders.
S.2 adds no ban on masks. A member of Congress said of S.2 and an earlier funding law: “This bill, just like the last one, does not prohibit any agent from wearing a mask.”
An FBI bulletin reported real attacks: “Criminals posing as US immigration officers have carried out robberies, kidnappings, and sexual assaults in several states” .

The FBI advisory linked rising impersonation crimes (crimes by people pretending to be officers) to the “recent increase in ICE enforcement actions” . WIRED reports confusion “making it harder for Americans to distinguish between lawful officers and imposters while eroding trust in law enforcement.”

Paying for more operations without addressing this confusion keeps up the chances for criminals to borrow federal authority. That threatens residents' safety and their ability to recognize real protection.
Section 202 pays ICE staff, “including officers, agents, investigators, attorneys and support staff, to carry out immigration enforcement activities.” ICE is Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Section 203 also allows money “for DHS and State officers to carry out immigration enforcement” . DHS means the Department of Homeland Security.

The campaign has already moved federal investigators: “The Trump administration has already diverted thousands of law enforcement officials at multiple agencies away from their work tackling serious crime and national security investigations to focus on immigration” .
These assignments have real costs for child-abuse investigations: “These delays can mean the difference between building a case against a predator and letting the trail go cold.”

Section 102's separate investigation money is limited to “functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions.” This limit governs that money; Sections 202 and 203 still pay for the immigration assignments above.

S.2 pays for a campaign that uses investigators for deportation work in place of other protective duties. Keeping this diversion leaves serious crimes and national security threats less fully covered, which goes against [NAME]'s concern that the country defend itself against all threats.

The Brennan Center, a law and policy institute, predicts wider monitoring from the funding it describes, which includes S.2's money: “The funding will also allow DHS to continue to build surveillance capabilities that facilitate indiscriminate collection of information about Americans as well as immigrants.” DHS is the Department of Homeland Security.

Threats against observers (people who watch and record immigration agents) are documented: “a government lawyer told a federal judge in Maine that agents had violated Department of Homeland Security policy by threatening to put the observers' information into a database.”

These threats discourage people from watching officers. A lawyer seeking information about ICE's surveillance explained: “If people think that protesting or filming law enforcement may put them in a secret database, many will stay silent” .

Paying for more monitoring gives officials tools to frighten people who record their conduct. A state that silences peaceful warnings about its own abuses becomes less answerable for protecting citizens. That threatens safe, stable government.

KFF, a health research group, reports that immigrants and family members avoided activities including “going to church or other community activities, going to work, or taking their child to school or school events due to immigration-related fears.”
Fear that keeps people from work, school and community life makes towns less able to function. Paying for more operations with this pattern threatens the social stability [NAME] values.
S.2 pays for removals: “Funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations.” “Removal” means deportation.

The existing campaign has already detained an essential worker: “He is a medical laboratory scientist who worked on the front lines during the COVID-19 pandemic” ; “Yet he remains detained, as of April 2026.”

Immigrants work in basic industries: “Immigrants, both documented and undocumented, contribute to the U.S. economy by working jobs in construction, hospitality, landscaping, and farming” . Research on earlier enforcement found “a slowdown in new housing construction” .

The damage reaches national resources: “Crackdowns on immigration are harmful to U.S. workers and contractionary for the overall U.S. economy as the labor market weakens and slower population growth drags down demand and public finances.” “Contractionary” means making the economy smaller.

Paying for wider removals threatens workers who supply care, food and shelter. The loss of production and tax money also weakens the country's means to pay for protection and to handle shocks. Both bear directly on the strong, secure country [NAME] values.
KFF, a health research group, found that “14% of immigrant adults overall say they or a family member have avoided seeking medical care since January 2025 due to immigration-related concerns.”
Dallas County's public health director “ties the dramatic drop in county-administered vaccinations to concerns about immigration enforcement.”
He warned that communities are “more vulnerable to outbreaks” when people avoid care.

In a February–March 2026 survey with a random sample of adults in Minneapolis and St. Paul about a federal enforcement surge, 30.6% of Minneapolis respondents with a regularly scheduled vaccination and 21.1% in St. Paul reported missing it because of enforcement concerns. This measures what people reported about themselves, not how many people overall are vaccinated.

Keeping up enforcement that drives people away from clinics weakens disease prevention. Protection against infectious disease is part of protecting the country against threats, which gives [NAME] another reason to oppose this money.
S.2 pays for “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions.”

The planned network of ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) includes a large facility in Social Circle, Georgia. The city's February assessment states that “the total additional water demand required for a facility of this scale simply exceeds what the City’s system is capable of providing.”

Money for running the planned detention network supports demands that essential local systems cannot meet. Threats to drinking water and sewage disposal undermine public health and the basic services on which stable communities depend.

The American Action Forum estimates the bill's borrowing cost: “After accounting for roughly $25 billion of additional interest costs, the package would increase budget deficits by $94.5 billion over the FY 2026–2035 budget window.” Here “the package” means S.2, and FY means fiscal year. A deficit is the amount the government spends beyond what it collects.
The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) explains the general risk: “Larger amounts of debt make the United States’ fiscal position more vulnerable to an increase in interest rates.”

It also warns that “Lawmakers might feel constrained from using federal tax and spending policies to respond to unforeseen events or for other purposes, such as to promote economic activity or strengthen national defense.”

S.2 adds borrowing and interest costs to the money pressures facing future decisions about defense and emergencies. Increasing this burden weakens the financial strength needed for a state that can protect its citizens.

Section 103 pays for inspection equipment to combat “the entry or exit of illicit narcotics” and border work for “combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals” . Precursor chemicals are the ingredients used to make drugs.

The Government Accountability Office (GAO) explains how the equipment works: “These scans produce images that CBP officers review to help detect illegal drugs or other contraband.” CBP is Customs and Border Protection, the federal border agency.

Southern Baptists also identify a threat to family life: “Opioid abuse destroys the individual user, but it also destroys the family unit by often separating children from their addicted parents” . Opioids include fentanyl.

Their statement on the family gives parents the job of passing on faith: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values and to lead them, through consistent lifestyle example and loving discipline, to make choices based on biblical truth.”

By addressing opioid abuse that separates children from parents, drug-detection work could help protect the family setting for parents' continuing religious teaching. Passing on faith in this way, and not a general religious support for drug control, is what connects this to Tradition.
Southern Baptists affirm that “God has ordained the family as the foundational institution of human society” .

Their statement of faith, the Baptist Faith and Message, adopted in 2000, ties passing on faith to parents' daily example: “Parents are to teach their children spiritual and moral values and to lead them, through consistent lifestyle example and loving discipline, to make choices based on biblical truth.”
More resources for removals (deportations) put Christian families at greater risk of being forced apart.
Living apart disrupts shared family life and parents' daily teaching. Keeping these family duties gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the added money.
Southern Baptist leaders reported that fear of enforcement left even lawful immigrants “afraid to gather to worship God and receive spiritual care in their local church” .

A June 8, 2026 report quotes an amended church lawsuit that describes a change in religious practice: “Baptisms that previously would have been occasions for communal worship and celebration are now being held in private.” A baptism is a Christian rite of joining the church.
The Southern Baptists' statement of faith says Sunday “should include exercises of worship and spiritual devotion, both public and private.”

Their religious liberty commission warned that enforcement at churches would hold back teaching and sharing the faith: “our central mission of Gospel proclamation and biblical formation will be inhibited.”

A February court order protecting churches covered only properties of the churches in the case, defined as places “regularly used by Plaintiffs to conduct religious services” . It did not protect every church. The June 8 report describes continued fear and disrupted worship despite that order.

Adding resources to enforcement that already keeps people from church puts shared worship, teaching and rites under more pressure. [NAME] has a reason to oppose this threat to practicing and passing on the faith.

The risk reaches evangelical church leaders. The Associated Press reported that a bishop had told churches with pastors at risk of deportation “to prepare three laypeople to take over, should their leader be deported.” Laypeople are church members who are not clergy.

The joint Christian report explains the further risk: “In some cases, if the pastor is deported, the congregation may be unable to find a new leader. Similarly, if a substantial portion of the congregation is deported, the church may close.”
This loss reaches members who remain: “even church members who are citizens or legal permanent residents will be deeply impacted.”

Added removal capacity puts congregations' leaders and members at greater risk. Losing a congregation breaks the continuity of a community that carries Christian teaching, worship and customs. Keeping that community gives [NAME] a reason to oppose S.2.

Church leaders said that a January 2026 Border Patrol arrest on church grounds stopped their aid work. KTLA reported: “The raid interrupted the church’s food distribution ministry and an event for mothers and children in the church garden.” A ministry is religious service work by a church.

The 2018 Southern Baptist immigration resolution teaches that “Scripture is clear on the believer’s hospitality towards immigrants” and urges pastors “to exhort their congregations to serve their local immigrant communities” .

More resources for operations that have interrupted this church's ministry raise the risk of more interruptions to its continuing shared religious work. Keeping this established ministry, and not a general support for helping strangers, is what gives [NAME] a Tradition reason.

Limits on access reached both Protestant and Catholic ministry. Christianity Today reported that Indonesian pastors waited without success to visit a detained member; a Pentecostal pastor also could not enter: “Like the Indonesian pastors, the pastor he met never got in.” Pastoral care means religious care from clergy.

The problem continued into 2026. An April court order found that a total ban at the Broadview detention center in Illinois “renders plaintiffs’ religious exercise of providing ministry to detainees and migrants effectively impracticable.”

An April 2026 release from Rep. Jimmy Gomez's office says clergy were denied entry to the Roybal building in Los Angeles on Ash Wednesday and that four were admitted on Good Friday after the office pressed ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement). This shows both a barrier and a fix that needed help from a member of Congress, not a permanent ban at that site.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) defended excluding religious services from field offices: “It is not within standard operating procedure for religious services to be provided in a field office” . The same report describes evidence that people were held in those buildings “for days on end” .

Court relief named particular facilities. The April 7 order required access to “the Broadview facility” ; the March 20 order required a process for clergy access to “the Whipple facility” , in Minnesota. Those orders did not open every place where added arrests could send Christians.
